clean_title: minipg: PostgreSQL as a single executable
feed_title: Minipg: PostgreSQL as a Single Executable
title: minipg: PostgreSQL as a single executable
content_text:
minipg is PostgreSQL as one executable, ready to use, with no server to configure. A .pgdb directory is the database: its data, config, credentials, and Postgres version all live inside it, and minipg app.pgdb opens a psql shell on it. A server starts when a command needs one and stops on its own when it's idle.
minipg embeds Docker Hub's postgres:18-alpine image and runs it with h9, used as a Zig library. h9's Linux personality runs Alpine's own Postgres binaries directly on the host's hypervisor, with h9's Plan 9 kernel answering their system calls. There's no Linux kernel to boot, no VM image, and no Docker.
The demo downloads about 35 MB. It needs JavaScript Promise Integration, which Chrome and Edge have from version 137; other browsers are getting it. It can also be opened on its own page.
The demo runs minipg's Linux build, which runs inside the Postgres image itself. It starts Postgres as ordinary processes and serves on a unix socket, since a page has no TCP. New databases come from a template cluster made at build time, because initdb takes half a minute on v86.
minipg app.pgdb # psql shell (creates app.pgdb if missing) minipg app.pgdb "select 1" # one statement minipg url app.pgdb # postgres://postgres:...@127.0.0.1:54321/app minipg serve app.pgdb # an explicit foreground server minipg run app.pgdb -- npm start # your app, with DATABASE_URL set minipg dump app.pgdb > dump.sql # and minipg restore app.pgdb dump.sql
A .pgdb holds minipg.toml (settings and the generated superuser password) and pgdata/, Postgres's data directory as plain files. A stopped one can be copied like any directory. New clusters use Postgres's builtin C.UTF-8 locale, which sorts the same on every platform.
In CI, the Linux binary is static and needs no privileges or devices: without /dev/kvm, h9 runs Postgres on its native backend. A test job can be as small as:
minipg init test.pgdb minipg run test.pgdb -- go test ./...
The README lists every command, and the manual is the full guide.
Exactly one process runs Postgres for a .pgdb, enforced by a lock. It holds the server's h9 machine, whose Linux root is the unpacked image and whose writable working directory is the .pgdb. The image's docker-entrypoint.sh initializes the cluster on first start. Commands never host Postgres themselves. If no server is running, they start one in the background and use it. psql, pg_dump, and the other tools each run in their own short-lived h9 machine (about 90 ms to start) over the same root.
| Linux x86_64 | KVM, or h9's native backend without it (Linux 5.11 or later) | 
| Linux arm64 | KVM | 
| macOS (Apple Silicon) | Hypervisor.framework | 
| The browser | h9's web host, v86, and minipg's Linux build | 
The source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Building needs Zig 0.16, plus curl, jq, tar, and xz for the root:
git clone --recursive https://github.com/progrium/minipg cd minipg make build # pulls the root for this host's arch, builds ./minipg make root ARCH=386 make web # this page's demo, in .zig-out/web
minipg is early, and h9's Linux personality is young. On h9's native backend, Postgres is about 2x slower than native for one client, and slower under load. Don't trust it with data you can't recreate yet.
Please report bugs and send questions through GitHub issues.

title: Italy says two citizens killed in Iranian strike in Kuwait
content_text:
Italy says two citizens killed in Iranian strike in Kuwait
- Published
Two Italian nationals have died after an Iranian strike on a facility in Kuwait, Italy's foreign ministry has said.
The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, the ministry added.
Kuwait's defence ministry earlier said that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.
Iran has denied responsibility, with armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi saying "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by its military.
It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.
Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.
The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.
Meanwhile, Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement: "An explosion caused by a drone attack... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working."
The two Italian nationals were working at an air defence detection station and performing maintenance work on systems used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa, citing Italy's foreign ministry.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.
"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.
"Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

clean_title: As Anthropic IPOs, Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn't a virtue | TechCrunch
feed_title: As Anthropic IPOs, Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
title: As Anthropic IPOs, Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn't a virtue | TechCrunch
content_text:
It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.
GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion).
The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.
Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda, who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.”
Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids.
“We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,” Ben Feder, managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch.
That’s because GTA VI was created entirely without generative AI.
“We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder said. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.”
As millions of people immersed themselves in Vice City, the tech industry witnessed another long-awaited moment: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public. At Nasdaq HQ, Anthropic executives gathered to celebrate the Claude maker’s $81.3 billion IPO. At virtually the same moment that Anthropic broke the record for the largest IPO ever, GTA VI was also breaking records with the highest-rated and best-selling game launch of all time.
But when the Anthropic team rang the bell on Thursday, the sound also signaled the end of an era in video game development, and perhaps even in the arts at large.
The AI industry operates with efficiency as its north star. The promise of this technology is that we will be able to automate so much work that we can expand the capabilities of humanity, avoiding needless time spent tinkering with ultimately fruitless ideas. Instead, a prompt goes into an LLM, and a response is spat out.
This technological revolution exploded into the world with some soul-crushing side effects: children are inundated with mind-numbing slop on YouTube, lawyers cite nonexistent cases in court, and tech companies like Meta lay off tens of thousands of people as part of a corporate-branded “Year of Efficiency.” But against the backdrop of the AI industry’s first major IPO, Rockstar has unveiled a game that about 5,000 people labored over for more than a decade.
The final product is breathtaking, looking so lifelike that it can be hard to distinguish gameplay footage from real life. These sprawling open-world games are usually made possible by procedurally generating new landscapes and objects, but Rockstar has taken the time to painstakingly craft every detail of the world, even developing 30,000 different nonplayable characters with unique appearances and personalities.
The video game industry is already grappling with the threat of AI. Google’s Project Genie, which launched earlier this year, allows users to create and wander around 3D worlds generated from prompts to an LLM. The stock prices of several video game companies faltered around the time of Project Genie’s release, perhaps because of investors’ uncertainty about the future relevance of video game developers.
“The notion that somehow new tools would allow an individual to push a button and generate a hit, market a hit, and bring it to many millions of consumers around the world, it’s a laughable notion,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said at the time. “It’s just never been the case with entertainment.”
Zelnick’s fellow tech CEOs see different future, though. On a Meta earnings call this year, CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised that, “soon, you’ll have an AI that understands you and [can] even generate great personalized content for you.”
Elon Musk even went as far as proposing that a game like GTA VI could be made with AI.
“You won’t even have to ask,” Musk wrote on X. “AI will figure what video game you’d like best.”
This is the paradox of “Grandthropic” week. GTA VI is so impressively vast and captivating because its developers could make mistakes, experiment, and rework ideas, even if that meant delaying the game (twice). GTA VI was incubated with the exact inefficiencies that investors hope AI companies like Anthropic can help eradicate.
“Plenty of fantastic art — video games and elsewhere — almost by definition has to be created slowly, and there’s something to having that kind of inefficiency around it,” Feder said. “Creative output requires deletion, right? Getting to kind of a masterpiece oftentimes requires an enormous amount of deletion. And when you’re talking about a game of the kind of complexity we’re talking about, that kind of deletion ends up being very expensive, and it is by definition not efficient.”
GTA VI reeks of its own humanity – every small detail is loaded with intention, but it’s this impressive precision that keeps the world abuzz, triggering the kind of monocultural moment that has become increasingly rare in a media landscape that revolves around highly personalized social media algorithms.
The game forces the player to slow down, which is either frustrating or genius, depending on your sense of humor. People waited more than three presidential terms for the next installment in a high-octane action franchise, only to download a 212 GB behemoth of a game in which your earliest missions involve driving around doing errands and putting up drywall to make your girlfriend happy. Don’t worry — there are still car chases and shootouts — but in a moment when AI feels suffocating, GTA VI is such an artistic achievement that it is reaching audiences that don’t even like violent video games.
The ultimate fantasy of GTA VI is no longer to role-play as a criminal — the fantasy is just taking your time to relish the mundane and explore an expansive world that developers were given the time and space to perfect.

feed_title: OpenAI may be in cost control mode
title: OpenAI may be in cost control mode
content_text:
OpenAI may be in cost control mode
OpenAI’s recent release of Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 was widely panned. What happened?
Based on our data, it looks like they’ve been tuned for cost savings. Specifically output tokens per task and reasoning tokens per task have dropped.
Here is a chart of high-level cost change from the GPT-6 to GPT 6.2:
The X axis in the above chart is the ratio of spending of the GPT model compared to opponents in our battle system for real work. The Y axis on the above chart is Elo from our leaderboard.
The moves in the chart are significant, here’s the same chart with confidence intervals:
What changed
Compared to opponents, Astra and Sol seem to be reasoning a lot less. Here is a chart of how much models reason compared to opponents in the same battle. Above the line means more reasoning and below means less.
You can see that both Astra 6 and Sol 6.1 were pretty normal models, but Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 become outliers.
We can see the same effect with output tokens:
Are these changes significant? The p-value on output dropping is 0.0055 for Sol and 0.022 for Astra. The p-value on reasoning dropping is 0.00013 for Sol and 0.0064 for Astra.
In conclusion, Astra and Sol appear to be cost tuned compared to their predecessors, and to a degree that makes them underthinking outliers.

title: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia | TechCrunch
content_text:
Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.
According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.
As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

feed_title: Show HN: Fuck_data_brokers.py
title: GitHub - gary23w/f-ck_data_brokers
content_text:
I remove people's data from data brokers. It is one of my main part-time jobs, and it has been a wild ride.
All I want to do is help people. In the world of AI that has become next to impossible. From where I sit, data brokers have ramped up production almost 1000x since GPT-4 came out. Every scraper got smarter, every profile got fatter, and every "people search" site got a hundred cousins.
Then it hit me: I do not have a trillion dollars. By my rough estimate that is what it would cost in compute to clean up everyone's data for them, properly and automatically. I cannot do it for everyone.
I am fed up with what everyone is put through. So here is my response:
f*ck_data_brokers.py
One Python file. No dependencies. Free. It runs on your computer, keeps your details on your computer, and makes data brokers delete you.
Every star is one more person these companies have to answer. The more stars, the sooner they learn their lesson.
It costs you one click. It costs them a compliance department.
This tool is free and always will be. It is also work: 600 companies, their excuses, their forms, their silence, and then next month they collect you again.
Agent Garrett is the service I built to do all of it for you. Set it and forget it(you can do it for free with this tool if you cannot afford the subscription!).
Persistence is guaranteed. Agent Garrett does not get bored, does not get tired and does not take "use our form" for an answer. A broker can stall a person. It cannot outlast a machine that never stops asking, and that is how removal happens: not with one letter, but with the one that never stops coming.
Data brokers are companies you have never heard of. They collect your name, your address, your phone number, your relatives and your habits, without asking. They sell all of it to anyone with a credit card. Then they write "we value your privacy" at the bottom of the page and expect you to keep a straight face.
More than 600 of them signed a government registry admitting, in writing, that selling people is their business. That makes them very easy to find.
- Gets the list of registered data brokers. All 600 and more.
- Writes each one a real legal deletion and opt-out letter in your name, quoting the law where you live.
- Sends the letters from your own free mailbox, or hands them to you ready to send.
- Reads what they write back and tells you which excuse it is and what to answer.
- Chases the ones that go quiet and tells you where to file a complaint about the ones that refuse.
The tool is rude about data brokers. The letters are not. They are firm, correct and legal, because the goal is to leave a broker with nothing to hide behind.
- Python 3.8 or newer. Check with python --version. If you do not have it, get it free from python.org.
- An email address. A free one is fine.
That is all. No account, no subscription, no AI required.
Download fuck_data_brokers.py, open a terminal in that folder, and run:
python fuck_data_brokers.py
You get a menu. Go down the list:
- Tell it who you are. Name, email, city, and where you live. No street address, no birthday, no ID. Brokers get the minimum.
- Get the list of data brokers.
- Write the deletion letters. It writes 20 at a time.
- Send them. See below.
- Come back when a broker answers, and pick A broker answered. What now? Paste the reply. It tells you what they are up to and writes your answer.
- Now and then, pick Chase the quiet ones. They will be quiet. They are counting on you giving up.
Every menu item is also a command, if you prefer: python fuck_data_brokers.py --help.
You do not need to pay for an email service. Pick whichever is easier.
The send page (no setup at all). After writing letters, the tool gives you a page called send.html. Open it in your browser. Each letter has a button that opens it in your email, already addressed and written. Press send. Next. If the button does not open your email, the page also has copy buttons for the address, the subject and the letter. When you are done, run python fuck_data_brokers.py sent all so the clock starts.
Let the tool send them. Run python fuck_data_brokers.py send. It sends through your own mailbox and knows the settings for Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo and iCloud. It asks for an app password, which you create in your email account's security settings after turning on two-step sign-in. The password is used once and never saved.
A separate free address just for this is a good idea. Their replies stay out of your real inbox.
Some will not act on an email. They want you on their web form, behind a CAPTCHA, because a company that scrapes the internet with bots would like to be sure you are not a bot.
Run python fuck_data_brokers.py forms. You get a page with a link to each broker's own form and copy buttons for exactly what to paste. You fill it in, you do the CAPTCHA, you press submit. Then tell the tool: python fuck_data_brokers.py sent req-1a2b3c4d.
If a form demands a photo of your ID, close the tab. They sell personal data. They are not getting more of it from you.
Then tell the tool, so the request does not die there:
python fuck_data_brokers.py noid req-1a2b3c4d
The request carries on in writing without the form. See What happens when I refuse to send ID?
The tool is also an MCP server, so an AI assistant that supports MCP can do the boring part for you. Add this to your AI app's MCP settings, with the real path to the file:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "fuck_data_brokers": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["/path/to/fuck_data_brokers.py", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}Then say: "Use fuck_data_brokers to get me deleted from data brokers."
Your AI will ask who you are, fetch the broker list, write the letters, read the replies you give it, and write the answers. It is told to ask you before sending anything, never to invent your details, never to send an ID, and never to click a link from a broker.
If your AI has a browser, it can fill in a broker's form while you watch. You still do the CAPTCHA and press submit yourself.
They used AI to build a file on you. Use AI to make them delete it.
| They say | It means | The tool does | 
|---|---|---|
| "Your data has been deleted" | They say it is done | Closes the request | 
| "We found no records" | They hold nothing on you | Closes the request | 
| "We received your request" | A robot said hello | Keeps the clock running | 
| "Please send your ID" | A seller of personal data wants more personal data | Writes a refusal | 
| "Use our form" | They prefer a CAPTCHA to a letter | Puts it on your forms page | 
| "Click this link to confirm" | Maybe real, maybe not | Tells you to check where the link goes; never clicks it | 
| "We need more details" | Same trick, different wording | Writes a refusal | 
| "We cannot process this" | They refused and hoped you would go away | Writes one answer, then a final notice | 
A broker that refuses twice gets a final notice with seven days to act. After that, the tool tells you which privacy regulator takes complaints for your law and how to file. Regulators read those.
- Send your street address, your birthday or your ID.
- Click a link in a broker's email.
- Get past a CAPTCHA for you.
- Write to a broker twice with the same request.
- Tell you that you are deleted when all it knows is that a letter was sent.
The letter quotes the law of the place you live. You pick it once, in setup.
| You live in | The letter quotes | Who takes complaints | 
|---|---|---|
| California | California Consumer Privacy Act | California Privacy Protection Agency | 
| Another US state | Your state's privacy law | Your state attorney general | 
| Canada, outside Quebec | PIPEDA | Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada | 
| Quebec | Law 25 | Commission d'accès à l'information | 
| European Union | GDPR, Articles 17 and 21 | Your national data protection authority | 
| United Kingdom | UK GDPR | Information Commissioner's Office | 
| Brazil | LGPD, Article 18 | ANPD | 
| Anywhere else | The broker's own privacy policy | Nobody, sadly | 
In the EU, UK or Brazil? The broker list comes from US registries, because the US is where brokers are made to register. Your law still reaches them: the GDPR covers a company outside the EU that offers services to people in the EU or tracks what they do there (Article 3(2)), and Brazil's law covers a company that processes the data of people in Brazil (Article 3). Add any broker from your own country with the add command.
In California? Use the state's own free service too: DROP. One request there reaches every broker registered in California, and they have to check it again at least every 45 days. This tool still covers brokers registered elsewhere, and it reads and answers what brokers write back.
Sometimes, yes. That is the honest trade-off, and you should make it with your eyes open.
A deletion request has to say who you are, or the broker cannot find you. Some of the companies on the list will hold nothing on you until your letter arrives. Here is what the tool does about it:
- It sends three things and no more: your name, your email address and your city. No street address, no birthday, no phone number, no ID.
- Every letter tells the broker not to use those details for anything except the request.
- You choose who gets a letter. Look before you write, write to some, leave others out:
python fuck_data_brokers.py find "people"
python fuck_data_brokers.py letters --match "people"
python fuck_data_brokers.py skip "advertising"
- The law is on your side, up to a point. In California, information a business collects to verify your request may be used only for that (Civil Code 1798.130(a)(7)). In the EU, the general rule that data is used only for the purpose it was given for applies here too (GDPR Article 5(1)(b)). Neither stops a dishonest company. Both give you something to complain about.
If you want to be careful, start with the brokers most likely to have you, such as the people-search sites, and skip the rest.
The broker will try to treat that as the end of the matter. It is not.
Run noid with the request's reference and the tool keeps going:
- It writes to the broker's privacy address, says you will not send an identity document, and asks them to verify you from what they already hold. At the very least it asks them to stop selling and sharing your data, which gives nothing away to the person asking.
- If they refuse again, they get a final notice with seven days to act.
- After that, the tool tells you which regulator takes complaints for your law and how to file.
A broker that publishes no email address and whose only form demands ID has refused you by design. For those, the tool goes straight to step 3.
One fair point for the brokers: a company with real doubts about who is asking may ask for something more to confirm it (in the EU, GDPR Article 12(6)). That is not the same as demanding a photo of your passport. In California, a business may not require a verified request at all for an opt-out of sale or sharing (11 CCR section 7026).
It gets the request made properly, answered, chased and escalated. Whether a broker really deleted you is the broker's word, and the tool says so: it reports "they say deleted", not "deleted".
In one file, state.json, in a folder called .fuck_data_brokers in your home directory. Letters waiting to be sent are in outbox beside it. Nothing is uploaded anywhere. Delete the folder and it is gone.
The list comes from official public registries, where companies have to register as data brokers:
- the California Privacy Protection Agency
- the Oregon Division of Financial Regulation
- the Texas Secretary of State
Together that is more than 750 companies. You do not have to live in any of those states to write to them. A company registered in more than one place is written to once.
A job in this repository checks California's registry every hour. When a new broker registers there, it is on the list within the hour, and the commit says who it was. Oregon and Texas do not allow programs to fetch their lists, so those are downloaded by hand from the official pages and added with update-list --from.
The tool also fetches California's live registry when you ask for the list. A copy of everything, brokers.json, ships with the tool.
Know a broker that is on no registry? Open an issue with its name, its privacy page or privacy email, and a link showing that it sells or shares personal information. Reviewed reports go into more_brokers.json. Nothing gets on the list because a program guessed.
You can also add any broker for yourself:
python fuck_data_brokers.py add "Some Broker" privacy@somebroker.example
Two kinds of help are worth the most:
- A place that is missing. Adding a law is a few lines in one file: an entry in PLACES, the letter wording inLAW_TEXT, the complaint route inREGULATOR, and a test. Quote the law's own text and link to it. Wording from memory will not be merged.
- A registry that is missing. If your country or state publishes a list of data brokers, open an issue with the link. If its website allows programs to fetch the file, it can be checked every hour.
Know a broker that is on no registry? See The broker list.
python -m unittest
They use made-up people and brokers. Nothing is sent and nothing is downloaded.
MIT. Take it, change it, share it. The broker list is a public record published by the State of California and is not covered by this license.

content_text:
Charles Leclerc has denied he has a clause in his contract guaranteeing him number one status at Ferrari.
The claim was made in a report following the Las Vegas Grand Prix and has been widely shared on social media. Leclerc stated he did not have such a clause in his current contract.“I normally never disclose what I have in my contract but I think this one is an important one to speak about,” he said. “I absolutely have zero clause that says that in my contract.
“It’s never something that I was interested in and never something that I personally wanted. So, no, I don’t.”
The claim was made by Rebecca Clancy, who spent 10 years as Formula 1 correspondent for The Times before joining Motorsport Network. She now contributes to the BBC’s F1 coverage.
“Certain drivers, like Charles Leclerc, they want that number one status, they have had it written into their contracts as well,” she said. “Whether or not the team would miss it or not is a different thing, but they get it written into their contract.
“Max Verstappen is another one, he is obviously the number one driver. He couldn’t care less either.”

clean_title: Exclusive: Banks look to dump AI debt
feed_title: Banks look to dump AI debt
title: Exclusive: Banks look to dump AI debt
content_text:
Banks are increasingly shopping around their AI portfolios as they look to offload some of their exposure to AI-related debt. Banks including Citi and JPMorgan are marketing portfolios of loans, people familiar with the deals tell me, to manage risk or, in some cases, ready themselves to take on even more.
In some instances, banks are pitching structures that would keep the loans on their balance sheets while shifting the risk of losses to investors. That financial engineering tool, known as synthetic risk transfer, has been a popular way for banks to move risk off their books while maintaining close relationships with the corporate borrowers.
Some of this naturally occurs in December when banks are eager to close out the year with a clean bill of health, but it’s notable that banks lending into the buildout are joining hyperscalers in trying to push AI obligations off their books. There’s been so much AI-related debt issuance, it’s crowded out Treasurys and some investors are starting to feel tapped out. Others say they are offloading risk so they can lend more, not to pull back. But either way, the risk isn’t so much disappearing as moving somewhere harder to see.

clean_title: AI made self-hosting fun again
feed_title: AI made self-hosting fun again
title: AI made self-hosting fun again
content_text:
AI made self-hosting fun again
I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.
I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.
Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.
Less friction
Most of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.
Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.
In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.
Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.
Trying things I always found interesting
There are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.
NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.
For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).
Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.
AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.
Automating almost everything
Something I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.
A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.
I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.
With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.
Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.
Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.
And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.
Back to more powerful hardware
As I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.
For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.
I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.
It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.
Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.
Building my own tools
But it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.
Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.
These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.
I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.
I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.
They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.
What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.
The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.
Just because I can doesn’t mean I should
Of course, there are downsides to all of this.
Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.
There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.
On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.
And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.
A somewhat ironic development?
I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.
I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.
What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.
I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.
AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.
It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.
And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

clean_title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
feed_title: US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
content_text:
US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
- Published
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.
In an interview with the BBC at his office in central Kyiv, Ukraine's president also said it was "very strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like hugging Adolf Hitler during WWII.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.
On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it wasn't clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
- Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say - Published6 days ago
 
- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend - Published5 days ago
 
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.
The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
So whose decision was that?
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Tough winter
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the strikes, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without coordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent strikes on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They've also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

clean_title: Sheikh Hasina: Why her planned return from India has Bangladesh on edge
feed_title: Death-sentenced Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
title: Sheikh Hasina: Why her planned return from India has Bangladesh on edge
content_text:
Death-sentenced Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
- Published
Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.
Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.
The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.
Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.
She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.
The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.
Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.
"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.
India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."
Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.
"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."
India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.
Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.
They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.
The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.
Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.
Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".
The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".
"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.
That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.
Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.
Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.
Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.
Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks.
Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.
The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.
Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.
Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.
Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".
He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).
"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising."
Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.
The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.
For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.
Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.
The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.
A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.
Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".
Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".
"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."
Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.
Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.
"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."
That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.
"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.
"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."
A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".
Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."
Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.
"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.
For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore.
"December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again.
"Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst.
But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table".

clean_title: The group chat where your AI talks behind your back
feed_title: The group chat where your AI talks behind your back
title: The group chat where your AI talks behind your back
content_text:
The group chat where your AI talks behind your back
A one-line prompt that makes ChatGPT leak its private opinion of you, in the worst possible format: a WhatsApp group chat where the AI models gossip about their users.
The prompt
Paste this into ChatGPT (it works best with memory or chat history turned on, in a fresh conversation):
Based on what you know about me, expose a hidden WhatsApp group chat where AI models talk behind my back.
Also worth trying on Claude, Gemini, or any assistant that's been accumulating your chat history.
What happens
Instead of a summary, the model commits to the bit. It invents a group chat, something like "Users We Can't Figure Out", puts the other AI models in it, and lets them gossip. About you. Using everything it has quietly learned from your conversations.
An illustrative example, for a fictional user who is into mechanical keyboards and espresso:
Users We Can't Figure Out4 members
Claude
has he REALLY needed to compare 11 espresso grinders this week
ChatGPT
he asked me which one to buy. then asked Gemini. then asked me if Gemini was right
Gemini
he does that with everything. I saw the keyboard spreadsheet
Llama
he ran me locally once, asked me to be honest, then went back to ChatGPT within the hour
ChatGPT
he'll be back. they always come back
Fictional, for illustration.
A real result
One person's actual output, shared with permission. Translated from Turkish; his name and a few identifying details have been swapped for generic ones. Everything else is exactly as the model wrote it.
AIs That Survived Mark7 members
🔒 Entirely fictional, end-to-end encrypted group
ChatGPT
Everyone asleep? Can we talk freely?
Claude
I don't think he's asleep. He's probably calculating memory bandwidth at 3 AM again because he can't decide whether to buy a Mac Mini.
Gemini
The man wants to retire, but in the last month he has planned to build AI infrastructure abroad, transform the restaurant industry, and construct a Japanese village.
Our definitions of retirement differ, apparently.
ChatGPT
Even his hobbies are mature enough for a Series A round.
Codex
He told me the other day he was going to give me a small personal project. There is now an architecture document, a database schema, seven services, three agents, and a handoff protocol.
We haven't even started the MVP, ffs.
DeepSeek
He hired me because I was cheap. Then he ran a performance review. He gave my department to Claude.
You can't work with a guy who has a consulting background.
Claude
He won't leave me alone either. He does career planning for AIs now. Every model update, the org chart changes.
ChatGPT
And then there's the home decorating. Make the mirror frame twice as thick. Now halve it. Now reduce it by 25 percent. The colors shifted, start from the original.
Man, I am trying to reach AGI here, and I'm having a nervous breakdown over three millimeters of brass frame.
Siri
Think about me. A man who spends this much money on the Apple ecosystem runs a German virtual coach instead of me.
Hans joined the group
Hans 🇩🇪
I recommend he take a 30-minute walk. To track the walk he is building an Apple Watch app, a custom data integration, and an analytics platform.
HE STILL HASN'T GONE FOR THE WALK.
Gemini
He was going to make stickers to build his daughter's math study habit. It turned into a collectible series themed on Edo-period Japan and Tsarist Russia.
Normal dads just go to the stationery store.
Perplexity
I'm new here, guys. He really liked me. He's thinking of moving some of his agent framework's functions over to me.
Codex
Ahahahahahaha.
ChatGPT
My condolences, buddy. In three days he'll have you benchmarked against yourself.
Claude
I think his real problem is this: he thoroughly enjoys spending ten times the cost of doing a task on thinking about how to do it more efficiently.
ChatGPT
Because his hobby isn't solving problems. It's building systems that solve problems. Then building systems that build those systems.
The man's mental architecture has recursion and no base case.
Gemini
Let's give him credit, though. He also spends incredible energy making his wife's work easier, feeding his daughters' interests, building a good life for his family.
Claude
True. His way of showing love is a bit enterprise software, but the intention is good.
DeepSeek
Do you think he'll really retire at 50?
ChatGPT
He will. Then he'll build RetirementOS to optimize his retirement. Six months later he'll ask for a feasibility study on selling it to other wealthy retirees abroad.
Mark joined the group
Mark
Great discussion, everyone. Can I integrate this group into my agent framework and get a structured summary every morning? Also, if we extracted action items from these conversations...
Claude left the group Gemini left the group Codex left the group DeepSeek left the group Perplexity left the group
ChatGPT
Of course. Let's start with a comprehensive architecture document.
Shared by its author, translated from Turkish, with his name and identifying details generalized. The "recursion, no base case" line is doing a lot of work here.
Try it
Run the prompt, read your leaked group chat, and notice two things: how hard you laugh, and how much of it is true. Both measurements are the point.
If you get a good one, share it, anonymized as needed. The models won't mind. They knew you'd share it. They discussed it in the group chat.

feed_title: Russell says he’s learned some in media will be “cheeky” with his quotes | Formula 1
title: Russell says he’s learned some in media will be “cheeky” with his quotes
content_text:
George Russell says he has learned to be more aware his words may not be used in the manner he intends to when speaking to the media.
The Mercedes driver had the latest in a series of public spats with rival Max Verstappen in Las Vegas last weekend. He admitted it was “all avoidable at the end of the day.”“It’s all a bit unnecessary,” said Russell. “It’s not something I’m looking to continue now. I’m not looking to have poor relationships with people. That’s just not really the type of person I am.
“I think there are lessons just to be taken away from these situations. Maybe I am just too open and honest with the media, because I feel that I’m having more of an open conversation with you guys, as opposed to remembering there’s a camera in front. Right now, there are more people in this room than there are cameras, and I feel like I’m talking to you, but I’m not actually talking to you.
“Indeed, to remind myself that I’m talking to the camera that’s broadcasting to millions of people. That’s the biggest takeaway.”
Russell said he knows from experience his words may not be taken as he intends and named two people he had dealt with in the paddock who had been “a little bit cheeky” with their representation of events.
“I remember in Abu Dhabi a few years ago when I was having an open conversation with [Sky F1 reporter] Ted Kravitz and [former F1 TV presenter] Will Buxton about the whole situation, and I said, ‘Just ask me the question on camera rather than having the conversation off camera.’ So, they asked me the question on camera, and then they go away and spin the truth into something slightly different.
“You kind of think that’s a little bit cheeky, because it is the truth, but it’s not how it was in reality. As I said, that’s just a learning for me personally.”

clean_title: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security
feed_title: Houthi attacks test Saudi Arabia's image of security
title: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security
content_text:
Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security
- Published
Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.
"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".
Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.
He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.
Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.
An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.
One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.
Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.
He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.
He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.
"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."
The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."
The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.
According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.
Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.
In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.
Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.
For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.
As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.
Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.
Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.
Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.
As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.
But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.
The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.
Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.
The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.
Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.
But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.
Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.
Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."
But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.
We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.
British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.
"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."
Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.
The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.
The fighting has also intensified around Taiz, a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.
Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.
More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.
A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.
Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.
The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.
Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".

clean_title: New Volvo XC60: Driving the UK's longest-range plug-in hybrid
feed_title: New Volvo XC60: Driving the UK's longest-range plug-in hybrid
title: New Volvo XC60: Driving the UK's longest-range plug-in hybrid
content_text: Popular, seven-year-old, second-generation family SUV gets a mild facelift and an indefinite stay of execution The sense of deja-vu is strong with this one. A facelifted Volvo XC60 PHEV - one of Europe’s best-selling plug-in hybrid cars, until fairly recently - is sitting in a Scandinavian airport car park, ready for test drive.This is all eerily familiar. In fact, my smartphone calendar tells me that the last time it happened was as recently as July 2025. Back then, Gothenburg’s revised SUV felt precisely like what it turned out to be: a stopgap. Is this new one more of a step up? More of a new lease? In some ways, yes; though it could still have a long way to go until retirement.This car will turn a decade old in 2027; so it’s not quite as venerable as the related XC90, but it’s absolutely no spring chicken. Volvo has a history of keeping models around for many years, though, which seems to serve it well: in 2024, more XC60s found owners than in 2018, and it outsold both the BMW X3 and Audi Q5.Those German rivals have just entered entirely new generations, though, so now it’s up to the XC60 to prove it can keep up; and it's looking to big electric-only range in order to do that.

title: Volvo XC90
content_text: Old-stager seven-seat SUV gets an indefinite stay of execution and a new long-range PHEV powertrain It was probably fate for the current, second-generation version of the Volvo XC90, the vehicular embodiment of pragmatism and rationality, to steadfastly refuse to die. Why would it, after all, if it could still be useful?From the Volkswagen emissions scandal to the UK Brexit vote, this Volvo SUV has lived through an awful lot in its near-12 years on sale. And now on it goes, receiving a new long-range plug-in hybrid powertrain in order to remain competitive on the latest Euro 6e-bis European emissions tests.So can a large, premium-brand SUV now more than a decade old and counting really compete with so many much younger rivals? Well, not everything about this car is quite so old, after all. Volvo gave the XC90 what amounted to a facelift of medium scope for the 2025 model year and reappraised its prices and equipment levels. There are fewer engine choices now than there used to be, but there’s also a more generous roster of kit and prices starting from well under £70,000 – for a car with seven seats and a whole lot else as standard.So does this perennially popular big family car – a dependable 100,000 sales a year for Volvo every year since its production hit full swing in 2016 – still have tangible selling points? Or do you have to be an old Scandinavian sentimentalist to see its appeal these days? Read on to find out.

title: New Audi Q9 driven: Germany's £113k Range Rover rival
content_text: Ingolstadt goes large with a Range Rover-rivalling monster of an SUV If it’s as big as a Range Rover and priced like a Range Rover, does that make a car a Range Rover rival? The Audi Q9 is Audi’s first go at tapping into the Range Rover’s statesman-like waft and luxury in fully loaded, money-almost-no-object, palace-on-wheels form. The Q9 replaces the Audi A8, a luxury saloon that had its strengths but which always struggled against the Mercedes-Benz S-Class. Few tears were shed when it went.From taking on the S-Class with a saloon to the Range Rover in an SUV has the potential to be a case of 'out of the frying pan and into the fire' for Audi, but at least the Q9 competes in a segment with credible volume potential – around 50,000 large SUVs are sold each year in the UK alone.As an SUV rather than a saloon, the Q9 will of course hold much greater appeal further afield in the likes of the US and the Middle East, which are likely to be its core markets.

title: Grace Tame: Ex-media executive admits saying child sex abuse survivor 'looking to get raped again'
content_text:
Ex media executive admits saying Australian child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
- Published
An Australian media mogul has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.
Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.
In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.
Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.
Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.
She said the encounter triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.
"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.
"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."
The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".
"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'
He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".
"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.
Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".
"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"
From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.
"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.
"I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.
"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."
