clean_title: Connectivity conundrum: Do you really own a software-driven car?
feed_title: Connectivity conundrum: Do you really own a software-driven car?
title: Connectivity conundrum: Do you really own a software-driven car?
content_text:
A radio station in Cumbria broadcasts a time signal 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
The 'Time from NPL' (the National Physical Laboratory) broadcasts a signal derived from three atomic clocks at the transmission site at Anthorn. It's the UK's national time reference, and has been broadcast from various locations in a similar form since 1950, though the UK first began broadcasting a reference time as long ago as 1927.
It's receivable throughout the UK and most of northern Europe, but there are other time broadcasts from elsewhere too. In the US a radio station called WWV, now in Colorado and with a sister station in Hawaii, has been broadcasting the time since 1945. (It also broadcasts a tone at 440Hz, the A above middle C in modern musical pitch, which it started doing at the request of American musical organisations.)
At source, WWV's time is accurate to within 0.001 milliseconds of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), which obviously gets a little delayed the farther away from source you are but is ultimately likely to be no more than a few milliseconds off throughout North America.
The signals are used by all kinds of organisations and companies and products. I have a Casio G-Shock watch that receives its time from NPL, or elsewhere if I'm travelling (there are also transmitters in Japan, Germany and China), which it synchronises with late at night, daily. So it always tells the right time, and because it's also solar-powered, I can effectively forget about maintaining it. Because fundamentally I'm lazy, that makes it one of the very best things I own. I wear it all the time.
It is, perhaps, a bit scruffy, though, so I thought I should get one that's tidier but just as convenient, so I bought a shiny metal G-Shock that I thought would look more acceptable at work dinners or shown on video.
Fark. It turns out, and I didn't read the bumf well enough beforehand so this is entirely my fault, that it doesn't update itself automatically from a quaint radio signal that can trace its history back 100 years. Instead, it wants to pair with an app on my phone, via Bluetooth, a miserably unromantic way of the thing on my wrist keeping its accuracy. So today, like most days, I'm wearing the plastic one.
I've found, in other words, the exact level of technology I'm comfortable with: I can't be bothered to wind one; I don't want to pair one.
And I have a similar feeling about where I'd like my cars to be. I'm beginning to suspect that I'm not alone. Which could be problematic.
Today, if you want to buy a watch, you can get one that you have to wind yourself, all the way through to varying degrees of smart that will tell you if you need to have a lie down. Whereas if you buy a new car, with the odd exception, you'll get no choice about not just how it arrives but possibly how it acts in future too.
Most new cars you can buy will update their software during your time with them. According to BMW executives, this could happen as often as every three months in its cars, because they think that spamming software updates more frequently than that would be too annoying. But such updates could extend to even changing the layout of the touchscreen and its apps, should a company think that it finds a better way of doing things, owing to customer feedback.
So, who knows, perhaps the presentation of the climate control page could adjust after an update into a form that the owner didn't sign up for when they bought the car. An owner wouldn't have to allow every piece of software to download, but if they did allow it - because there were crucial changes that they couldn't or shouldn't ignore - and didn't like the changes, it's unlikely they would be able to change it back to the previous one again.
Car makers might say that this is not just normal, but critical; that there are so many components to a car, the most regulated and complicated consumer product in the world, that keeping it in optimum operating condition is essential. Which might be correct. But I can't shake the feeling that we don't quite have ownership of something we've bought. And that the choice of interference in our lives is being ever reduced.

clean_title: Antonelli quickest by half a second on medium tyre compound in first practice
feed_title: Antonelli quickest by half a second on medium tyre compound in first practice | Formula 1
title: Antonelli quickest by half a second on medium tyre compound in first practice
content_text:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli was emphatically quickest in the opening practice session for the Qatar Grand Prix.
The new world championship set his best lap time of 1’23.217 on the medium tyre compound. No one was able to beat that time, even on the softer rubber.Teams found the tyre performance dropped off more quickly than expected around the Losail International Circuit. Lewis Hamilton’s race engineer Carlos Santi told him tyre degradation was “much higher than expected on all compounds” at the end of the session.
George Russell made it a one-two for Mercedes, though his best time on the soft rubber was over half a second off his team mate’s best.
Isack Hadjar was next for Red Bull, though both he and team mate Max Verstappen were stunned by the lack of front grip they had as the session progressed.
“Is the front wing still there?” Hadjar asked at the end of the session, while Verstappen at one point said he needed “10 clicks more” on his front wing angle.
The two McLaren drivers split the Red Bull pair. They opted not to use their new-specification floor for the first day of running, which appeared to be a wise move as several drivers ran wide and kicked up sparks on Losail’s punishing kerbs.
Charles Leclerc, seventh fastest, ran wide onto the kerbs at least twice during the session. Hamilton, who came eighth, also went off at one point.
Arvid Lindblad and Pierre Gasly completed the top 10. The latter had one of the more spectacular impacts with the kerbs, sparks flying from his Alpine’s tail.
Only one team ran a junior driver in the session. Jak Crawford took over Fernando Alonso’s Aston Martin, making his sixth appearance in a practice session this year.
The stewards will investigate Red Bull after the session after ruling a member of the team personnel was “in an unsafe position in the pit lane” while attending to Hadjar’s car.

title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
content_text:
a ball will fall. trade on where it lands.
I made this game! Some technical details:
The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome.
There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky.
Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.

clean_title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
feed_title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
content_text:
Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
- Published
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their funadamental rights.
Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely-watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.
On Friday, the Supreme Court ruled that Quebec's use of the "notwithstanding clause" is valid, except for a section of Bill 21 that bars elected officials from wearing a face covering.
The court found that this provision of the law violates a section of the Canadian Charter protecting the democratic rights of all citizens, which is not covered by the notwithstanding clause.
Barring elected officials in Quebec's legislature from wearing a face covering would infringe on an individual's right to run for public office, the court found.
The court's majority also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the rights Charter even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

clean_title: Erin Patterson: Mushroom murderer launches last-ditch High Court appeal
feed_title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson launches last-ditch High Court appeal
title: Erin Patterson: Mushroom murderer launches last-ditch High Court appeal
content_text:
Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson launches last-ditch High Court appeal
- Published
Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.
Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.
Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole – saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".
She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.
Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday.
She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.
After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.
Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.
He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.
Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.
Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.
She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.
Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.

- Published7 July 2025

feed_title: Hollow Knight: Silksong's first big expansion, Sea of Sorrows, comes out in two weeks - and seems to include a fishing minigame
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong's first big expansion, Sea of Sorrows, comes out in two weeks - and seems to include a fishing minigame
content_text:
Hollow Knight: Silksong's first big expansion, Sea of Sorrows, comes out in two weeks - and seems to include a fishing minigame
Needle things.
Hollow Knight: Silksong developer Team Cherry debuted a special 'Cherry Time Special Presentation' today (27th November), with the aim of bringing more information to light about the game's first big DLC offering, Sea of Sorrows, but also provide a nice little springboard for some other indie titles.
But first, the reason we're all here: Sea of Sorrow is "an expansion like we've never done before", says Team Cherry, before showing off a trailer for the content - which will be free for all players, in case you've forgetten. The trailer confirms the release date for the DLC, 11th December, and teases some new environments, enemies, bosses and - right at the end - what looks like a fishing mini-game. But of course, this is a nautical-themed expansion, after all.
Team Cherry has hinted at the future of Silksong before. Recently, and more than a year after its initial release, physical versions of Hollow Knight: Silksong finally began arriving on players' doorsteps. These editions seemed to tease previously unconfirmed "free content packs" (note the plural). "The world of Hollow Knight: Silksong will expand with free content packs," the booklet read in the physical editions. "Prepare for even more adventures filled with new friends, new abilities, and new ferocious foes!" We have no hint on what will happen next for Silksong, though, off the back of this presentation.
Check out the full livestream below.
At the start of the show, the two founders of Team Cherry (that's William Pellen and Ari Gibson) used their platform to show off three cool little indie games from other developers in the scene:
- The first was a fun little title that began as a graphic novel that turned into a narrative adventure game, called Blokkan: Secret of the Walking City.
- The next was a a 2D pixel art side-scrolling game called Radio Rain, which is "all about exploring the ruins and listening to music", and it looks neat. It's supposed to feel like "listening to a radio station and hearing music you haven't heard for years", and is inspired by 80s music.
- The third game comes from an animator/illustrator/voice actor/game developer called The Botanist and the Translator, in which you travel to a distant planet to solve a plant-based mystery. It's all inspired on Sailor Moon, and aims to be "cute, charming, and appealing."
In September last year, Eurogamer gave five stars to Hollow Knight: Silksong, calling it "pretty and charmingly mean-spirited" whilst praising it as a "game filled with revelations and genuine personality". I'm excited to get my hands on more of this sumptuous Metroidvania.

clean_title: If you're not using Auto Drive and Cinematic Camera in GTA 6, you're missing out on some of the best experiences in the game (and a cheeky, free 'fast travel' alternative, too)
feed_title: If you're not using Auto Drive and Cinematic Camera in GTA 6, you're missing out on some of the best experiences in the game
title: If you're not using Auto Drive and Cinematic Camera in GTA 6, you're missing out on some of the best experiences in the game (and a cheeky, free 'fast travel' alternative, too)
content_text:
If you're not using Auto Drive and Cinematic Camera in GTA 6, you're missing out on some of the best experiences in the game
Highway Star.
Spoilers for Chapter 1-3 of GTA 6 follow.
I have just successfully busted a Kingfisher operation just north of Cottonmouth Lake in Mariana County. It was beautiful. Jason took point, armed with a shotgun liberated from an M7 clubhouse, guarding a chokepoint as hordes of rednecks threw themselves at him in an unceremonious, slightly humiliating pantomime of existential futility. Lucia, confident in her improving gunmanship, stood behind, aimed over Jason's broad shoulders, and took out stragglers with a custom hunting rifle pilfered from the Kingfisher's own safehouse. Not so safe anymore, is it, losers? This one's for Donnie, I think as I kneecap the final goon and rifle through their safe.
"That one was for Donnie," Lucia says to Jason as they get in their favourite car - Jason's sunset yellow Declasse '72 Tulip, with a suped up engine and custom parts. God damn, I think, this game can read my mind. And I'm not sure if I would have had this intimate little moment of grief and reconciliation if I hadn't got in the habit of using the game's Cinematic Camera. Your dual protagonists can chat even when you, the player, are in the driving seat - of course - but there's so much going on in the world of Leonida (and so many pedestrians and motorists that like to behave like maniacs and cut you off) that I find their conversations are often cut short or terminated altogether by the chaos of the world.
So, hopping into the car, hitting 'down' on the D-Pad and then hitting 'Start' will instigate the Cinematic Camera, and if you've already set a destination on the map or via the handy new quick navigational menu (simply hold 'down' to see this), your chosen lovebird will start automatically driving to their next location. For me, in this example, it was the Pelican River to Vice City's Bayside, and Boobie's apartment. Probably about 15 minutes of real-world time; enough space to fuss my dog, grab a drink, reply to my editor, and really take the time to soak in the absurd level of detail Rockstar has crammed into its opus. On this specific journey, I also heard a really touching, sweet interaction about Jason's insecurities regarding Lucai's mum. Goosebumps.
GTA 6 is an action-packed game; there aren't a lot of menial jobs going for Jason and Lucia - they're on the run, after all, so I don't think a traditional PAYE-compliant nine-to-five is really on the cards. As such, even the smaller money-making activities on offer are quite stressful: dirt-track events, street racing, pawn store robberies, hit-and-runs, stick-ups… there's only so much a bit of meditation in a park can do to decompress you. So I've taken to enjoying life on the roads. After a big, somewhat impromptu heist on two Kingfisher operations, I need a bit of time to slow down and smell the proverbial roses (or should that be Tulips?).
Jumping into Jason's car, turning the radio to The Chamber 106.6, and letting the star-crossed lovers meander their way home listening to Slayer's Kerry King and Tom Araya play a selection of metal tracks from the past four decades is good for my brain. I actually think these moments of leisure are essential to the rhythm of GTA 6: dial it up, cool it off. It creates this almost tidal ebb and flow, the resultant flotsam and jetsam ending up fenced or stashed as the rhythm dictates.
I'm usually a very active and fussy player when it comes to games; I can't stand long cutscenes taking control away from me, and I absolutely will skip story scenes on a second playthrough if it's getting in the way of hands-on controller time. So I'm quite surprised at the ease with which I've given up my agency for these longer rides. But it's a testament to Rockstar's writing. I want to see what Jason and Lucia are saying to each other. I want the camera to show me the world passing me by outside my window as I get from A to B. I even sometimes schedule and phase in little detours to C and D, to be honest, because I feel so zen as I watch the bruise-coloured sky sets over the Keys (and I want to hear the end of Symphony of Destruction, maybe).
My Lucia is dressed a bit like someone you'll see cutting about outside Nottingham's Rock City club - cute little tank top, leather jacket, nose and ear piercings galore. One afternoon, after driving out to Hamlet to have a long overdue catch-up with her mum, I set the Cinematic Camera and auto-drive settings on to take her back to meet Jason at a bar (another place, incidentally, you can turn on the Cinematic Camera and just watch them hang out together). On her way back home, with the sunlight dipping below the horizon, the fiery orange ambience caught the whites of her eye and the metallic zip of her leather jacket. She smiled to herself as Tool's Sober came on the radio. Christ, I thought, I'm there.
GTA 6 has this odd capacity to transport me. I think it's because the levels of simulation in Leonida are so artisanal, so well-pitched, and so well-executed. I can believe I'm there. I want to sit in this muscle car, no doubt smelling of leather and oil, listening to Tool with Lucia. I want to feel the humid air of Watson Bay coalescing on my skin, warm air blowing through my hair. I want to join in on Jason and Lucia's in-jokes, laugh as they do little impressions of each other and coo as they make up and hold hands during the longer drives. I want to stick my head out the window like Lucia does and smell the Cuban food grilling in the food trucks, or hear the kids partying on the beach.
With the Cinematic Camera turned on, I have the chance to do that. I don't have to worry about making money, paying back favours I owe, checking in with Brian, topping up my BuckMe account. I can just engage in this fantasy - this simulation - Rockstar has built for me. And in these moments where I take my hands off the wheel, hang out with these people I've dressed up and ride around in the car I've built, it really does feel like it's been made just for me. I can't remember the last time a game made me feel that way.

clean_title: Stanford Physicist Uses AI to Tackle Quantum Gravity Problem
feed_title: Stanford Physicist Uses AI to Tackle Quantum Gravity Problem
title: Stanford Physicist Uses AI to Tackle Quantum Gravity Problem
content_text:
Stanford Physicist Uses AI to Tackle Quantum Gravity Problem
Insider Brief
- Stanford physicist Venkatesa Chandrasekaran proposed a quantum theory of gravity that uses the paths of light to calculate how spacetime can fluctuate.
- The approach yielded a finite result for a graviton-pair calculation that diverges under an approximation and reproduced a known quantum correction to black hole entropy.
- Chandrasekaran said he developed several calculations and proofs through months of work with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, using about 400 million tokens.
A Stanford physicist has proposed a quantum theory of gravity that uses the paths of light to get a finite answer for a calculation that can otherwise run to infinity.
If the approach holds up, it could help reconcile quantum mechanics, which governs the behavior of matter and energy at small scales, with Einstein’s general relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime. The study also reproduces a known quantum correction to the entropy of a black hole.
In a preprint posted on arXiv, Venkatesa Chandrasekaran calculated what happens when two gravitons, the hypothetical quantum units of gravitational waves, are created and then disappear. The calculation gave a finite answer even after accounting for waves of arbitrarily short wavelength. An approximation applied to the same calculation produced an infinity.
Chandrasekaran said in the paper’s acknowledgments that he developed several of its calculations and proofs through months of back-and-forth work with GPT-6 Astra, an OpenAI model. He put the total at about 400 million tokens, the units of text AI models process, and said OpenAI provided the computing resources.
The work addresses a problem of reconciling general relativity with quantum theory, a problem that, as mentioned, has vexed top physicists for decades. General relativity treats gravity as the curvature of spacetime. In plain terms, quantum theory allows physical quantities to fluctuate. If spacetime itself fluctuates, the geometry that ordinarily tells physicists where and when something happens also becomes part of what they have to calculate.
Chandrasekaran’s proposal uses the boundaries of finite regions of spacetime to set up those calculations. The boundaries follow paths that light could take, and their shape can change with the gravitational field. That gives the calculation a way to specify where something happens even as the geometry changes.
The study also finds that a region bounded this way, with a specified maximum size, can hold only a finite number of mutually distinguishable quantum states. In a separate calculation for a large black hole, the approach recovered both the standard relationship between a black hole’s entropy and its surface area and a previously calculated quantum correction.
It’s important to note that the paper is theoretical and presents no experimental test.
Using Light to Set the Boundaries
To calculate how gravity behaves when spacetime itself can fluctuate, Chandrasekaran starts by defining the region he wants to study. He uses the paths light can take between two events to set its boundaries.
One way to envision this is to imagine a flash going off and a detector set to record light at a particular moment later. Light spreading out from the flash marks one boundary. Tracing the possible paths of light backward from the detector at that moment marks the other. The two boundaries enclose a region called a causal diamond. Any point inside it can receive a signal from the flash and send one in time to reach the detector.
In general relativity, gravitational waves can distort those boundaries. The paper treats the surface where they meet as part of the system and locates quantities relative to it. Chandrasekaran first solves the classical equations that constrain which combinations of boundary data are possible. He then applies quantum rules to the remaining variables, which include the two ways a gravitational wave can be polarized.
To describe a larger stretch of spacetime, the paper joins regions along shared boundaries. It matches the gravitational data on the two sides and sums over the quantum states that can occur at an intermediate stage. Chandrasekaran shows that these intermediate sums converge within the construction. In fact, they converge even when the set of possible states is infinite.
The order of operations matters, as the graviton-pair calculation shows.
In practice, physicists often start with a rough answer and refine it by adding corrections based on the strength of the interaction.
In this example, expanding in Newton’s gravitational constant before adding the contributions from different wavelengths produces a term that grows without bound. Keeping the constant at its physical, nonzero value and doing the sum first gives a finite answer. At very short wavelengths, contributions that would otherwise drive the divergence partly cancel.
Counting States Inside a Black Hole
For the state-counting result, Chandrasekaran imposes a maximum size on a macroscopic causal diamond using what he calls a gravitational clock. The clock is a distance-like reading defined along the paths of light. Gravitational radiation changes that reading by affecting how neighboring light paths converge. Putting an upper limit on the reading also restricts which wave states can fit within the region.
The study concludes that a causal diamond with a fixed size limit can contain only a finite number of distinct quantum states. That means the area where the two light cones meet can take only certain values, with gaps between them.
The black hole calculation uses a surface where a bundle of outward-directed light rays momentarily stops spreading. The local gravitational data are enough to identify that surface and begin counting states on its interior side.
By summing over interior states, Chandrasekaran recovers the leading term in the Bekenstein-Hawking formula, which makes a black hole’s entropy proportional to its horizon area. Entropy describes how much microscopic information is compatible with the same large-scale description.
For a large, nonrotating black hole, the study also found a small adjustment to the standard entropy formula that grows slowly as the black hole’s surface area increases. The result matches an earlier calculation by physicist Ashoke Sen that held the black hole’s mass fixed and accounted for small variations in its spin.
Next Steps
A lot of work remains.
The four-dimensional theory covers gravity in a vacuum, where gravitational waves can propagate. Extending it to include matter would widen its scope. The calculation also recovers Einstein’s equations in the low-energy limit for initial quantum states concentrated around a classical geometry. It calculates the first quantum correction in that regime, including how fluctuations in gravity in turn affect the average geometry.
One question Chandrasekaran leaves for future work is whether different choices in building the quantum state space lead to equivalent theories for the same range of clock readings. Another test would be to carry the black hole and low-energy calculations beyond the first quantum correction.
For a deeper, more technical dive, please review the paper on arXiv. It’s important to note that arXiv is a pre-print server, which allows researchers to receive quick feedback on their work. However, it is not — nor is this article, itself — official peer-review publications. Peer-review is an important step in the scientific process to verify results.

title: Spotlight: Some F1 broadcasters choose not to attend Qatar Grand Prix
content_text:
After months of discussion over whether Formula 1’s final two rounds in the Middle East would go ahead, first practice for the Qatar Grand Prix took place today.
But not all of F1’s broadcasters chose to attend. France’s Canal+ does not have correspondents at the Losail International Circuit.
Sky’s German coverage team are also not attending the race. “We have decided not to send an editorial team on-site,” the broadcaster told Sport1. “Commentary will be provided from Unterföhring, and pre-race coverage will begin 60 minutes before the start of the race.”
As Formula One Management provides a stream from the track, broadcasters do not have to be present at the circuit to air live coverage of the sessions.
This article will be updated.

clean_title: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in
feed_title: John Simpson: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in
title: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in
content_text:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.
Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.
The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.
The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?
Surviving blackouts
Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.
Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.
I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.
To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.
Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.
Raving through the war
I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.
We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.
Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.
What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.
Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.
Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.
It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.
There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.
How does it all end?
The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.
So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.
But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.
Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.
And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."
Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.
Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.
At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.
The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

content_text:
Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
- Published
Touring musicians from across the US who descended on New York City to perform at the Macy's Thanksgiving parade have turned to fundraising to cover their costs, after getting stuck when the event was rearranged due to a storm.
A band from Texas told the BBC's US partner, CBS News, it had raised some $350,000 (£267,000) to pay for an extended stay for its 500 members. It saluted the kindness of its supporters.
A group of student musicians from Hawaii, meanwhile, voiced their relief after friends and family rallied around to cover their additional hotel, coach and meal costs.
The parade, a famous annual event, is now scheduled to take place on Saturday.
Earlier this week, organisers said they would it push it back by two days, in part due to the concerns around flying giant inflatables in strong winds.
The balloons were temporarily deflated for a few days - and so too were the spirits of those who had journeyed to the city to watch the action.
The move represented the first time the event had been postponed, although it was suspended altogether during World War Two.
Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, some of them from high schools, to provide music for the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions of people in person and on TV.
- Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather - Published1 day ago
 
The leader of the Texas band described his emotions as costs for his delegation were met.
"It's been exhausting and emotional to figure this out, but it has been incredibly humbling to see an outpouring of kindness," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band at Pearland High School, near Houston, in Texas, told CBS.
Demkovich said contributions had arrived from businesses and individuals in the band's home community, with the help of a social media push.
Meanwhile, the Hawaii group, the the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it would still be able to participate in the parade, as a result of the efforts of families, friends, and other supporters who raised more than $500,000.
Speaking to the BBC earlier on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.
The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It had travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.
"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional, for our students," Badua said.
But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".
The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.
Badua was hopeful his group would get the same experience he had when he first performed in the parade in 2003, as student drum major.
"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."
Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it was trying to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.
"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Prof Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.
While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain that were brought by a storm to eastern areas of the US.
Hundreds of thousands of homes lost power, and coastal areas were flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.
Additional reporting by Jessica Murphy

feed_title: Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
title: Brazil pushes back on Emmanuel Macron calling its meat 'doped'
content_text:
Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
- Published
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron who called Brazilian meat "doped".
France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry which took effect in September.
In its statement, the Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".
Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat and poultry owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.
In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.
Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.
"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.
Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".
Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".
Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

feed_title: Clashes mar European games as Macron condemns violence
title: European games marred by clashes as French President Emmanuel Macron condemns violence
content_text:
Clashes mar European games as Macron condemns violence
- Published
Violent clashes marred a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French President Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.
There were also incidents at games between Turkish side Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Be'er-Sheva in Georgia and Sunderland's 1-1 home draw with Poland's Jagiellonia Bialystok.
Uefa says it has appointed ethics and disciplinary inspectors "to conduct investigations into the incidents and examine all available evidence" from the Marseille-Levski Sofia and Besiktas-Hapoel Be'er-Sheva games.
European football's governing body said it "strongly condemns the serious incidents of violence and disorder" at those ties.
It added: "Violence, aggression, hatred and any form of provocative, discriminatory or extremist behaviour have no place in football.
"Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety."
In Marseille, the build-up to the Europa League match at the Stade Velodrome was affected by incidents in the stands, including the throwing of projectiles and flares between the two sets of supporters.
With 10 minutes to go until kick-off, several Marseille fans ran from a home stand, appearing to pursue a group of Levski Sofia supporters.
They breached the stand designated for away fans, which housed around 500 supporters of the Bulgarian domestic champions.
"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," said the Marseille police prefecture. "Six others were treated on site for various wounds."
Macron spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev about the incidents, with the French president condemning "with the utmost force these acts of violence, which have no place in sport or in public space", and reassured him that "these acts would not go unpunished".
According to news agency Reuters, Radev thanked Macron for his personal involvement following the "attack on Bulgarian citizens" and for the medical assistance provided to the victims.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova said she found video footage of the incidents "shocking" in a statement posted on social media.
"The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world," she added.
"Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety."
Ligue 1 club Marseille said it was "working to understand the precise circumstances of these incidents".
The police source said all the people injured were Bulgarian and there was "no information at this stage regarding any arrests".
Security personnel managed to restore calm, allowing the game to kick-off on time, although there were a few further flare-ups between the fans, notably during the half-time break in a match Marseille won 1-0.
"It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football," said Levski Sofia coach Julio Velazquez
Marseille boss Bruno Genesio added: "We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable."
Meanwhile, the Turkish Football Federation has strongly condemned the "unacceptable" actions of Georgian police towards Besiktas fans who unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during their Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er-Sheva.
Besiktas say they have lodged a complaint with European football's governing body Uefa over "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.
The match had been moved from Istanbul to Batumi, Georgia for safety and security reasons but had to be suspended in the 25th minute after clashes involving Besiktas supporters and local police.
Both the officiating team and the Besiktas players left the field, but play was able to resume 30 minutes later.
Besiktas won the match 2-1.
"We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the Uefa Europa League match," said a statement from the Turkish federation.
Turkish outlet NTV reported that Georgian police had gone into the stands and used pepper spray on the Besiktas fans.
The report added that there were anti-Israeli chants from the Turkish fans and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters to try to calm matters before play restarted.
Hakan Fidan, Turkey's minister of foreign affairs, spoke to his Georgian counterpart Maka Botchorishvili following the incident.
"All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights," a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
At Sunderland, there were crowd disturbances after Jagiellonia Bialystok fans were found in areas of the Stadium of Light with home fans, despite Uefa having imposed an away supporter ban for the Europa League game.
Police and stewards attended some disruption early on during the match.
"In the build-up to the match, the club had put measures in place in line with this sanction and maintained regular communication with our supporters, Jagiellonia Bialystok and Uefa," said a Sunderland statement.
"Unfortunately, Jagiellonia Bialystok failed to engage and cooperate on this matter.
"We are disappointed that these measures and communications were disregarded by some visiting supporters and we will review the circumstances surrounding their entry into the stadium."

feed_title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
title: Paul Mackenzie: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
content_text:
Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
- Published
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.
The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves.
The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the Shakahola cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.
The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

clean_title: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
feed_title: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
title: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
content_text:
Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
- Published
Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.
His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life. A post mortem examination was due to take place on Friday.
In his eight-page note, De Gennaro, 78, vehemently denied obstructing the inquiry into the murder of anti-mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in Sicily in July 1992.
The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino's killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone two months earlier.
But several fruitless investigations were later launched into potential cover-ups by high-ranking officials.
In a recent inquiry De Gennaro, who in the 1990s worked in the anti-mafia directorate and later became Italy's police chief, was accused of misdirecting the initial investigation.
The allegations shocked many Italians, as De Gennaro had worked closely with Falcone and was seen as being on the front line of the fight against organised crime.
"In a few minutes I will be gone, so you understand well that a 'man condemned to death' cannot lie," he wrote in the letter, published by Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I have never betrayed my oath of loyalty to the Fatherland."
"I hope that, amid the avalanche of falsehoods now overwhelming me, the truth will ultimately prevail," he added.
The case, and the media furore that has surrounded it, have re-opened the wound of the Mafia killings of the early 1990s, which remain an emotionally charged issue in Italy.
The story has dominated Italian headlines since De Gennaro's death, with several of the country's most senior political figures publicly commenting on the case.
On Thursday Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she had been "deeply shocked" by the case.
"His words struck us deeply, and I think the most important think we can do now is to help prosecutors who are working to clear things up," she added.
The letter was found next to a hard drive which he said contained notes from his 40-year career.
According to Italian media, investigators seized two hard drives, one from the home of De Gennaro's son and one from a former member of his security detail, and two USB sticks held by a close collaborator, who is also under investigation.
The sticks are reportedly labelled "Stato-Mafia", a likely reference to the alleged relationship between the Italian state and the Mafia, and "Massacres".
Forensic specialists are now expected to examine whether any files on the hard drives or USB sticks were altered or deleted, reports say.

clean_title: Credit card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sites — InfoHawk News
feed_title: Credit card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sites
title: Credit card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sites — InfoHawk News
content_text:
Credit card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sites
All the sites we contacted took action; but the larger consumer web ecosystem should be prepared to mitigate these attack vectors
A card-skimming script was planted on the online stores of Lascana, Samsonite, American Tourister, Revolve and FWRD in the week before Black Friday. After our reports to affected companies, all have had the script removed (on November 24th or 25th) ahead of Black Friday. We observed it in action on one of the five websites: Lascana, where it sent our test card's details to a 3rd party. We believe the script was built to take a card number, expiry and security code, along with a user's name, address, phone and email, and send them to malefactors as a user entered their payment credentials. It did this before the store checked the payment, so a card could be taken even if the order was declined or cancelled, and nothing would look wrong to the shopper. Across all of these sites, we do not know how many, if any, shopper details or payment credentials may have been captured.
Which sites were affected
| Consumer site | Delivery method | Status at time of publication | 
|---|---|---|
| Lascana www.lascana.com | Altered Quorum* marketing pixel | Both Lascana and Quorum replied and removed the code on the 24th, see details below | 
| Samsonite shop.samsonite.com | Edited Seers† cookie-banner setting | Neither party replied to us, but the code was removed on November 24th at 14:25 UTC | 
| American Tourister shop.americantourister.com | Edited Seers† cookie-banner setting | Neither party replied to us, but the code was removed on November 24th at 14:25 UTC | 
| Revolve www.revolve.com | Altered file on Revolve's own CDN | Revolve confirmed removal on November 25th | 
| FWRD www.fwrd.com | Altered file on Revolve's own CDN | Revolve confirmed removal on November 25th | 
On November 24, we notified all of the named parties in this article and others, including: Amazon Web Services about the storage buckets serving the script, Cloudflare about the services the malefactor used, the domain registrars, the pixel vendor, the consent-banner provider and the affected retailers and platforms. Lascana replied to us and removed the Quorum pixel from their site by November 24th at 15:48 UTC. Quorum confirmed the identified malicious code was removed from their pixel tracker, and they restored the clean marketing pixel as of November 24th at 21:09 UTC.
Revolve provided this statement on behalf of REVOLVE and FWRD: “On November 25, InfoHawk notified our team of a potential security issue impacting mobile and tablet versions of our websites which we resolved the same day. We appreciate the outreach, and are actively investigating the issue to determine any potential impact.”
* Quorum is an ad-attribution platform that links ad views to store visits and online sales (quorum.inc).
† Seers is a cookie consent management platform and data privacy compliance company (seers.ai).
How the attack works
This attack uses WebRTC, the technology that allows you to make video calls in your web browser. WebRTC lets a web page open its own channel to another party and pass data (e.g. audio/video packets) over it. It has likely been used (both to load the skimmer and to send the stolen card details out) because security rules and monitoring tools often do not watch this communications channel as closely. For example, Meta briefly used WebRTC in a creative way in 2025, according to researchers looking at the technology as a compromise vector. This form of attack appears to target mobile devices, and we only saw the server enable the skimmer on checkout pages, so desktop checks and homepage scans would likely not see it. The skimmer's traffic appeared to run through Cloudflare's relay, so it would blend in with the WebRTC traffic and hide its true endpoint.
The skimmer and card details both traveled over WebRTC
    How the kit is designed to work on a store page, in 7 steps. Only step 4 is
    an ordinary web request, which a connect-src rule can block;
    steps 5 to 7 run over the WebRTC data channel, outside
    connect-src.
  
- 
      Store pageBootstrapping the attackThe loader gets onto the page through a consent-banner setting, a retailer CDN file, a shared marketing pixel or the store's own HTML. 
- 
      Store pageLoading scripts from S3 bucketsIt loads Insds.jsorgtage.jsfrom an Amazon S3 bucket.
- 
      Store pageTargeting the attack to mobile checkoutsIt runs only on small or touch screens. The Samsonite version runs on /checkoutonly.
- 
      Web request · connect-src can block itEstablishing the WebRTC connectionGET /_cf/icefetches the relay details, andPOST /_cf/relsends the WebRTC offer, to a brand-namednorthbridgeads[.]comhost.
- 
      WebRTC data channel · outside connect-srcData exchange via TURN relayEvery exchange that returned relay details used turn.cloudflare.com. The malefactor's answers listed only Cloudflare relay addresses; through that relay it sends code and receives data.
- 
      WebRTC data channel · code inAttack code is loaded and executedThe skimmer arrives in chunks over the channel, is checked against a SHA-256 digest, then run with eval.
- 
      WebRTC data channel · data backData goes back the same wayAt Lascana's checkout‡, the skimmer sent our test card details this way. 
‡ This was the only example of live card details being sent off-site that we captured.
Worried that your card was compromised?
Check your recent statements for charges you don't recognize, especially on debit cards. Call your bank or card issuer right away, report the fraud and ask for a new card number. Follow up with a written dispute within 60 days of the statement that shows the charge.
Our understanding of US federal law is that your liability for unauthorized credit card charges is capped at $50, and is generally zero if only your card number was stolen, as in a skimming attack like this one. Debit cards have weaker protections that depend on how quickly you report, so act fast. For more information, see “Additional resources” below.
What site owners should immediately do
connect-src rule that lists only the hosts you use.
  That blocks the two web requests the script needs before WebRTC opens. Without them the skimmer never arrives, whichever file was tampered with.
What security teams should look for
We saw the skimmer delivered in three different ways across five websites run by different companies, and all of them appear to rely on the same attacker infrastructure. That makes it likely that other sites are affected too, so we encourage online retailers to check their own sites for the signs below.
- 
      Script sources: search page source, tag managers, consent-banner
      settings and CDN files for scripts from
      <brand>-static.s3.amazonaws[.]com(filesInsds.js,gtage.js). We believe this is the malicious code.
- 
      Tracking pixels: if you load
      qscripts.s3.amazonaws[.]com/pscript.js, check its last line for one of the above CDN buckets, and if present, remove the tracking pixel. We recommend reviewing all similar tracking pixels and their exposure to sensitive fields or actions on your website.
- 
      Seers banners: If you have integrated Seers, open your banner
      config
      (cdn.seersco.com/banners/<account>/<domain>/cb.js) and check that every URL field holds only a URL. In the affected configs, the privacy-policy link field also held a hidden image, whoseonerrorevent handler loaded the malicious code.
- 
      Checkout traffic: on a phone-sized touch screen, at the payment
      step, look for /_cf/iceand/_cf/relrequests to*.northbridgeads[.]comand a relay-only WebRTC connection used by the malicious code. Desktop checks miss it.
- 
      Strings: KghRtc,rtc-signal-v1andquickfetchare referenced in the malicious code and may warrant further investigation if present.
The industry is not ready for the scale of supply chain attacks coming
This attack takes advantage of a few critical design decisions in websites that, if improperly configured, allow malicious actors to broadly deploy and trigger exploits across the open web.
- Websites load third-party code, often through a tag manager, from servers they don't control. The vendor can change that code at any time, and it can pull in further third-party code the site never reviewed.
- That code runs as an ordinary script with the same rights as the site's own code. It can read and rewrite the page, watch what users type, and load more code.
- Login, personal-information and payment pages often load the same marketing scripts as the rest of the site. Card fields should sit in an isolated payment frame, and third-party tags should be kept off these pages entirely.
Loading third-party tracking pixels on checkout, payment and login pages is far too common a practice today. Each pixel can run whatever code its vendor's file holds, including a skimmer, and whoever controls that file can change it without the site noticing. Every site should review which tracking pixels load on pages that take payment or sign-in details, who can change those files, and whether they need to be there at all.
A similar weakness was exploited at scale on 16 November 2026. An attacker reportedly used a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation product to add malicious code to customers' projects, and Optimizely's own servers delivered it to visitors of 178 organizations' sites, including Zoom, the BBC and CNN, with no change to those sites' own code.
Additional resources
- Mastercard, "What is digital skimming? Your guide to staying safe while shopping online". Published October 10, 2024, it explains how criminals sneak malicious code into e-commerce websites to steal the payment data of customers who use their cards there.
- Visa, "Why hackers are prioritizing account data attacks in digital payments". This describes how hackers inject malicious code onto the checkout pages of merchant websites to harvest payments account data and personally identifiable information (PII) entered by customers.
- Visa Zero Liability
- Mastercard Zero Liability
- CISA/FBI E-Skimming fact sheet. It explains how cyber criminals introduce skimming code on e-commerce payment card processing web pages to capture credit card and personally identifiable information and send the stolen data to a domain under their control. It's from 2020, but it's still the clearest government explainer.
- FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center

clean_title: SAP Confirms Cyberattack, Source Code Reportedly Compromised
feed_title: SAP confirms a cybersecurity incident; report: hackers obtained its staffers' authentication tokens, letting them copy and alter source code stored on GitHub (Eduard Kovacs/SecurityWeek)
title: SAP Confirms Cyberattack, Source Code Reportedly Compromised
content_text:
Enterprise software giant SAP has confirmed it is investigating a cybersecurity incident following reports that threat actors targeted its development infrastructure.
German publication Der Spiegel [paywalled] broke the news on Thursday, citing SAP insiders and an internal notification sent to employees.
SAP told SecurityWeek that it had detected suspicious activity and implemented measures to protect customers and secure its services. The German company did not disclose details of the attack.
“Based on our investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data,” SAP told SecurityWeek.
German news agency DPA reviewed internal SAP communications that revealed the suspicious activity had been identified within GitHub.
According to an insider cited by Der Spiegel, the hackers obtained SAP employees’ authentication tokens, enabling them to copy and alter source code stored on GitHub.
SAP publishes developer tools, sample applications, and open source projects on GitHub. It’s unclear whether the threat actor accessed any proprietary code.
Separately, Handelsblatt reported that SAP’s emergency security measures have affected numerous teams. The software giant has reportedly replaced signing keys, limited access to GitHub, and suspended automated development operations.
None of the reports indicate that tampered code was incorporated into software delivered to SAP customers.
Sources cited by Der Spiegel suggested that the attack may have been assisted by AI. While AI involvement has not been confirmed, several major organizations, including the European Commission, have recently disclosed AI-assisted cyberattacks.
In late October, the Gentlemen ransomware group listed SAP on its leak website, pointing to the company’s Latin American operations. File listings reviewed by SecurityWeek suggest the hackers obtained SAP-related software and source code, but it is unclear whether SAP itself or a third party was compromised. The two incidents do not appear to be connected.

feed_title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
title: Paul Mackenzie: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
content_text:
Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
- Published
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.
The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves.
The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the Shakahola cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.
The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.
More about Kenya's doomsday cult from the BBC:

clean_title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
feed_title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
content_text:
Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
- Published
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.
Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."
The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.
On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.
The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.
While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.
Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".
Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.
- Canada's top court to rule on Quebec's ban on wearing religious symbols - Published6 hours ago
 
Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.
Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.
"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.
The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.
"It wasn't the result we were looking for," Ortona told reporters. "But we do take solace from a lot of the declarations that were made by the court."
Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laïcité - as a core component of its identity.
Earlier this year, the province passed another bill expanding its secularism rules to subsidised daycares and post-secondary institutions. It also restricted public prayer with fines for non-compliance.
The leader of the Bloc Québécois, a federal party that advocates for Quebec sovereignty, said Friday's ruling upheld the province's right to protect its values.
"We are now more than ever in a position to move forward with the preservation of the very elements that profoundly define the distinct nature of Quebec society," he told reporters in French.
