title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 gets a model painter demo, so you can make a mess of your Orks, Necrons, Space Marines and AdMech before they even hit the battlefield
content_text:
Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 gets a model painter demo, so you can make a mess of your Orks, Necrons, Space Marines and AdMech before they even hit the battlefield
Tired: grimdark. Wired: orangebrown
In the grim darkness of the week before the release of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4, developers King Art and publishers Deep Silver have released a demo model painter. It's your chance to pre-emptively run a brush over units from the new strategy game's four major factions – Orks, Adeptus Mechanicus, Necrons and Space Marines. The Imperial Guard are in the game too, but mostly as a tutorial army. What a slap in the face for the Imperium's vanilla humans.
Deep Silver are calling it "the most powerful Painter in Dawn of War history", which doesn't seem all that dashing a boast given that Dawn of War 3 came out almost 10 years ago and today's PCs have a fair bit more RAM in them. You can opt for Basic Painter mode in order to quickly knock together livery for entire armies, or fire up the Advanced Painter and get stuck into the weeds of individual armour and body parts, with a choice of materials, patterns, decals and weathering. Here be trailer.
Gosh, don't your units look splendid, after literal moments of tinkering! What a colossal waste it would be to buy the full version of DOW4, import your custom designs, and watch them get all scratched and blown to pieces! Although that is obviously the idea - this is bog-standard preorder bait. You can also send your designs to other players using codes, which is nice. I plan to fashion my very own line of Space Marine chapters with colour schemes that can be deduced from the title alone: the dreaded Magpie Men, the valiant Traffic Lightbearers, and the Emperor's own Paisley Pillagers.
There is surely no greater insult for a table-top Warhammer player than having your opponent show up to the battle with an unpainted army. Somebody did this to me once, which is partly why I don't play tabletop Warhammer anymore (the main reason, of course, is that tabletop Warhammer is mind-bogglingly expensive). I'd spent hours on my own High Elves, getting the blue of the pennants and the gilt of the heraldry just right, and here's some guy with an army of grey plastic and pewter. Might as well have moulded his troops out of chewing gum and saved himself £50!
Well, there'll be no excuse for showing up with a blandly dressed army in Dawn of War 4. Find the model painter on Steam. As for the actual warmaking component of DOW4, Julian worries the devs are playing it too safe.

It's your chance to pre-emptively run a brush over units from the new strategy game's four major factions – Orks, Adeptus Mechanicus, Necrons and Space Marines. The Imperial Guard are in the game too, but mostly as a tutorial army. What a slap in the face for the Imperium's vanilla humans.

Deep Silver are calling it "the most powerful Painter in Dawn of War history", which doesn't seem all that dashing a boast given that Dawn of War 3 came out almost 10 years ago and today's PCs have a fair bit more RAM in them. You can opt for Basic Painter mode in order to quickly knock together livery for entire armies, or fire up the Advanced Painter and get stuck into the weeds of individual armour and body parts, with a choice of materials, patterns, decals and weathering. Here be trailer.

title: Go fishing and fire Hornet out of a cannon in Silksong's December-bound Sea of Sorrow expansion, which Team Cherry say is "unlike anything we’ve done before"
content_text:
Go fishing and fire Hornet out of a cannon in Silksong's December-bound Sea of Sorrow expansion, which Team Cherry say is "unlike anything we’ve done before"
Lost and drowned
Honest to goodness news for Hollow Knight: Silksong expansion Sea of Sorrow? That I didn’t invent in a dream? Scarcely believable, yet entirely true. The watery DLC is releasing on December 11th 2026, a scant two weeks from now, and as with original Hollow Knight's expansions it’ll be free to those who own the base game. There’s also a new trailer, showing some of the gunpowder-jumping and fishy boss-battling Hornet will get up to while exploring those sorrowful seas.
Keen ramblers through Silksong’s sonorous Pharloom kingdom will note the new, aquatic locales: coral-coated ruins, damp algae forests, and bioluminescent cliffs that crackle with strange blue lighting. A piratical sub-theme also flashes up in a few places, particularly one yarr-ing jellybug boss and Hornet’s newfound talent for launching herself out of cannons as a movement aid.
There also looks to be at least another one of Silksong’s deviously tricky 'Climb a shaft while being chased by rising Bad Liquid' sections, as well as a moment when Hornet tries her claw at silk-fishing. I’m not the most accomplished Silksongist on the planet but I’ve played enough to know that whatever she catches will probably have two phases and a title card.
Or will it? In introducing the release date and trailer, as part of a Cherry Time showcase on the developers’ YouTube channel, Team Cherry claimed Sea of Sorrow is "unlike anything we’ve done before" – so further surprises are likely in store, even if I’d still wager that most of them involve needle violence. More fundamentally, Sea of Sorrow does look considerably larger in scope than any of Hollow Knight’s freebie DLCs, which at most – Godhome, basically – added a small handful of new locations and a smattering of boss challenges. Silksong’s first expansion appears to be showing off multiple new regions, legions of new enemy types, extra traversal mechanics, and that most desired of prizes among soulslike and soulslike-adjacent fans: untold lore.
And it’s out in two weeks? Time to get back in the water.

title: Keep the lighthouse on and the villagers obedient in Glagstone, an eerie island city-builder with Macintosh-style graphics
content_text:
Keep the lighthouse on and the villagers obedient in Glagstone, an eerie island city-builder with Macintosh-style graphics
Now coming to Steam, following a Playdate prototype
Glagstone's "1-bit" aesthetic is a homage to Macintosh games of the late 1980s, cut with elements of art deco, Expressionism and film noir, but it looks like that mainly because it began life on lo-fi indie handheld Playdate.
In transplanting this eerie, story-driven city-builder to Steam, developers Valerii Krasnoselskii and Evgenii Kirichenko have fleshed out the tasty throwback art and shored up connections between the game's management and story layers, while leaving the crux of the experience untouched: you are the newly appointed governor of a remote northern island, contested by rival nations. You have come here to harvest the island's rich mineral resources, and now, the island is trying to drive you nuts.
You start by building homes and roads, getting fish to the warehouse, and churning out coal for the Crown. You'll also need to get the local lighthouse operational, so that you can see the city you're maintaining amid recurring fog, storms and darkness.
According to the devs, who've written a longer account of their project for 80.lv, it's supposed to feel like a simple sandbox, at first. But it has a creeping undertow. Visiting ships bring both opportunity and peril – admitting them to port is a gamble. The coastline is worryingly indefinite, in ways that can't quite be attributed to the tides. The locals are secretive, demanding and a little sinister. They talk of strange masked rituals, Silver Ladies, Shed Skins, and coves where you don't go during an eclipse. The Crown's orders, meanwhile, make less and less sense, and the waves keep coughing up peculiar objects. Sometimes, you could swear you hear singing through the surf.
A lot of the associated Dreadful Lore appears to arrive in the form of notebook marginalia, item descriptions, and sailor anecdotes that need to be coaxed forth with the promise of liquor. There are also pop-up events that may shape the morale and loyalty of your townsfolk. Those masked festivals, for example: they'll cost you production, but the glint in the village elder's eye suggests that refusing to give people time off for the Old Listening might be… reckless.
It all feels like an elaborate port fable from Failbetter's Sunless Sea. Or a standalone episode from fellow "1-bit" coastal sojourn World of Horror. You probably don't need me to tell you that Poe and Lovecraft are among the explicit influences. The developers – who are based in Belgrade and Basel - have also taken inspiration from the Svalbard and Novaya Zemlya archipelagoes. I've just googled Svalbard. It has very pretty reindeer. Haven't dug up any reports of kraken and mermaids just yet, but I'm sure they're out there.
Glagstone is coming to PC next year. Catch it on Steam - they're accepting playtest requests. Speaking as a fan of impenetrable marine murk, I think this looks wonderful. The 80.lv piece is worth reading through, however self-promotional - it includes some savoury titbits on how they've modelled the play of radiance between lighthouse beam and roadside lantern. Did you try the Playdate original? Any comments?

clean_title: The Story So Far
feed_title: Show HN: I restored Palm's last device, and brought its OS to other platforms
title: The Story So Far
content_text:
In socializing recent innovations for the platform, I began to realize that there are people out there who don’t really know what webOS was. I guess I’ve lived with it so long that it never occurred to me that the rest of the world has moved on. While I had intended to write a post about the future for the platform, maybe a little primer on the past is in order – for the more casual explorer…
Long before the iPhone, the Palm Pilot was the “it” gadget that everyone wanted to have. Palm’s own OS made these devices useful and responsive, but by 2004, both the company and its platform were in a tough place. Efforts began to re-imagine both, and a completely new “web OS” was created to be contemporary of the original iPhone.
Under Apple alum Jon Rubinstein , Palm attracted some of the best designers and developers (many even from Apple), to create a fluid and beautiful new experience on limited hardware, by leveraging open technologies, like Linux, WebKit and JavaScript. The original Palm Pre, with its slide-out keyboard, was followed up by the Pre 2 and Pixi while they were still Palm, but the valiant efforts of the team were not enough to take on Google and Apple. They needed a new owner, with a bigger wallet.
HP decided they wanted to be that owner, and acqui-hired the Palm team . Work resumed on the diminutive Veer slide-out, the impressive Pre3, and the TouchPad tablet line under HP’s brand. The leadership promised webOS everywhere, and it looked like there might be a chance. The TouchPad launched against the iPad, with an updated version of webOS, innovative features that wouldn’t be copied by others for years, and a small but useful App Catalog… and then disaster struck.
HP had a leadership change, and foolishly decided to write off the Palm purchase . The dev team worked quickly to spin off a fully Open Source derivative, Open webOS , and accelerated efforts to make the SDK libraries usable cross-platform. The TouchPad went on fire sale , and most of the Pre3s never made it to market. The little group of innovators who dared to take on the Apple/Google Duopoly were defeated.
LG bought what was left of the commercial OS, and moved quickly to make it the platform for their Smart TVs. Other experiments, including a Smart Watch, only briefly glimpsed daylight. The Palm brand moved to TCL, and HP moved on to selling crappy Android and Windows 8 tablets. It seemed like the end…
But the famously active and dedicated Community weren’t willing to give up. webOS had been defined by Homebrew and the hacker ethos . Community members archived as much of the App Catalog as they could salvage before it was shut off. Open webOS was promptly picked up and became LuneOS – a community re-write that worked on the TouchPad and could be ported to other hardware. The TouchPad itself got some updates through Luna Community Edition, providing launcher features Palm never got to deliver.
Over the ensuing decade, though, the small contributions of the community were not enough to fight back the tide of progress. The ancient Linux kernel, WebKit and OpenSSH stacks became a challenge for the modern web. Previously open APIs that enabled apps and features got closed off as Meta and Google consolidated their iron-fisted control over our screen time. And app devs moved on to more profitable platforms.
In 2018, shortly before the world got shut down by Covid, I started work on restoring the SDK . I liked the fact that my TouchPad and Pre3 couldn’t do much – that meant Google wasn’t tracking my every move. It became a challenge to find a way to proxy, re-route, or update calls so I could keep apps alive, or restore them to functionality.
Community members with app archives, and a partially implemented App Museum, were quick to engage in my novice efforts, and work began in earnest to restore what we could. Coordinating on the (now dead, but archived) forums , and in occasional Zoom meetings, we collected our preserved bits into the “webOS Archive.” A new version of the App Museum made downloads “just work”, and I poured over repositories and zip files and questionable MegaUpload links to link together binaries with their scraped meta data.
Then a respiratory virus locked us all indoors, and I really started coding. Publishing as either webOS Archive (for platform-wide features) or codepoet (for hacks and restorations), I began building new functionality again. With a working app delivery mechanism, we started to get an idea of how many people were interested. I committed to making sure the platform was never as creepy as Google or Meta, but anonymous stats, opt-in features, and self-identifying users on our Discord server, gave us a picture of a small, but very real community still using their devices.
Still, it was a tough road. The move to TLS 1.3 increasingly made it difficult to do anything online, and while I hosted a SSL-bump proxy that made anonymous access possible (but insecure), actually logging-in to anything was also limited by so called “modern sign-in” like OAuth2 flows, that couldn’t render in the ancient browser. By 2024, I was about to give up…
Then two things happened, almost at once:
- Out of the LuneOS effort, long-time community member Herrie gave us an OpenSSH update.
- AI assisted coding got good – and it had in its training data all the documentation I’d built and restored for the platform.
There’s lots bad to be said about AI, and in my personal life, I’m conflicted about it. But the fact that Claude knows my passion project as well as I do has been an incredible accelerator. A decades worth of ideas started coming together in weeks or even days. The foundation we’d preserved, and the tools we’d put together, made it possible to do new things with our 15-year old platform.
While Palm’s phones died a different death with the 3G shut downs, WiFi-enabled devices, and particularly the TouchPad – which was remarkably powerful for its time – sprung back to life, as problems were knocked down one-by-one.
The Pre3 got a modernization suite that largely brought its original functionality (sans the mobile carriers) back online. The TouchPad got all that and more. This past summer I released webOS Community Edition 3.1.0 , replacing HP’s final system image (usually 3.0.5) with a firmware bundle including all of the Community’s additions, updates and fixes. Using that as a foundation, I started work on the last still-broken piece: the update server.
With Claude’s help, we reverse-engineered the signed and secure communication between the device and Palm/HP’s servers. A new key, included in 3.1.0, made sure that TouchPad’s would trust community server’s instead, and the new OS baseline made it possible to compute a delta update between the initial release and a bundle of updates.
webOS Community Edition 3.2.0 is available as flashable firmware OR as an Over the Air Update to TouchPad users running 3.1.0. Every non-commercial part of the platform has an open source, community run equivalent. webOS, as originally envisioned by Palm, lives on!
But even with bit-rot addressed through community software. The reality remains that the TouchPad, while the last and best Palm device, is showing its age. The CPU is slow, the RAM ceiling low, and the WiFi chip can’t connect to WiFi 6 and newer, faster networks. We need a way to run webOS on other hardware.
Lunacy for Android , and LuneOS from webOS Ports, are that way forward. In Part 2, I’ll talk more about how the community can engage in those efforts…

clean_title: Don't expect a GTA set outside the USA anytime soon, as Rockstar has "not had a lot of conversations over doing it anywhere else"
feed_title: Don't expect a GTA set outside the USA anytime soon, as Rockstar has "not had a lot of conversations over doing it anywhere else"
title: Don't expect a GTA set outside the USA anytime soon, as Rockstar has "not had a lot of conversations over doing it anywhere else"
content_text:
Don't expect a GTA set outside the USA anytime soon, as Rockstar has "not had a lot of conversations over doing it anywhere else"
"There never ceases to be a more interesting place."
Would Rockstar really set a future Grand Theft Auto game outside of the United States? The concept's been mooted recently, particularly in reporting on a recent Rockstar interview with The Guardian, where co-studio head Rob Nelson quipped: "Never say never." But speaking to Eurogamer in another interview since then, I would say it's unlikely.
During our conversation, I asked Nelson about the choice of the US as an ongoing setting for the games, and what in particular drove Rockstar's continuing infatuation with the country across both GTA and Red Dead Redemption.
"I don't know," Nelson said initially. "It's just that there never ceases to be a more interesting place to think about setting it. I just think that it's constantly changing, there's constantly stuff for us to respond to, and it works from a gameplay standpoint in terms of what we want to do."
A little more conclusively, he added: "We have not had a lot of conversations over doing it anywhere else."
That doesn't quite settle it for good, of course. Nelson's "never say never" comments still stand, but coupled with his follow-up response to The Guardian, where he noted "there's still so much to do in America," it seems we can pretty confidently pin the next GTA's location as somewhere, once again, within the United States.
I also wouldn't be surprised if there were early ideas as to where exactly within the US the next GTA might end up. The decision on Florida was one of the earliest Rockstar made this time, for instance. As Nelson explained to me, with GTA 6: "You first decide on place, for GTA – where are we going to set it?"
That was "quick", this time, he noted. "We had three major cities established, this was the one that we hadn't been back to recently. It's also felt [amongst the team]: if you want to reflect something about contemporary America, Florida is a pretty good place to give you a wide range of craziness, and sort of variety in terms of experience."
That then led to early research trips to Florida, Nelson explained, which in turn informed the game's characters and mechanics – including the more interactive, thoughtful, empathetic world Nelson also explained to me, and the decision around the big character moment in the early minutes of the game's prologue.
For much more on GTA 6's setting, meanwhile, our full GTA 6 map and extensive GTA 6 walkthrough might come in handy. And all this said, frankly, I'm more than happy to stay here in Leonida for some time - as was probably made quite clear in our five-star GTA 6 review.

clean_title: Court of Appeal rejects Audi’s call for Tsunoda penalty in Italian Grand Prix
feed_title: Court of Appeal rejects Audi’s call for Tsunoda penalty in Italian Grand Prix | Formula 1
title: Court of Appeal rejects Audi’s call for Tsunoda penalty in Italian Grand Prix
content_text:
The International Court of Appeal has rejected Audi’s attempt to have a penalty applied to Yuki Tsunoda in the Italian Grand Prix.
Audi argued the Racing Bulls driver should have received a stop-and-go penalty for causing an aborted start.The ICA upheld the stewards’ decision not to penalise Tsunoda.
Audi brought the case after Gabriel Bortoleto finished 11th behind Tsunoda in the Italian Grand Prix. The original start of the race was abandoned and an extra formation lap ordered by the race director and the stewards noted Tsunoda had not lined up in his grid box correctly.
However the stewards ruled Tsunoda’s position in his grid box was not the cause of the extra formation lap, meaning he should not receive a penalty. Audi contested the decision and Bortoleto said they had a “straightforward” case against the Racing Bulls driver.
The FIA is yet to issue the full reasoning for the ICA’s decision to uphold the stewards’ original decision.
Tsunoda made the second of his three appearances for Racing Bulls at the Italian Grand Prix. His 10th place finish was the only point he scored during his stint substituting for Liam Lawson.
Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and
This is the second decision by the ICA concerned a grand prix this year. In September the ICA overturned a decision by the stewards of the Monaco Grand Prix and re-applied two penalties to Pierre Gasly, dropping him from third place to seventh.
FIA statement on ICA’s decision
The following hearing of the International Court of Appeal took place on 25 November 2026 in Paris:
Hearing
A Case ICA-2016-14: Appeal lodged by Audi Revolut F1 Team against Decision No. 69 of the Stewards of the 2026 Italian Grand Prix, dated 6 September 2026, counting towards the 2026 FIA Formula One World Championship.
On 6 September 2026, at the end of the formation lap during the race restart following a red flag, the Race Director ordered an additional formation lap.
Following the race, the Stewards investigated a potential breach of Article B5.9.4 of the 2026 FIA Formula 1 Sporting Regulations by Mr Yuki Tsunoda (Driver of Car No. 22), which requires any driver who caused an extra formation lap to start from the end of the pit lane. Failure to do so, a Stop-and-Go penalty should be imposed on the Driver. In Decision No. 69, the Stewards decided to take no further action against Mr Yuki Tsunoda.
On 9 September 2026, Audi Revolut F1 Team lodged an appeal against that decision, arguing that Mr Yuki Tsunoda had caused the extra formation lap and should therefore have received the prescribed Stop-and-Go penalty.
Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and
Decision of the International Court of Appeal
The Court, after having heard the parties and examined their submissions, decided to:
– declare the appeal admissible;
– dismiss the appeal on the merits;
– uphold the Decision No. 69 of the Stewards of the 2026 Italian Grand Prix, dated 6 September 2026, counting towards the 2026 FIA Formula One World Championship;
– and order the competent Sporting Authority to draw, as appropriate, the consequences of this ruling.
The International Court of Appeal was presided over by Mr Laurent Anselmi (Monaco), and included, Mr Mark Kletter (Austria), Mr Philip Moser (United Kingdom) and Mr Laurent Nuss (France).
The full decision will be available at a later date.

title: Social Media: Alonso pays tribute to retiring Moto GP champion Marquez
content_text:
Fernando Alonso paid tribute to Moto GP champion Marc Marques, who has announced he will retire from the series at the end of this weekend.
Marquez, 33, won the world championship for this eighth time in his career this year. This weekend’s race in Valencia will be his final appearance.
“One of the things I’ve enjoyed most about watching you race is that I never knew what you were going to do,” said Alonso in a post on social media. “Even when it seemed like the race was already decided, I’d still keep watching to see what you’d do!
“It’s going to be hard to get used to Sundays without that. I’m so lucky to have seen you race, Marc. Thanks for everything, and enjoy this next chapter! Thanks a million!”

clean_title: Rumored The Simpsons: Hit & Run remake might be in trouble as a New Radical Games developer says their "mind-blowingly awesome" project has been cancelled
feed_title: Rumored The Simpsons: Hit & Run remake may be in trouble after one developer says their "mind-blowingly awesome" project is cancelled
title: Rumored The Simpsons: Hit & Run remake might be in trouble as a New Radical Games developer says their "mind-blowingly awesome" project has been cancelled
content_text:
Rumored The Simpsons: Hit & Run remake may be in trouble after one developer says their "mind-blowingly awesome" project is cancelled
I'm Groening.
A rumored remake of The Simpsons: Hit & Run (the internet's most-wanted video game revival) may be in trouble.
Just earlier this year, Radical Entertainment made somewhat of a comeback as New Radical Games - with the original studio's co-founder (Ian Wilkinson) and former developer (Tim Bennison) serving as New Radical's CEO and COO, respectively. The company best known for Prototype and the well-remembered open-world Simpsons game was back, in some sense.
Whatever project the studio was cooking hasn't been so lucky, it seems. New Radical Games senior game designer Darren Evenson recently said an upcoming project at the company had been scrapped, and he's now looking for new work, per a LinkedIn post.
"It seems that not even a fantastic project with an absolutely incredible team is immune from the current state of the industry right now, as what we were working on at New Radical Games (although mind-blowingly awesome) was part of a whole gaggle of cancellations," Evenson wrote. "A gaggle, I say!"
"Oh, you silly suits with spreadsheets... will you EVER learn? If you don't make the game, you can't make the money... and if you don't make the money, then you don't get the power... and... well, there's more to that quote, but I digress."
"For the first time in my career, I am Available For Work and looking for a new exciting opportunity where I can make some fun games with some great people," he added. "Please reach out, shout out, or perform some interpretive dance if you know of an opportunity that a hip cat like me could groove to."
New Radical Games has never formally revealed its plans, but a couple clues pointed to something Simpsons-shaped. As VGC noted, Evenson's statement echoes a few popular lines from the iconic animated sitcom. "Will you ever learn" is suspiciously close to a particular Troy McClure quote, for one.
Then there's seemingly a Scarface riff in the developer's statement - one that was also parodied in The Simpsons, of course: "In America, first you get the sugar, then you get the power, then you get the women." It's worth noting Radical Entertainment did also make Scarface: The World Is Yours, so this one could go either way.
But the most eyebrow-raising clue came from original Simpsons co-showrunner and creator Matt Groening. During a Disney D23 panel this summer, Groening and current showrunner Matt Selman were asked about the possibility of a Hit & Run comeback.
"I don't know [if] I'm speaking out of turn, I think the original game is coming back in some form," Groening said at the time, before Selman quickly chimed in: "Or not…"
"Hit & Run is so interesting. I'm a thousand years old, and when I was in my mid to late 20s, I helped write Hit & Run," Selman said back in March. "I had no idea it would become a cult game, a cult success. Of all the games, the thousands of Simpsons games... that one..."

clean_title: Antonelli leads another Mercedes one-two despite red flag interruptions
feed_title: Antonelli leads another Mercedes one-two despite red flag interruptions | Formula 1
title: Antonelli leads another Mercedes one-two despite red flag interruptions
content_text:
For the second practice session in a row, Andrea Kimi Antonelli topped the times despite setting his best lap on the mediums compound tyres.
He and several of his rivals had to abandon their flying laps on soft rubber due to a pair of red flags.
Antonelli exchanged quickest times with team mate George Russell early in the session on the medium tyre compound. He set his quickest time on 1’23.077 on his seventh lap.
The Red Bull drivers were unable to improve their times when they switched to the soft rubber. The McLaren pair did lap quicker but were unable to beat the two Mercedes drivers.
Russell began his first run on the soft rubber strongly, setting the quickest times through the first two seconds. As he approached the final corner he looked set to take the fastest time, but he had to back off as race control threw a red flag.
The session was interrupted to allow marshals to clear away gravel and a piece of debris left when Charles Leclerc had a dramatic spin at turn seven. That forced the Ferrari driver to pit for floor repairs.
Soon after the session restart, Antonelli took to the track on a set of soft tyres. But in a repeat of what happened to his team mate, the red flags flew as he neared the end of his lap.
This time Pierre Gasly was responsible. The Alpine driver dropped his left-hand wheels into the gravel at the exit of turn 14 and lost control, spinning into a gravel trap from which he never emerged.
That put paid to Antonelli’s hopes of improving his lap time, but nor was any other driver able to do better. He therefore ended the session on top, followed by his team mate and the two McLarens.
Max Verstappen, fifth fastest, was unimpressed to be overtaken by Lewis Hamilton as he began one lap. “You saw that under braking?” he asked his team. “My God.” Verstappen had overtaken Hamilton approaching the finishing line moments earlier. The stewards chose not to investigate the incident.
Hamilton ended the session eighth-fastest behind his team mate. However the Ferrari driver suffered a power unit problem shortly before the chequered flag appeared.
The two Racing Bull drivers made it five consecutive pairs of team mates in the top 10, Liam Lawson ahead of Arvid Lindblad.
Despite his spin, Gasly set the 12th fastest time behind Gabriel Bortoleto. Franco Colapinto took 15th after a near-missed with Carlos Sainz Jnr at turn one.

clean_title: Rumoured Simpsons: Hit & Run remake could be dead in the water, as New Radical Games devs suggest their unannounced game's been cancelled
feed_title: Rumoured Simpsons: Hit & Run remake could be dead in the water, as New Radical Games devs suggest their unannounced game's been cancelled
title: Rumoured Simpsons: Hit & Run remake could be dead in the water, as New Radical Games devs suggest their unannounced game's been cancelled
content_text:
Rumoured Simpsons: Hit & Run remake could be dead in the water, as New Radical Games devs suggest their unannounced game's been cancelled
Simpsons creator Matt Groening appeared to lend credence this summer to chatter about a potential return for Hit and Run
Earlier this year, New Radical Games rocked up on the scene. A successor to Simpsons: Hit & Run and Prototype studio Radical Entertainment, with original Radical co-founder Ian Wilkinson as CEO, New Radical looked to be trying to trade on some of that pedigree. So, naturally, when Simpsons creator Matt Groening seemed to indicate during a panel that Hit & Run could be making some sort of return, remake speculation began churning. Sadly, whatever New Radical were working on, it looks like that game's been cancelled.
A couple of New Radical developers have put up similar LinkedIn posts about needing to look for new work over the past week. "It seems that not even a fantastic project with an absolutely incredible team is immune from the current state of the industry right now, as what we were working on at New Radical Games (although mind-blowingly awesome) was part of a whole gaggle of cancellations," senior game designer Darren Evenson wrote. "A gaggle, I say!
"Oh, you silly suits with spreadsheets... will you EVER learn? If you don't make the game, you can't make the money... and if you don't make the money, then you don't get the power... and... well, there's more to that quote, but I digress."
"Alongside other projects, I'm sad to say our project was cancelled by the Publisher this week," fellow New Radical senior game designer Bob Churchill wrote in his own post a few days earlier than Evenson. "A huge shout out to everyone at New Radical Games. What we achieved in those four months was nothing short of amazing. I wish everyone could see it."
The comment from Groening which seemed to hint at Hit & Run making a return was made during the Disney fan convention D23 in August (thanks, VGC). "I think the original game is coming back in some form," he said, prompting current Simpsons showrunner Matt Selman to go into what seems like 'Ah bollocks, better sarkily suggest we didn't just let that slip' mode.
Assuming the right deals could feasibly be made to render it possible, a Hit & Run remake would seem like an obvious opportunity to rake in a tonne of nostalgia bank, given how many folks my age and older have fond memories of running around Springfield in it. The Simpsons' relatively recent cameos in Fortnite also seem to have gone down pretty well, suggesting the very long-running series isn't something the kids of today turn their noses up at.
Whatever these New Radical Games devs were working on, hopefully they're able to land on their feet in new work soon.

title: After drawing ire for selling new Mass Effect merch following BioWare closure, EA is now flogging new Dragon Age tat too
content_text:
After drawing ire for selling new Mass Effect merch following BioWare closure, EA is now flogging new Dragon Age tat too
Nevarra dull moment.
Seemingly unperturbed by the criticism it faced after selling new Mass Effect merchandise following the shock closure of developer BioWare, EA is now flogging new merchandise for the studio's other big series, Dragon Age.
EA's decision to close BioWare and cancel the long-awaited Mass Effect 5 in October was met with shock and condemnation from fans and games industry veterans alike. Legendary designer Warren Spector slammed the closure, and fan efforts to save the studio - including calls of support from Mass Effect voice acting talent - have continued in the aftermath.
EA, apparently aware of the potentially poor optics, quickly scrubbed a number of Mass Effect-themed cosmetics from Battlefield, but eyebrows were raised when, just weeks later, new Mass Effect merchandise - including a $175 wearable LED helmet - was released onto its BioWare Gear store on 'N7' day, the annual celebration of BioWare's space series. Unsurprisingly, more criticism followed. As one fan put it at the time, "This is such a bad look".
And now here we are again. EA'S BioWare Gear store has sprung to life once more, this time (thanks IGN) to promote a new "Seven Swords of Nightmare" hoodie inspired by BioWare's Dragon Age: Inquisition.
"Unless you reopen BioWare, EA, then no money for you," one person wrote in a social media response indicative of the general sentiment from others. Some users also used the opportunity to share the #savemasseffect hashtag beneath the BioWare Gear post - a related community initiative has so far seen over 330,000 fans sign a petition to save the series.
The community has been energised by glimpses of what could have been following Mass Effect 5's cancellation. At one point, a flashy internal trailer appeared online, and award-winning composer Austin Wintory also shared music he'd pitched for the game. Elsewhere, content creators claiming to have seen a work-in-progress version of Mass Effect 5 have called it "incredible" and claimed it would have drawn lessons from The Witcher and Baldur's Gate 3.
BioWare's closure in October came as part of the first round of layoffs at EA since the publisher's $55bn acquisition by a consortium including Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, investment firm Silver Lake, and private equity company Affinity Partners earlier this year. The move resulted in the loss of 400 jobs, with layoffs occurring across multiple studios, including Apex Legends developer Respawn, The Sims studio Maxis, and EA Motive.

clean_title: "We just wanted to provide some clarity" - Yooka-Laylee studio explains upcoming Definitive Edition's absence on Xbox to 'frustrated' fans
feed_title: Yooka-Laylee studio explains upcoming Definitive Edition's absence on Xbox to 'frustrated' fans
title: "We just wanted to provide some clarity" - Yooka-Laylee studio explains upcoming Definitive Edition's absence on Xbox to 'frustrated' fans
content_text:
Yooka-Laylee studio explains upcoming Definitive Edition's absence on Xbox to 'frustrated' fans
"As a small team, we hope you guys can understand the challenges we face."
Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair: Definitive Edition is notably skipping Xbox Series X/S consoles, and the studio blames "technical challenges and costs."
The Definitive Edition is bringing support for 120fps, revamping the platformer's lighting, updating textures and shadows, and packaging in the Trowzer's Top Tonic Pack DLC next month. But a large question mark hung over the lack of an Xbox version.
"Hi folks, just wanted to say a massive thanks to everyone on here for the support for Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair: Definitive Edition. The response has BEE-n incredible, and we can't wait for you to experience the game all over again on December 15th," developer Playtonic Games said in a new social media post.
"We are aware of feedback regarding the lack of Xbox Series S/X support, and we just wanted to provide some clarity on the reasoning behind this decision. Bringing Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair: Definitive Edition to PlayStation 5 and Nintendo Switch 2 has been an exciting adventure… Unfortunately, we've had to prioritise our efforts given the technical challenges and costs presented in the creation of this updated version of the game and as a result, we are unable to commit to any additional platforms for the foreseeable future," it continued.
Playtonic said it understood Xbox players' frustrations, but the development costs associated with bringing the game to more platforms "just isn't viable for us at this time." Playtonic is still an independent game studio, after all, and Xbox console sales have been lagging behind the competition for quite a while.
"As a small team, we hope you guys can understand the challenges we face. Please know that this wasn't an easy decision to make, and we apologise to any of you affected by this. We only wish things were different, and we value every single one of you and your feedback," the statement went on.
Digital Foundry's John Linneman chimed in to tell folks that the omissions isn't a huge deal, because Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair already looks pretty great on Xbox consoles. "The Xbox One X version of this game is already native 4K," he tweeted. "The upgrade seems minor, thus it's already excellent on Xbox. Was the best console version by far."
The original Yooka-Laylee was a collectathon throwback in the same vein as Banjo-Kazooie, but this follow-up took more inspiration from Rare's Donkey Kong Country games instead - and the results were pretty stunning.
"It's the new in Impossible Lair which impresses, the tightness of the game's 2D controls and intricately designed levels which stands out, and which seems better fitted to Playtonic's toolbox," Eurogamer's review said. "It's a far more polished game than the studio's predecessor, and one well worth exploring through."

title: “Not worth thinking about” being able to beat Mercedes even with new floor – Norris
content_text:
Lando Norris says Mercedes are too quick for McLaren to be able to compete with them in this weekend’s Qatar Grand Prix.
Andrea Kimi Antonelli lapped four tenths of a second faster than Norris in second practice. However Antonelli set his quickest time on the medium compound tyres and had to abandon his later lap on the softs.Norris says McLaren are in good shape compared to the rest of the competition but Mercedes are comfortably ahead of the field.
“It depends how you want to look at it,” he said. “I don’t think we’re too bad relative to most, but to Mercedes, I don’t think we’ve been further off.
“They just seem in a different category comparing to us today. Quicker in every single corner by a mile.
“I would say the battle’s for [third] and we seem in relatively decent position. We seem similar in pace to Red Bull and similar-ish to Ferrari. So I would say there’s things we need to improve and things that can certainly be better but I guess you always look to the top. So when you look at ourselves comparing to to the Mercedes we need to improve a lot everywhere.”
McLaren did not run their latest floor specification in practice due to concerns over potentially damaging it on Losail’s punishing kerbs. But Norris doubts they will be significantly closer to Mercedes when they fit the new floor again tomorrow.

clean_title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
feed_title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
content_text:
Hi HN!
I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious.
So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves.
I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging (https://declarative-dragging.github.io/) on the front page of HN and the spark came back!
It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions.
A few more points: - There are no ads, no trackers, no accounts (it's a static website and progress is saved in the browser cache). - Teachers can create their own problem sets, encoded in the link. - I plan to add more chapters (trigonometry, complex numbers, some calculus) but I first need to figure out the 'right' mode of interaction. - I just started working on the experience from mobile, so there may still be some rough edges there
I'm curious to know what you think, if you have suggestions for content, if you spot anything that I should fix, if you have feature requests! Thank you in advance

clean_title: Rayshader 1.0: Exit the Matrix
feed_title: Rayshader 1.0: Exit the Matrix
title: Rayshader 1.0: Exit the Matrix
content_text:
Be sure to read to the end for what I can guarantee is the most exciting and cinematric R package bibliography you’ve ever seen. Everything you see in the below blog post was rendered in R with the rayverse.
Eight years ago, rayshader started as a small experiment in making beautiful maps in R. The first version was based on a simple question: what if we combined raytracing and cartography? I had always been interested in learning both about mapping and pathtracing, and what better way than to combine the two ideas into a single R package? The big “aha!” moment came when I applied that method with interactive 3D terrain for the first time and took it for a spin.
The surface was no longer just a shaded map: it felt tangible and real, a 3D rectangle twirling like a Little Debbie cosmic brownie on a microwave turntable. The combination of cartographic hillshading and 3D raytraced terrain looked spectacular in a way that, at the time, mostly lived in bespoke Blender scenes or other advanced 3D modeling tools. And unlike Blender, you didn’t need to learn a whole new ecosystem to visualize your data in 3D: it lived in the same place your data did (R!), which allowed for a gentler learning curve.
But as time went on and the package and userbase expanded, I had a nagging feeling: rayshader was still too hard.
Not always, of course: plenty of people were using it, quite effectively. Simple use cases were fine: pass in a matrix, add a few layers, call plot_3d(), and suddenly you had a cool-looking 3D landscape. If that’s all you needed: great! But if the story you were trying to tell was about data within the landscape–well, that’s where the friction began to burn.
Beauty is table stakes
I built rayshader for people who wanted to make data beautiful without leaving R. Beauty has a real purpose in the world: it draws people’s eyes. It doesn’t matter how accurate or well-constructed your map is if the reader swipes on by: in the market for human attention, beauty and form are table stakes.
Journalists understood that quickly, and were some of rayshader’s earliest adopters.
The Wall Street Journal’s The Future of Arctic Shipping used detailed shipping, bathymetric, and ice coverage data to explain the complexities of the Northern Sea Route. The piece was recognized by the Information is Beautiful Awards, which described it as a deeply researched story built from shipping, bathymetric, and ice coverage data. It appeared only a few months after I released rayshader: talk about an introduction! Bloomberg’s 2024 Gaza rebuilding story, Gaza Reduced to 42 Million Tonnes of Rubble. What Will It Take to Rebuild?, used R, rayshader, and rayrender as part of the visual system for communicating the scale of destruction and debris in Gaza. And in June 2022, a rayshader 3D flood visualization appeared on the front page of The Sydney Morning Herald, inset into coverage of the Lismore flooding.
That last one stuck with me (and not only because a rayshader map was featured “above the fold” in a major newspaper!). Rayshader had started as a way to make beautiful data visualizations in R, but here it was being used in deadline journalism to help explain a disaster to a general audience. The package had left the domain of “fun engaging social media posts” and entered the visual language of public-interest reporting.
But getting a reader to stop scrolling is only half the problem. Working with journalists taught me how much friction stood between having the data and making the final product. A newsroom deadline is a very good detector of bad API design. If adding buildings takes half a day of coordinate fiddling, that feature might as well not exist. If a 3D path requires a hand-rolled coordinate transform pipeline, nobody is doing that 30 minutes before a deadline. If a pathtraced render looks great but takes too long to converge, it is not going to make it to print. Especially if the editor needs a slight tweak: “Oh, sure–just give me 8 hours to re-render the animation.” Ha. Nope.
Working with journalists taught me how much friction stood between having the data and making the final product.
The problem wasn’t so much with rayshader itself: it was how much spatial bookkeeping and manual fiddling you had to do to get data into rayshader before you could do all the fun stuff. And at the root of all that bookkeeping was the humble matrix, rayshader’s original choice for representing terrain.
The problem with matrices
Rayshader used matrices to represent terrain because it simplified a lot of the work that went into turning a bunch of elevation values in a 3D object. But most real data does not arrive nicely packaged as a plain rectangular numeric array. It arrives as georeferenced rasters, polygons, lines, and points. It arrives cloaked in an unknown coordinate reference system. It arrives in meters, feet, yards, degrees, or German legal metres. Choosing the matrix as the base input made it easy for me, the developer, by putting the spatial problem (mostly) on the user.
Is there an… illegal german metre?
Convert the raster to a matrix. Save the extent. Transform the vector data. Save the CRS. Crop the linework. Pass the heightmap again. Pass the extent again. Wait, is the extent format lat/long/lat/long or lat/lat/long/long? I never remember–whatever, try both. The first choice is (somehow!) always wrong. Pass zscale again. Resize the overlay. Pass the CRS again. Check whether the map is oriented correctly. No? Surprise! Errant minus sign. Yuck.
This was not just annoying for beginners. It annoyed me, and I wrote the damn thing: now that’s a usability red flag! The new version of rayshader includes a series of changes that gets rid of all of this overhead and allows you to focus on presentation instead of the data processing.
rayshader has gained object permanence
The big change in rayshader 1.0 is this: rayshader no longer has short-term amnesia. Rayshader now keeps track of all the spatial details from your underlying map so you don’t have to worry about it any more.
This changes the user experience from:
Transform and pass in your data into an aligned matrix coordinate system, and rayshader will render it in beautiful 3D.
To:
Transform andPass in your datainto an aligned matrix coordinate system,and rayshader will render it in beautiful 3D.
The black diamond learning curve is now a gentle bunny slope. Terrain can stay a spatial raster. Road can stay a spatial line and will automatically be converted to the correct coordinate system when plotting. Buildings can be passed in as spatial polygons and will automatically be cropped to the underlying map’s extent.
A rayshader scene now extracts and caches the important metadata from the input data: heightmap, extent, CRS, zscale, vertical exaggeration, and rendered-object metadata. That cache lets downstream render_*() calls do the thing users always wanted them to do: simply drop data into the scene.
Most of the functions can now add to the scene simply by passing the data, plus an optional argument that specifies altitude or height, either directly or through a column in an sf object. The rest of the arguments then focus on how you want to style the data.
For example, let’s load in some road and elevation data and see what the new API looks like. The code below defines the helpers and loads the data into R. There’s no rayshader in it, so you have absolutely no obligation to read it :).
Transform to a UTM CRS (so everything is in meters)

Pretty straightforward… just kidding, loading geospatial data is always a pain. Nothing I can do about that! But the real question is: how complex is visualizating all this data once it’s loaded?

Not complex at all! You call the function named after the type of data… and it renders the data in the scene. Any additional arguments are just for styling the data to your liking.
And the payoff is not just less typing: it lets us get to the fun part of 3D data visualization faster. The coolest part of rayshader has always been building strikingly beautiful 3D landscapes from your data. But the third dimension raises the cognitive cost of entry: before you can play director and cinematographer, you have to build the set. When every point, path, and polygon needs the user to track the CRS and extent info themselves and transform the data appropriately, many users never get to the stage where they can experiment with lighting and composition, styling the data (costume design!), or focus on editing the overall narrative.
But also, less typing!
The third dimension raises the cognitive cost of entry: before you can play director and cinematographer, you have to build the set.
This release automates almost all of the behind-the-scenes work. The boring parts–CRS juggling, extent passing, heightmap repetition, matrix conversion, and other bookkeeping–stay in the package internals. The user is then free to jump to the enjoyable creative roles: the executive producer of the analysis, the production designer of the world, or the sound designer of a multi-sensory data experience.
Spatial data: free yourself from the matrix!
Rayshader now accepts many more spatial inputs for the heightmap. The plot_3d() function can now accept a heightmap as a matrix, a terra::SpatRaster, a raster object, or a raster filename. When the input is spatial, rayshader extracts and caches the extent and CRS. If zscale is not supplied, rayshader derives it from raster cell resolution. If the raster is geographic longitude/latitude, rayshader estimates the meter-per-cell scale at the raster center. The data was always there; it just had to be piped around to the right place! Now I do the plumbing for you.
Let’s look at an example. The same DEM and main-road data feed both versions below. The difference is who’s now doing the spatial bookkeeping (hint: it’s not you).

Internally, rayshader still converts the raster to something it can render. Externally, the scene remembers enough to let the render_*() functions just work.
There is now also a cleaner division between physical scale and visual exaggeration. zscale now describes the relationship between horizontal and vertical units, while vertical_exaggeration describes the stylistic exaggeration. For spatial rasters, rayshader can derive zscale from the raster itself, placing the data at its physical scale. You can then adjust vertical_exaggeration to emphasize the terrain without changing the underlying unit conversion.
And this spatial data directionality can now be reversed. spatialize_image() turns a rayshader image, matrix, RGB array, or RGBA array back into a georeferenced terra::SpatRaster. It can inherit the cached extent and CRS from the active scene, convert rayshader’s linear color values to sRGB, and optionally append the source heightmap as an additional raster layer. So rayshader’s output can now feed back into other GIS software, rather than just assume rayshader is the final destination itself.

This release lets rayshader fit into a real spatial workflow: spatial input, then rayshader styling, followed by spatial output. So you can generate beautiful hillshades and terrains in R, and then bring them into other spatial software like QGIS or ArcGIS. Work in the GIS interface you already know, render the terrain in R, and drop the result right back into your map.
A watershed moment for rayshader water
Rayshader’s water was always a bit of an afterthought: it was good for rendering an ocean with bathymetry data, but it didn’t really work if the water was localized to one portion of the map. A lake halfway up a mountain shouldn’t require flooding everything below it to see the water, but rayshader’s old water meshing method assumed one water level for the whole map. Which was perfect if all you needed was that one large body of water: set a level and fill the scene to that height. Separate lakes, reservoirs at different elevations, and imperfect shorelines called for something more flexible.
Now water can arrive as a raster or a polygon, high in the mountains or below sea level. render_water() uses the terrain and coordinates already stored in the scene to properly place and render the water in a sane way.
The old single-level behavior remains available as water_render_method = "legacy", as it is much faster and is perfectly suited for coastlines and topobathymetry data.
Water can follow grid cells with water_render_method = "raster" or preserve polygon boundaries with the default, water_render_method = "polygon". Both draw a watertight mesh at the footprint and elevation you supply, even when that means an exposed vertical water wall where the supplied shoreline doesn’t quite meet the terrain. Fast, flexible, and suitable for the rare case where you need to visualize Moses crossing the Red Sea.
Another (much cooler, IMO) option is water_render_method = "optimized". It fits a closed shoreline to the actual 3D terrain mesh, adjusting the water elevation to match the supplied area. Using the elevations beneath your water footprint to seed candidate levels, the optimizer searches for a contour that comes as close as possible to the supplied water area without spilling out of the terrain. The animation below shows how candidate levels change the flooded area.
If no closed water body is possible—for example, the supplied water would flood the entire map—rayshader falls back to raster water.
A different problem arises when a DEM has no bathymetry: the lake bed and its surface occupy the same plane. shift_terrain() is a new function that can lower the terrain beneath a lake polygon before you add water, making room for the lake instead of letting the surfaces overlap. It can also raise terrain SimCity 2000-style (no tornados or alien invasions… yet).
Additionally, in render_highquality(), water can now use a rough dielectric material to spread reflections into the broad highlights you expect from a rippled lake. A perfectly smooth dielectric surface behaves like glass: reflected light stays coherent, so lakes and rivers can turn into polished sheets. Real water has small wind-driven ripples, each reflecting light in a slightly different direction. The microfacet material models this give a more realistic appearance to bodies of water, especially when viewed at a low angle.
Rayshader: now streaming!
Streams need to follow the terrain as they wind downhill. render_streams() takes spatial line data, samples the elevation along each path, and builds ribbons of water that hug the surface. Widths can vary by feature, and connected streams can be merged to reduce visible seams in high-quality renders. Put those streams together with lakes and you have a hydrologic scene driven by data.
Load and prepare Mono County terrain, lakes, and streams
Note that there’s no complex GIS concepts on the rayshader side: all the complexity is related to defining the visual style and appearance. As it should be–rayshader is a visualization package! The remaining complexity is just standard data complexity present in any analysis: get the data loaded, cleaned, and in a form that represents the thing you care about.
The road to believable roads
3D maps might seem like a fun little toy rather than a serious class of data visualization, but the third dimension is often surprisingly important for understanding geospatial data. This becomes less surprising when you realize that the most common mapping tool used by regular people–GPS apps–use 3D quite extensively. When you’re traveling through a city, buildings give you landmarks to match to your surroundings; on a walking or cycling route, the terrain shows where you’ll be climbing; and at a complex highway interchange, seeing which roads pass over one another helps you follow the right ramp and choose the right exit.
I already had surface-hugging polygons working for streams. Swap the water for asphalt and there’s a road! Easy, peasy, right?
No! What’s the issue? We’re spoiled with our GPS apps: we’re used to roads looking like roads. A strip of grey asphalt needs lane markings for someone to know it’s a road. With the help of some fun repeating UV coordinate tricks and our new spatial-first workflow, we can paint properly-sized lines on the road at the cost of a few small textures. And we can use the lane counts supplied in OpenStreetMap data to add the correct number of lanes to each road. Rayshader uses those counts to mesh and texture the road, while the scene’s spatial information keeps the markings correctly sized.
In Figure 11, each dash is 10 feet long and each gap is 30 feet. Those familiar markings do double duty: they improve the picture and act as little scale bars scattered through the scene. Beautiful! Pack it up, put a bow on it, and move on to the next feature, right?
The spacing is configurable for local standards.
No! Our roads are still smooshed together on one layer. At an interchange, that borders on uninterpretable.
OpenStreetMap doesn’t provide a full 3D road model. But it does carry one tiny (but extremely useful!) nugget of vertical information needed to draw roads correctly in 2D: drawing order. Draw layer 0, then layer 1, then layer 2, and the right road appears on top. That tells us which road crosses over which; it doesn’t tell us their heights or how the ramps return to ground level. Is this enough information to fully reconstruct our 3D roads?
The tempting shortcut is to turn each layer into a fixed height: find the crossings, lift each road by a standard overpass height, and ease it back toward the ground with some sort of ad hoc relaxation rule. What could go wrong?
Everything. Everything can go wrong.
Simple hacks? Don’t work here. Turns out the world is filled with little annoying complications like a bridge crossing a sunken highway (the highway is already below ground, so the bridge needs no change in elevation), or short segments in interchanges that are technically not stacked but fall between stacked layers, or places where the road is technically stacked over a traversable water body (which also counts as a layer!), or a thousand other pesky little details.
What are we to do then? How can we implement realistic highways? It’s not like there’s a manual with explicit guidance and standards for how roads should be built in 3D—wait, what is that? There is an explicit manual?
Figure 14: AASHTO’s A Policy on Design Standards—Interstate System
The American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO) has a design manual for Interstate highways. Two of the things it covers are exactly what our map is missing. How much room does a truck need under a bridge? How steep can the road get on its way up there? Now that rayshader knows the scale of the scene, I can give the solver a clearance in feet and a maximum grade in percent. Here are the default settings I gave the road solver (these are customizable):
Keeping crossing road surfaces at least 14 feet apart
Limiting the road grade to 7%
Ensuring roads default to hugging the ground when not part of an intersection and do not rise unnecessarily
We can turn these requirements into constraints on the road heights. While the rules aren’t guaranteed to generate roads that match the real-world roads exactly, it’s going to be pretty close: excursions from the bare minimum allowable ruleset will usually only increase cost, and we’re talking government contracts here. Around each interchange, we discretize the roads into short segments and solve for their elevations together: maintain the crossing order and clearance, limit the grades, and keep the roads close to the terrain wherever possible.
It’s not like there’s a manual with explicit guidance and standards for how roads should be built in 3D—wait, what is that? There is an explicit manual?
For example, a road can weave over and under several others. Lifting one crossing changes the grades leading into the next, so solving each crossing independently won’t work–we have to solve all the linked constraints at once. We build a graph of the road connections with {igraph}, locate crossings with {sf}, and follow the constraints along connected road segments. Each connected optimization region gets a sparse quadratic problem, assembled with {Matrix} and solved with {osqp}. It turns out, R has everything you need to build and optimize road profiles.
Figure 15: Roads at a Bernese Oberland interchange with teal profile control points and orange rings at seven crossing constraints.
It’s pretty cool how closely a set of road-design rules and OSM’s layer ordering can recreate a complex interchange. The layer tags tell us which road goes over which, and the rules guide how the ramps connect them. Here’s Houston, now modeled in a sane way:
Figure 16: Elevated decks separate the crossings, with Houston buildings providing context. Now, the merges still need work, but that’ll have to wait for the next update :)
Beautiful. And since I went to Houston for this year’s Posit::conf, I was able to drive over specific intersections I rendered here and confirm that yes: the roads were accurately meshed. Minus the traffic.

“I know ggplot2.”
The original plot_gg() was based on a simple idea: take a ggplot2 object, turn a fill or color aesthetic into height, and map the original plot onto that extruded surface. This made it possible to create 3D ggplots without learning a separate 3D plotting API. Just drop in your existing plot and poof! A 3D version would appear.
But this came with one limitation: the data had to be attached to the surface.
Floating data needs something to ground it. I originally kept the data attached to the surface deliberately: actual 3D data is harder to understand on a 2D screen, since depth is ambiguous. Extruded 2D surfaces provide a continuous underlying substrate, which makes interpretation easier–the surface itself provides depth cues, by nature of surface continuity providing cues on depth ordering. It’s not hard to plop down some floating 3D data in a box and call it a day: before rayshader, that was what pretty much every 3D plotting library I encountered did. In my opinion, that lazy approach helped give 3D dataviz its terrible reputation. Adding 3D data disconnected from that substrate requires additional care and thought to keep the data interpretable.
Which rayshader now provides!
In rayshader 1.0, plot_gg() is much more tightly integrated with the render_*() family of functions that add real 3D data to the scene. Rayshader now extracts the data extent from the existing ggplot2 scene. Basically, we now track how ggplot2 transforms data into the image, so we can use the same transformation for our 3D data. Downstream render calls can use that extent to place real 3D geometry in the correct part of the plot. The ggplot is no longer just a surface extrusion: it’s now the base coordinate system for a complete 3D scene.
And this can really help visually, as that surface extrusion wasn’t ideal for certain types of data. The original raster extrusion worked well for smooth surfaces, density plots, and continuous fields, but sharp polygon boundaries and abrupt vertical edges were harder.
Take Figure 19: it shows a map of US states with height mapped to population. States share an boundary in the source polygons, but when rasterized to row of pixels, you can see the colors bleed down the step between states. This is an unavoidable problem when you try to force vector data into a raster format. So we avoid it by drawing the actual 3D data. On the right, each state’s own polygon makes a crisp vertical wall.

The same integration lets individual points float above a flat ggplot2 substrate (enabled with plot_gg(..., flat_substrate = TRUE)). The ggplot establishes the scales and coordinate system, and rayshader adds the observed values as actual 3D points, positioned correctly. render_zaxis() gives those floating marks a scale you can read. It picks up the height scale from the ggplot, and you can put the axis inside a panel or along the outer edge of the plot. If you have facets, you can pick the panel. It works on regular terrain maps, too.
Figure 20: Each point is one car in mtcars. Weight and fuel economy are on 2D ggplot2 axes, and its elevation gives the horsepower (noted in the z-axis).
This removes a ton of visual compromises. Instead of forcing every feature to become part of the surface texture, we use the surface texture as the base and add the features as real 3D geometry. The plot layout and elements are still determined by ggplot2: we’re just adding data to the z-axis.
As a note, while it raises the bar on what you can do, it also lowers the bar for making bad 3D visualizations, but with great power comes great responsibility! Oh, wait, wrong movie.
Faceted plots can receive geometry one panel at a time. Spatial plots built with coord_sf() carry their geographic transform into the scene, too. Your base plot can use familiar geoms—geom_hex(), geom_point(), geom_path(), geom_raster(), or geom_sf()—while rayshader adds polygons, points, paths, and a labeled z-axis in those coordinates.
Figure 21: Each North Carolina county rises in proportion to the number of births recorded there in 1974. The z-axis gives the scale in births.
3D ggplots were always a cool, sometimes useful novelty. Now they can be a foundation for complex 3D visualizations. How complex are we talking about? Watch me demo it below with a data visualization showing ADSB flight path data over Washington, DC. Come fly over the National Mall with me and I’ll walk you through how deep the 3D rabbit hole goes.
The render_*() functions have been rewritten around the same principle: spatial data already encodes where it is, so there is no reason to throw that information out.
render_points() can accept spatial point objects. render_path() can accept spatial line objects. render_label() can accept points, multipoints, polygons, and multipolygons, converting polygon inputs to centroids when needed. render_polygons() and render_beveled_polygons() use cached heightmap and extent metadata. render_buildings() uses spatial footprints, roof materials, roof angles, height columns, and CRS-aware extent filtering. render_obj() can place OBJ models using spatial point data. You can see most of these in action in Figure 22.
New hillshading options
There’s some new basic hillshading options as well. haze_shade() adds an RGBA haze overlay based on an exponential atmospheric model. It is useful for low-elevation haze, valley haze, and scenes where you want the atmosphere to participate in the map rather than sit behind it. It is a good way to subtly separate mountain tops from valleys.
Add haze to the inland valleys
library(rayshader)# Crop the bundled DEM to the inland hills and valleys east of Monterey Bay.hills = terra::crop( montereybay_spatial, terra::ext(-121.73, -121.38, 36.20, 36.48))dark_terrain =create_texture(light_color ="#879581",shadow_color ="#15252b",left_color ="#54634b",right_color ="#283f42",center_color ="#354c41")hills |>sphere_shade(texture = dark_terrain, vertical_exaggeration =5) |>add_overlay(haze_shade(color ="#dfe8f2",optical_depth =1.5,scale_height =200 )) |>plot_3d(theta =220,phi =30,zoom =0.4,fov =50,background ="#20282f",solid_color ="#161e23" )render_snapshot()
Figure 23: Haze fades in and out as the terrain rotates, softening low valleys while leaving higher ground clearer.
radiance_shade() renders a top-down radiance pass from a cached hillshade context, the active 3D scene, or a supplied heightmap. It gives 2D maps and 3D ggplot2 workflows access to more visually-striking physically based lighting without forcing the entire project into a final path-traced render. This is a nice way to get higher-quality shadows on a model you can still rotate and revise quickly. The result is still an RGBA overlay, so it can be composited back into the usual rayshader map pipeline or exported to other programs.
Figure 24: A radiance pass composited back onto a 2D rayshader map, adding path-traced lighting while staying in the (fast) rgl workflow.
Earth’s curvature
For a small area, we can usually ignore Earth’s curvature. As a map grows to cover hundreds or thousands of kilometers, the bend of the Earth can become an important part of the story. For satellite orbits, long-distance flight paths, and regional coverage maps, curvature can help signal to the reader that we’re dealing with global-scale data without an explicit scale bar.
Setting earth_curvature = TRUE in plot_3d() adds that curvature to the scene. Mountains and valleys can look flatter beside the much larger bend of the Earth when no vertical exaggeration is applied, but the adjustment gives those other GIS layers a more useful spatial context.
Figure 25: Alaska and its neighbors with a flat surface (left) and Earth curvature enabled (right).
For example, Figure 25 shows three Starlink satellites cross Alaska along paths calculated from real orbital data. Their simulated beams track populated places below, switching targets as they move within reach. Both views show the same moment, but on the right, the surface and orbital altitudes are adjusted to match the global curvature. This helps give the viewer important context clues for the spatial scales we’re dealing with here that the flat projection does not provide.
Even higher quality render_highquality()
Want to realistically light a scene at a very specific time and date? Just give rayshader a date and time–it already knows the place. For a scene with cached spatial coordinates, render_highquality(datetime = ...) can infer the location and generate the corresponding sky and sunlight. You don’t need to look up the latitude, longitude, or sun angle again. Depending on the sky model, that can include stars, planets, and the moon’s phase and brightness.
As an example, around the equinoxes, the low sun lines up with the National Mall’s east–west axis—a favorite alignment for photographers. On March 25, 2026, at 6:56:11 p.m. EDT, the modeled shadow of the Washington Monument runs parallel to the Mall’s main paths. A few days past the equinox, the sun is still high enough at that alignment to keep the shadow within this view.
Figure 26: The Washington Monument at 6:56:11 p.m. EDT on March 25, 2026. Its shadow aligns with the National Mall’s main paths, and it only required passing the datetime to render_highquality().
And separately, text and annotation lines were physical objects in the rendered scene. Their letters and lines cast shadows across the terrain and buildings, giving annotations the same simulated weight as the things they were annotating. A label should help you read the map without becoming another object in it.
Figure 27: Mount Rainier, Mount St. Helens, and Mount Adams turn with the terrain, but their labels always face you. The leader lines stay anchored to the volcano locations. Terrain heights use 4× vertical exaggeration.
The labels in Figure 27 are drawn in screen space: their positions stay attached to the map, while the text keeps its size and faces the camera throughout the orbit, without casting shadows over the volcanoes. The horsepower axis in Figure 20 uses the same approach. The lines and text are composited in real time when you’re looking at the high quality preview render in rayrender, so you can set up the shot exactly how you want to. Oh, and you can set deferred_render = TRUE now as well, which removes the sample timer so you can have all the time in the world to set up your render. This is especially important now, since rayrender is now fully GPU-accellerated on ARM macs, leading to 30-50x speedups in rendering performance, so your render can often end before you got a chance to click on the screen. This blog post, however, is about rayshader, so I won’t steal its thunder talking about the awesome improvements in rayrender :)
1.0 and beyond!
It’s been a long, properly textured road–why 1.0 after eight years? I now feel that rayshader has firmly found its niche and purpose, and this overhaul feels like a graduation moment for the package. I’m no longer figuring out what a 3D GIS workflow in R should feel like–it’s now about making that workflow work for you. And thinking about all the people who used rayshader to produce everything from beautiful generative art and frameable cartographic works to scientific articles and award winning journalism made me decide to give rayshader the graduation it deserves, and make sure it knows: You’re number 1.0!
The grand finale and most exciting part of any publication: the bibliography.
Rayshader wouldn’t be possible without the work of all the packages and people that supported it and provided great user feedback during its development. In a normal blog post, this is where normally you’d have a list of citations and people to thank. But how often does R’s most cinematic package get a 1.0 release? I decided the people, packages, and data behind rayshader deserved the full cinematic treatment that rayshader has provided the R ecosystem. And that the cinematic treatment should be created entirely in R, using rayrender, of course. Please stick around and hit play for the credits below—and be sure to turn the sound on.

clean_title: AI researchers debate what we should do next – Daniel Kokotajlo and Ege Erdil
feed_title: Q&A with AI researchers Ege Erdil and Daniel Kokotajlo on the odds of an intelligence explosion before 2029, pausing AI, the US antagonizing China, and more (Dwarkesh Patel/Dwarkesh Podcast)
title: AI researchers debate what we should do next – Daniel Kokotajlo and Ege Erdil
content_text:
New podcast episode between Ege Erdil and Daniel Kokotajlo. I thought this was going to be a debate, but they ended up agreeing on a lot more than I expected.
Their main point of disagreement is how likely it is that we get some intelligence explosion that gives us AIs more competent than any human expert before 2029. Ege puts this possibility at around 20%, whereas Daniel thinks it’s higher than 50%.
They agree that there is not a huge difference in probability, and that, in either case, the situation is crazy enough that our civilization really needs to grapple with how the world might be transformed, and we need a plan that actually makes sense.
In particular, we should stop antagonizing China if we think some kind of global treaty will be needed to make superintelligence go well.
There was another important crux about how well we should expect future AIs (that swamp humans in population size and cognitive power) to treat us, and how relevant it is that current AIs, by and large, seem to be pretty nice.
We close off with predictions for 2027. Daniel, of course, expects superintelligence next year. Ege’s median for full automation is 2040, but by next year he expects AIs that can beat any video game on Steam, and which can control robots to get simple physical tasks (like folding laundry) done at roughly human speed.
Watch on YouTube; listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify.
