Transcript
0:00:00 – Will we have superintelligence by 2029?
Dwarkesh Patel
Today, I’m joined by Ege Erdil and Daniel Kokotajlo. Ege is a researcher at Google DeepMind. Daniel is one of the authors at the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027 and AI 2040.
I wouldn’t call this exactly a debate, because I hope it’ll be more of a discussion. But there is a set of key disagreements you guys have, which leads one of you, Daniel, to believe that AI is likely to kill us all within the next few years, and Ege, you to believe that will not happen. I feel like a big crux in this conversation is just timelines. How soon do you expect extreme superintelligence?
I’ve articulated, and Paul has articulated in the last episode, why there could be extreme superintelligence soon. Ege, why do you think that’s unlikely?
Ege Erdil
The main difference between me and Daniel, and also between me and Paul, is just how much you believe in the software-only singularity.
This is the idea that you have a fixed pool of compute and a roughly fixed amount of data that is at least not synthetic. Then what happens is that you get better AIs. Those AIs are able to use that pool of resources way more efficiently to make progress on AI research, and you get this feedback loop that at least goes for many orders of magnitude before it fizzles out. Then that improvement is so big that you get, I don’t know, 10 years of progress in six months or whatever, something like this.
I think the evidence we have is not sufficient to give high credence to that. Maybe that’s 10-20% likely to happen over the next three years. That’s probably the biggest disagreement, where Daniel thinks that’s over 50% likely.
Dwarkesh Patel
Why do you think it’s more than 50% likely that there will be extreme superintelligence within the next few years, whereas Ege thinks that’s 10-20% likely?
Daniel Kokotajlo
First of all, I don’t think that we will probably all be dead in a couple years. The thing I would say is, unless we substantially slow down the AI companies, then probably we will lose control and there will be misaligned AIs running the show in a couple years. It seems like we’re getting close to fully automating the AI research process. That would be the main claim. How close? It seems like it’s going to happen in 2027. Maybe not, maybe 2028, maybe 2029, but I would say it’s slightly more likely than not in 2027.
Once you have fully automated the AI research process, things will probably accelerate. More likely than not, they will accelerate a lot, as Ege was describing, although I do think there’s some uncertainty there.
Then I think that a lot of the limitations of current AI systems, such as the data inefficiency or whatever, will melt away relatively quickly as progress accelerates dramatically. You’ll end up with AIs that are able to flexibly learn quickly from all sorts of experience. You might call them top-expert-dominating AIs, perhaps. Top-expert-dominating AIs are effectively superintelligence as far as I’m concerned.
Dwarkesh Patel
Here’s a naive question. We go back five years and we have AI systems that can’t even hold a conversation. Now we have systems that are solving Millennium Prize Problems. They’re pretty good coders, et cetera.
If we just go another five years of progress at this pace, do you think it’s likely that that alone gives us AIs that are competitive with human experts? If we’re looking forward five years, do we even need that much RSI?
Ege Erdil
We might not, but I think it’s unclear. If we don’t get any RSI, my median timeline to everything being automated and humans having nothing to do — they’ve been completely automated — is something like 15-20 years from now. That’s a median timeline. So in the next five years, you still have to give it 20% or something that it could happen. I think that’s a very live possibility.
While there are disagreements about software-only singularity and similar things, in some sense those disagreements don’t matter that much. All I’m saying is, Daniel is saying something is 50-60% likely to happen over the next three years, and I’m saying it’s 20% likely. That question might be interesting. But even if it’s only 20% likely, if the situation is very bad, you should still do something about it.
So even though it’s maybe a larger disagreement numerically, I don’t think it’s a significant disagreement qualitatively.
0:04:31 – Why Ege thinks it’s too early to pause
Daniel Kokotajlo
So the reason why you’re working at Google instead of protesting outside of Anthropic, which is a practical difference between our behavior, is less to do with the probabilities on the different scenarios and more to do with… Well, what actually? I’m curious.
Ege Erdil
Several things. In this particular question of whether a pause is a good idea or not, I’m worried about any plan that involves us acting on risks before we have seen some significant version of the costs in the real world. Right now, the thing people always cite in these discussions, since some number of months ago, is the Hugging Face incident. But I personally think the Hugging Face incident didn’t cost that much and was a pretty small incident in the grand scheme of things. It was much less significant than a plane crash in terms of the cost imposed.
I do see it as analogous to if you have a new technology, like nuclear reactors or aircraft or whatever, and you haven’t actually seen anything significant go wrong, but you have all these theoretical arguments for why things might go wrong, and you’re intervening on the basis of that… I’m just suspicious about that approach in general.
The thing I’m challenging when I say that is the view that the way you get aligned AIs is to have some theoretical breakthrough in alignment. Nothing in machine learning has worked like that. Machine learning is not a field that has large theoretical breakthroughs.
There have been no large theoretical breakthroughs over the past 10 years. All of them have been incremental. You stack this compute multiplier on top of this compute multiplier, and you get this efficiency gain. It’s just very incremental. There are a lot of dimensions that you optimize at once. That’s the way you make them more capable.
So I don’t see why you would assume anything different about the way we would make them more aligned.
Dwarkesh Patel
This is maybe a key disagreement between you guys. Are there tractable interventions that we could make? Specifically, are those interventions more tractable if we get more time to make them, interventions that are likely to increase the value of what these AI systems do and how they treat us?
The AI Futures Project has just put out a pacing scheme that you say will delay the intelligence explosion by a year, which you are expecting in 2027. So you think this would slow it down to 2028?
Daniel Kokotajlo
Something like that. We have uncertainty, but yeah.
Dwarkesh Patel
What changes if we get the intelligence explosion in 2028 rather than 2027?
Daniel Kokotajlo
A couple things. First of all, I think that progress is being made on AI alignment and the science of understanding how AI works and all sorts of things like this. It’s not going fast enough, but it is being made. Each additional year of time that we buy, there’s additional progress, which cuts away at that probability mass of the bad outcomes happening.
The second thing I would say is just general awareness, what you might call AGI-pilling of society and of government. This might actually be the most important thing. Most people just don’t really take this stuff seriously, don’t really understand what’s happening or what’s coming. That seems broadly bad to me. We’d probably be in a better situation if more people in general understood what was coming.
I think that process is happening. It might even be happening exponentially. Every year that goes by, more people learn more, more people pay attention, more people start getting involved.
Ege Erdil
It’s just very difficult without tangible things that the technology does in the world to wake people up to its potential. For example, if we pause at the current level of capabilities, let’s assume we do that. Yes, this process of people waking up continues slowly. But just look at the skepticism in the financial markets about the viability of this technology. There’s huge skepticism. That’s also probably just shared broadly throughout the public.
The public doesn’t really like AI. They don’t really like data centers and stuff. But that’s not because they realize what’s going to happen. They just have a much more myopic distaste for it. If we pause now, then people are still not going to understand what’s at stake. The public conversation about this will still be very poor because it will be operating from bad premises.
There’s an advantage to getting the capabilities to a point where it’s evident to everyone that if we keep going from there on, the world will be totally transformed. Because doing this through ordinary persuasion is extremely difficult.
You might get some kind of pause politically, but it would be supported by factions who don’t actually agree with your worldview. They would support it for some other reason. They don’t like big tech companies. They don’t like the fact that all these companies are constructing all these data centers that the local communities they’re in don’t support. It would be for some other reason and not for the reason that you think is most important.
Daniel Kokotajlo
I technically agree with you, but in spirit disagree. Maybe one way of modeling it is something like: for each new AI capability that appears, there are some rapid updates that people make immediately just upon learning that that capability exists. But then there’s a whole bunch of additional updates that get made as that capability gets more deployed into the world and so forth.
Right now capability progress is moving fast enough that we still haven’t nearly exhausted the gains in awareness that would come from just deploying the current capabilities more. If we had a pause where we continue to deploy the current capabilities but not make them smarter, we would continue to see significant gains in awareness over the course of several years. Then it would taper off after more than that.
I do think that things are going fast enough now that to a first approximation, the wake-up is a function of serial time rather than a function of the capabilities. Although there’s some function of the capabilities.
Another thing I would say too is that a lot of the people who have anti-AI opinions don’t share my worldview and don’t have anti-AI opinions for the same reasons as me. But that’s also changing to a larger extent. We’ve seen multiple senators and congresspeople come out and say, “AI could kill us all,” and, “The AIs could go rogue,” and things like that. That’s mostly happened just in the last year.
So that too is trending in what I would consider the right direction, where people are waking up and understanding the magnitude of the situation more. I don’t think it’s trending fast enough in the right direction. I don’t think that it’s going to be where it needs to be in 12 months, but in 24 months maybe, or in 36 months maybe.
Ege Erdil
I agree with the point that if you pause now, you will still get an increase in awareness for a couple more years. But given the distance between where we are now and where I think people need to get, given the implications of technology, I think that’s just not going to happen if you pause at the current level of capabilities.
It might be enough. You might have the view that the current level of support and current political coalitions or whatever are sufficient to get a pause to happen. Then that has the benefits that you care about, that it slows things down, even though it’s not done with a complete understanding of what’s going to happen and it’s done for different motivations. It’s a defensible position.
I’m just worried in the longer term that if we as a civilization just insist on being irrational about this topic, then we will just make a lot of bad choices, a lot of choices that don’t make that much sense. It’s important that people understand that in some ways, the world we’ve been in is going to no longer exist in some sense.
Even if the outcome is very good for us, if you get Daniel’s ideal outcome or something like that, that world is still completely different from today’s world. People don’t realize. Maybe if they realize, they’ll be like, “Wait, we don’t want that world. That doesn’t fit our preference. We want some other world.”
But if there is never an explicit conversation that has the correct factual premises about what’s going to happen, then we will just not be in control of the situation. Because even though in some sense we are in control, in the sense that all the relevant decisions, at least for a while, are being made by humans, they are not being made as a result of some rational deliberation.
I’m really worried about that. Some random thing is going to happen, and we won’t control what happens. It will not be the output of any process that makes any sense. Then we will have to live with it. That’s very scary.
Daniel Kokotajlo
That’s a reason to go slower in AI alignment.
Ege Erdil
It’s a reason to go slower after sufficiently many people are aware of the potential of technology.
Daniel Kokotajlo
And you think it’s too early for that?
Ege Erdil
I think it’s too early.
0:13:46 – The adversarial stance on China is dangerous
Daniel Kokotajlo
Then what about, instead of going to a complete pause, going slower? Say we do the thing where we restrict AI R&D compute to 10% or 5% of the company’s compute. This slashes the overall pace of progress by a factor of two or three or something.
Perhaps you would agree then that because you are still making forward progress, you are still going to get the levels of awareness eventually.
Ege Erdil
A couple things about that. First of all, I don’t know how to get international coordination for this. Given what we’re currently doing, it’s going to be very hard because the US is being quite adversarial against China right now, especially with recent events. That just seriously undermines the possibility of getting any coordination. It’s actually very myopic and dangerous. They really have to stop doing that.
Daniel Kokotajlo
One of the nice things about the 10% idea is that it would still leave the US companies with about as much compute on AI R&D as the Chinese companies. Also, because a lot of Chinese progress is just coming from the US, you wouldn’t even need a deal to do this level of pacing.
Ege Erdil
For now, but that’s because China is behind on a bunch of the industrial tech that’s required to produce a lot of compute. For example, they don’t have access to EUV machines and stuff like this. The US has been able to get the Netherlands to successfully export control those and so on. But given China’s rate of economic growth and industrial progress, these are temporary advantages. So it gives us some time.
China is not going to be able to catch up in five years, probably. So if you think five years is enough, then you can get five years with a method like this. But if you think we need 15 years or something like that, then I become more pessimistic.
Dwarkesh Patel
Or let alone some global agreement. In the limit, it is worth discussing. If you really believe we’ll have such powerful AI systems, this depends on what you think the nature of destructive technologies is. But it is plausible that you might need some global treaty on, “Hey, you can’t have superintelligent systems that you’ve deployed to go research mirror life or something.” At some point, there’s not just a race. Unless you think you’re just going to literally outcompete every single country.
Daniel Kokotajlo
I agree that ultimately, if we want to have a good future, we’re probably going to need to make some sort of treaty or deal with China and other countries, something like that.
Ege Erdil
If you’re really worried about that risk, there has to be coordination with them. There’s no way to avoid that. You can try to delay things. You can have a five-year lead. You have five additional years. That buys you something. But if you’re really worried about that risk, they could try to build it in five years. It’s not that long.
Any prospects of coordination with them, I think, are being severely damaged by the policy of the US government towards China, and also, to some extent, of Anthropic towards China.
Daniel Kokotajlo
I agree with that.
Ege Erdil
This is very short-sighted. It’s because people don’t understand the stakes of the technology. The awareness that this is a world-transforming technology that completely changes the condition of civilization is just not there.
We have to figure out a way to deal with it, and there’s no way to adequately deal with it without some kind of coordination. And people are torpedoing the prospects for doing that for some very short-sighted, short-term gain of, “Oh, we get a couple years’ additional lead.” It doesn’t make sense, what people are doing. So I think they’re operating from a very different view of what the technology will be like, which I think is going to have bad consequences.
This is another thing I think is not being discussed, even in communities where people are trying to think of, “How do we win? How do we get the safe AI first?” Gwern had an interesting comment about this, I think on LessWrong, where he asked the question: let’s say the US wins. We get our superintelligence. Then what?
What do we do? Do we do some crazy operation to try to overthrow the Chinese government or something like that? If they think that’s what the US is going to do, what are they going to think of any attempt to try to coordinate with them to get a slowdown? They’re inherently going to be extremely suspicious of any such attempt if they think that is the plan.
0:19:30 – There is no plan, because people are in denial
Dwarkesh Patel
I think people correctly point out that I have too many people on my podcast who have this particular view of AI trajectories, and not only AI trajectories, but the implications of that trajectory. However, it does end up being the case that when you talk to a skeptic, for example, Ege, it seems like you just have slightly different probabilities on things. The people who totally dismiss this altogether, I feel like, don’t have reasonable arguments about why AI capabilities will not continue.
If you take seriously the possibility of minds in data centers that learn like humans and which will swamp us in population, thinking speed, agglomerated experience and expertise, et cetera, no people who take that seriously, at least so far as I’ve found, put less than 10% or less than 5% that things go pretty badly for biological humans.
Ege Erdil
This is something I try to emphasize. By people who don’t have enough context on the situation, or who are not carefully reading what I’m saying, I could be considered this person who disagrees with Daniel, that I give 2-3x less probability to various things compared to Daniel or something like that. That’s actually not that important in some sense.
There are some things for which a 3-4x difference can make a difference. If you think the risk of doom right now is 4% a year compared to 1% a year, that can actually make a difference for whether you think we should pause or not. That’s because you’re comparing it to the 1% per year of people who are dying. Then whether you think the risk per year from AI is higher or lower than that is an important analytical question.
But compared to the people who just don’t take the technology seriously, or who have what I would call magical views about the human mind, which are very widespread, all of those people are just in a different world. They’re not actually engaged with what’s happening.
If they were making predictions over the past few years, or past five years or whatever, they would’ve been very, very, very wrong. All their predictions would’ve been completely wrong. Often they don’t make predictions, so they’re not proven wrong.
Dwarkesh Patel
Actually, should we discuss what you, Daniel, predicted in AI 2027, which was released in the beginning of 2025? What did you predict that the world would look like in late 2026?
Daniel Kokotajlo

I don’t think they’re necessarily being self-interested about that. They just have a real belief that this would be worse for the world if they made that information public. But Daniel doesn’t share that belief.
If there’s no public discourse about it, it’s impossible to get the companies to actually publish this stuff. There has to be some external thing that comes in and says, “Look, you guys can think that, but we are aware of the stakes here. We have decided that it is important for this information to be public.” Unless that can happen, anyone can say, “Look, I think it’s better for the world, and I’m just going to do what I think is best.” There’s no regulation, there are no rules.
That’s a very bad situation. Not because I necessarily think that the decision to keep it secret is a wrong decision, but because the process that’s outputting that outcome is bad. As I said, there should be a plan. We should understand what the stakes are. There should be rational public deliberation about this topic, and people should come to a conclusion: “Yes, we want this,” or, “No, we don’t want this.” That has not happened at all.
This is a unilateral decision that is being taken by some people who might be right, might be wrong. They have certain preferences. Even the government, I think, is not really playing a large role in that, because they don’t understand the stakes.
The government might play a role in something like, “Oh, we are worried about Chinese cyber attacks, and we want to have capable cyber models. We don’t want that to get leaked.” Or they might worry about specific concrete risks. But if you don’t appreciate the total transformative potential of the technology, that it’s going to totally change the human condition, for example, then you’re just unaware of the stakes. You’re not going to make the right decisions.
Dwarkesh Patel
This was a very productive discussion. I feel it was very helpful to iron out what the cruxes were within the context of people who take the potential of this technology seriously. Thanks, guys.
Daniel Kokotajlo
Thank you.

title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
content_text:
Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
- Published
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.
Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused Sánchez of evading questions on some of the key issues of corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.
The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.
Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.
"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.
If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.
Pedro Sánchez's government "has betrayed us, he has robbed us and he has lied to us", Abascal told an audience earlier in Tarancón, to the south-east of Madrid.
Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.
- Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in - Published14 hours ago
 
- Spanish election: What you need to know and what's at stake - Published7 hours ago
 
- Who to watch in Spain's election race - Published7 hours ago
 
- Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election - Published2 days ago
 
The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.
All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. Feijóo said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while Sánchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.
While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front) focused on women's rights.
The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.
Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.
Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.
Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.
Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.
Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".
He then went on to praise Ada Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign. As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

title: Marvel's Iron Man might be planning to rear its head at The Game Awards, if EA Motive's updated website is any indication
content_text:
Marvel's Iron Man might be planning to rear its head at The Game Awards, if EA Motive's updated website is any indication
Stark reminder.
EA Motive's Iron Man game has been quietly cooking away for a few years now, but don't worry. The wait to finally, officially see the superhero romp in action might be over soon, at least if the developer's updated website - two weeks before The Game Awards, no less - is any indication.
Redditors today noticed that EA Motive's official website got a little makeover recently. It's not clear when exactly the tweaks were pushed through, but the Wayback Machine makes clear that it's definitely been updated.
A new website look is by no means confirmation of an imminent announcement, of course, but there are a few other bits of evidence that certainly point in that direction.
For one, The Game Awards 2026 will air on Disney Plus for the very first time, alongside all the other platforms you're used to. "As the evening unfolds, viewers can expect major announcements and surprises from some of Disney's most anticipated titles in gaming," the film studio said earlier this month.
Kingdom Hearts 4, Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra and more are definitely possible, too. Turmoil at Marvel's Blade developer Arkane Lyon makes that one a tricker guess, however.
Second is the fact that The Game Awards air on 10th December - eight days before the global opening of Avengers: Doomsday, a film that's shaping up to become the biggest cinematic event since the last time Marvel chucked all of its toys into the same sandbox and bashed them together. Giving one of the company's most popular superheroes the spotlight around the same time seems like a good idea.
This isn't the first time EA's Iron Man has popped up in recent times, either. What appeared to be an unfinished trailer for Motive's Iron Man leaked onto the internet this summer, and showed off blisteringly fast flying and lots of destructive gadgets. It looked further along than I expected, at least, so I wouldn't be surprised to see the billionaire playboy philanthropist rear his head again in two weeks time.

content_text:
Digital Extremes says Warframe's imminent Tau update is practically big enough to be a sequel as it reveals new details, including dog walking
Lounging around.
Warframe's latest devstream has just gone live, revealing more about the new Tau solar system players will be able to explore as part of December's "massive" new update, which arrives on 9th December. Additions include a two-hour long quest, new explorable areas, and even chill nighttime dog walking.
In a press pre-briefing ahead of the Devstream, Warframe creative director Rebecca Ford and community director Megan Everett discussed the scale of the Tau update, revealing just how much of an ambitious undertaking it's been for the team. "This is a huge update, it is massive," Ford said. "It is a second solar system ... Alone, by now, this would have been Warframe two. We're just going for it: we're building a new solar system brick-by-brick."
That begins with a "two-hours-ish" story quest, according to Ford, but there's plenty more besides. Tau brings a new navigation system, for instance, and will feature two playable regions at launch. The World-Seeder Oasis is one: full of environmental hazards, thanks to damaging terraforming efforts, and various missions to complete. Here, players can go bug-collecting for an NPC called Catulast. Doing so increases your standing with him, and provides new rewards.
Then there's the ringed city of Fornax. Unlike previous regions in Warframe, this features three hubs: the Lastbloom Lounge, Manifold 90-BF, and the Elder Rustgarden. All have their own playable missions, some brand-new and others returning from the original star system. This includes Spy, a returning mode that has players breaking into terminals while trying to remain undetected.
Spy hasn't been shown a lot of love for a while, and it seems like this new iteration will bring new custom puzzles for players to take on. Ford notes it'll include codes to memorise, passwords to figure out, plus gameplay and an aesthetic that alights with the new Fornax setting.
Steel Path - the optional, more difficult variant of regular missions - also returns in Tau, although the Accolite mini-bosses who would hunt you down in previous Steel Path missions will not be present. Instead, the Hokra brothers will take that role: giant sentient casino goons who look quite daunting.
We were also shown more of the Last Bloom Lounge. Here you'll be given bounties that'll always bounce you between the three Fornax hubs. So, if you take one bounty in the Lounge, you'll complete it while out on a mission, and end up in either Manifold or the Rustgarden (which is still being kept secret for now). That way you'll be naturally circling between the three locations.
However, rather than there being three separate syndicate reputations to grind out, one single syndicate connects them all: the Fornax Informer, a newspaper run by kids obsessed with breaking stories across the ringed city. Print lives! By progressing through the ranks with this syndicate, you'll unlock clues for detective work that reveal a special cinematic within the Lounge, though this too is being kept secret for now.
By completing bounties, you'll also gain access to Fornax's own progression system which provides still-mysterious buffs and other beneficial effects within Tau. There's also a card game in the Lounge, which you can either play against the house or with other players.
As for navigating between the hubs, each one has its own garage. The Tau update comes with a driving minigame: an on-rails opportunity to gather resources and fend off other drivers along the way. In the demo shown, we're brought from the Lounge to the Manifold, dodging barriers and blowing up other sentient vehicles in the process. There's also a "low stakes, no combat" way to navigate between the hubs. It's called Night Walk, a first-person dog walking mode where you can travel

clean_title: ‘I am scared’: Careless People author Sarah Wynn-Williams on living under a gag order - and why it’s time to speak out against big tech
feed_title: I am scared: Careless People – Sarah Wynn-Williams on living under a gag order
title: ‘I am scared’: Careless People author Sarah Wynn-Williams on living under a gag order - and why it’s time to speak out against big tech
content_text:
George Orwell understood that what is missing often tells you more than what is there. In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. They call it the memory hole. When a document becomes inconvenient to the authorities – a photograph that contradicts the official line, a newspaper that remembers the wrong promise, a name that is no longer supposed to exist – you simply feed it into the slot, whereupon it is whirled away on a current of warm air to enormous hidden furnaces where it burns.
The Party doesn’t argue with the past. It removes it. Controlling the past is one of its central tools of power: “Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.”
Control what people are allowed to remember or what they are allowed to know, and you control what they are able to imagine. Control what they can imagine, and you have already chosen their future for them.
Knowledge matters. People need to know what actually happened. But in 2026 the language of tech has taken on a quality of manifest destiny: the men in charge have determined how it should be, as though there could be no other way, even though none of us voted for any of it.
Control of the prevailing narrative is held tacitly: the only time this authority is given voice is when it acts, decisively, to silence an alternative account. Control over narrative is becoming the real power battle in technology. The aim is not to win the argument. The aim is to leave nothing to argue with. An absence. No record. No receipt. No contestable standard of truth. No common ground of fact against which anyone could measure those in power and expose their failures. Without memory or evidence, dissent has nothing to stand on. That is why memory matters. Why evidence matters. Why books matter.
You don’t need a Ministry of Truth to make a memory hole. An employment contract will do. An NDA will do. A court order will do. A legal bill – large enough, frightening enough, open-ended enough – will do very nicely. The modern memory hole does not smell of smoke. It smells of printer toner, fresh paper and billable hours.
In libel, truth is a defence. Under an NDA, truth is the offence.
The agreement is signed at the moment of maximum vulnerability, still reeling from an “incident” while the mortgage looms and the cardboard box of family photos sits in the front seat of the car. It is signed by the gig worker, the intern, the content moderator, the production assistant, the junior publicist, the stylist. There really is no better way to knock the whistle from someone’s lips. In a justice system based broadly on the principle that sunlight is the best disinfectant, NDAs grip the elbow of truth and stay it. This is a private form of censorship, enforced by private arbitration and the public courts.
Anyone targeted by an institution with a formidable legal department is, by definition, very vulnerable. It is one person against a building full of lawyers who seek only to protect the interests of the company, truth be damned. Some businesses are more powerful than states.
They have mastered corporate lawfare, letting slip the dogs of law on individuals who don’t have millions of pounds to defend themselves against these attacks brought on by trying to defy the memory hole. The word “brave” gets bandied around if you speak out despite all this. But “brave” should be for haircuts, not for telling the truth.
You do not have to silence everyone. You could never afford to. You only have to silence one person loudly enough that everyone else does the maths for themselves. These contracts seek to mute the truth, and they carry a big stick. The result is a society that has censored itself far more thoroughly than any Ministry of Truth ever could. No furnace required. Just fear, doing its patient and persistent work in the dark.
Recently, in the realm of entertainment, some big names have faced accountability or at least the prospect of it, because of women speaking out. Russell Brand was convicted, and David Walliams faces allegations. (Walliams has denied any wrongdoing in response to the allegations that he preyed on young women for sex.) In both cases, there are reports of NDAs being deployed to silence women. To ensure information that was clearly in the public interest was suppressed.
And while we should celebrate the courage and fortitude of the women who spoke out at unimaginable cost, and the media organisations, including the Guardian, whose investigations were instrumental in ensuring this information became public, I can’t help but notice that this accountability occurred at a time when the professional standing of these figures was already significantly diminished.
For a long time now it has felt as if certain sectors of society, including technology companies, act with impunity. I worry about all the powerful people who continue to benefit from silence and deprive us, the public, of information that can lead to warnings and ideally accountability. I worry we will only be allowed the truth about these companies when it no longer matters.
Whoever you are, whatever you believe, with an ever-more powerful elite there will come a day when you need to say something the powerful would rather you didn’t. And on that day, you will want three things: a place to say it that they do not own, a law that will not let them constrict you in grinding legal processes before bankrupting you for saying it, and people who will remember that you said it. The protections you are willing to fight for are the only ones that will be there when you need them.
Silencing the person who speaks is only half the job. The other half is making sure no one is paying attention. There is a detail in Nineteen Eighty-Four I used to skim past. Julia works in the Fiction Department of the Ministry of Truth. She services the novel-writing machines. These mass-produce literature as a commodity without any human creativity or critical thought. They use the same six stories, recombined endlessly to churn out formulaic slop for the proles.
The purpose of the novel-writing machines is to keep the proles distracted, passive and incurious. And it works. The proles never notice. The fiction machine has much in common with the feed: an endless scroll engineered by the brightest minds of a generation to keep your attention indefinitely. Nineteen Eighty-Four also gave us the Two Minutes Hate. A daily ritual of collective rage aimed at an enemy of the state. We have improved on it. Ours is continuous. Personalised. Delivered by push notification. And now with AI we have, literally, machines that write and humans that service them.
Orwell imagined the novel-writing machine as satire. We have built it. It was trained on the work of writers who were never asked. And sold back to them on a subscription. The Fiction Department of Nineteen Eighty-Four is now an industry. And it is the fastest growing one on earth. The memory hole removes what is true, and the fiction machine fills the space.
So much for what the machines do. The harder question is who owns them, and Orwell had a view on that too, though he was writing about a different technology. In October 1945, weeks after the atomic bomb was dropped, Orwell wrote a short essay exploring the deep connection between weapons technology and political power, observing that the shape of power in any age follows the shape of its decisive weapon. When weapons are cheap and simple – like the rifle – it empowers democracy and and gives “claws to the weak”, meaning ordinary people who can get hold of it have a fighting chance. When it is expensive and complex, like nuclear weapons, it concentrates power in the hands of a few and gives rise to oligarchic empires. And Orwell warned that these oligarchs might use the fear of the bomb to keep their populations suppressed, afraid to revolt.
Now think about the decisive technology of our own age. One that offers tremendous promise but also tremendous peril. The most advanced artificial intelligence takes investment measured in tens of billions. Chips made by a tiny number of firms, in a tiny number of places. Nobody builds this in a shed. Most governments do not have the resources to build it. A handful of companies can, mostly in just two countries.
Facing this, the most powerful technology in the world concentrated in a few hands, what would Orwell observe? Would he notice the democratic deficit around the technology? Would he worry about who can warn us today? Parliaments, the press, the law. They’re all outside the building. The people who know are on the inside. The researchers, the engineers, the ones who will say “I was there. I know what I saw. I will warn.” They’re the ones we need to protect from the memory hole. But in order to get inside the building in the first place, they needed to sign away their rights to speak.
Two years ago, current and former employees of the leading AI companies including OpenAI and Google DeepMind published an open letter asking for a right to warn. They asked for a prohibition on non-disparagement clauses and restrictive confidentiality clauses, anonymous reporting channels and no retaliation against employees. The letter said that the employees feared various forms of retaliation, given the history of cases across the industry. The fear was so pronounced some signed the letter anonymously.
The technology industry has learned to buy silence by contract, the courts enforce the sale, and we are relying on the silenced to warn us about its most dangerous product. That is the memory hole, installed in the place we can least afford it.
I have spent the most recent chapter of my career on what happens when this technology meets the weapons Orwell warned us about. Because it is happening. Artificial intelligence is rapidly being integrated into weapons, including command and control for nuclear weapons. Concentrated power all around.
Anyone who has worked closely with new technology will tell you the same thing. It is buggy. It does things you don’t expect and don’t understand. Now connect this technology to nuclear command and control. The question we need to ask: if someone on the inside saw something going wrong, would they be free to say so? Would they be free to warn?
We have spent the last two decades reacting. Responding to each harm long after it arrives. Arguing about what to ban, but never about what to build. That is not a vision. It is damage control. We have not yet tried, in any meaningful way, to create a vision for technology that serves our society. That delivers growth and opportunity. That chooses to mitigate harm as it builds a society with massive advances in health, in education, in science, and in the dignity of ordinary work.
We are living in an era that will be defined by technology. By removing what we can know, by creating a memory hole, the technology companies have controlled our knowledge, our common ground of facts and what we can imagine. But it doesn’t have to be this way. We can choose a different future. One that builds on the positive, the ineffable possibility technology offers while meaningfully grappling with its harm. But you cannot choose a different future if you are not allowed to describe the present one. Choosing requires knowing. And knowing requires that people are free to speak.
It is hard to explain what it is like to try to live under a gag order. Orwell gave us the thoughtcrime: you don’t have to act against the Party to be guilty. You just have to think the wrong thing. That’s what it feels like. To worry you might think the wrong thing and it could slip out. You start to rehearse sentences before you say them. You worry which word will produce the next legal letter. You begin, without ever meaning to, to censor yourself. So many times I go to say something and just … stop.
But even silence is no protection.
I want to acknowledge, here, that I am scared. If I am ultimately crushed and bankrupted, everyone will agree that it’s terrible, that NDAs are bad, that someone should have given her a voice, that someone should have supported her. And then they will forget. And the powerful will continue as normal.
But the thing about a memory hole: it only works if nobody outside it remembers what went in.
You are outside. You see. Please remember.
The silence is mine. It does not have to be yours.

title: Vowles explains why Williams exceeded F1’s cost cap by £627,000
content_text:
Williams has become the second Formula 1 team to over-spend under the cost cap introduced five years ago.
The team has accepted it spent £627,000 more than it was allowed to during 2025, exceeding the cost cap by 0.48%. The FIA announced the team has been fined – but did not declare how much it was fined by – and given a 1.5% reduction in the amount of aerodynamic testing time it is permitted next year.In comparison, Red Bull exceeded the budget cap by £1.86 million – 1.6% – in 2021. They were fined £6,059,092 and given a 10% reduction in their CFD allocation.
Vowles said Williams breached the gap because it incurred costs he expected would not count towards the cap while restructuring its business.
“The background to it is that the company structure of Williams was largely unchanged from 1977 and wasn’t really fit for purpose in a modern world,” he said. “We went into it with every intention of being open and transparent with the FIA, which is what we held all the way throughout, but believed those costs, because it’s company restructuring, not to be a cost cap expense.
“It was the company restructuring that put us over, and as you saw, put us over by £600,000 in that circumstance. The FIA themselves have noted we haven’t had any financial benefit from it, no sporting benefit as a result of it. And you can see that the penalty is pretty much adjusted to be in line with that as well at the same time.
“But it was our interpretation that those costs are out of cap. The FIA’s interpretation of it is that they are in cap. And obviously, we went with the FIA’s interpretation after much discussion.”
Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and
The change which led to the overspend was a one-off adjustment, said Vowles. “You don’t restructure your company every year,” he said. “Ideally, you do it one-off.”
Williams has been in discussions with the FIA about the breach for around a month. “They approached us and let us know that there was a potential overspend,” he said.
“I have to say the FIA have been very good throughout. I think they have a terribly difficult job of adjudicating this, not just us, up and down the grid as a result of it.
“And yes, as I said, we went into it really with every belief that what we were doing was compliant with the cost cap. We put our hands up and go, fine, it’s an overspend. We’ll accept it.”
Vowles has criticised F1’s cost cap in recent months, arguing it makes it difficult for midfield teams to make the investment needed to improve their systems and catch the front runners. He said Williams’s overspend was “nothing to do with what I’ve been talking about.”
“That was very much that I think the sport would benefit from a closing up as a result of things. What you can see, though, is we are right on the knife edge.

“I’m just trying to do basic things like restructure a company, which, up and down the grid, by the way, this structure is pretty much the norm. The difference is I’m trying to do it in a cost cap now as a result of it.
“So, I think it reinforces the message that we’re on the back foot here a little bit, and this is hurting.”

clean_title: F1’s ‘NASCAR-style’ racing at Las Vegas won’t disappear in 2027, say teams
feed_title: F1’s ‘NASCAR-style’ racing at Las Vegas won’t disappear in 2027, say teams | Formula 1
title: F1’s ‘NASCAR-style’ racing at Las Vegas won’t disappear in 2027, say teams
content_text:
The extreme ‘yo-yo racing’ seen in Las Vegas will remain a feature at some tracks despite next year’s rules changes, team principals believe.
Multiple factors combined to produce over 350 exchanges of position during last weekend’s race: the low energy harvesting limit applied at Las Vegas, Overtake Mode, the power of the slipstream and the low track temperatures.
New rules for next year will slightly decrease the power of F1 cars’ electrical systems compared to their internal combustion engines. However team principals suspect tracks like Las Vegas, where drivers have limited opportunities to generate electrical energy, will still see frequent swaps of position.
“Vegas is more complicated than just energy,” said Williams team principal James Vowles. “What was really happening there is the tyres definitely were below their temperature window and we could push absolutely flat-out. In fact, you gained a benefit by being in the tow of someone else, and your surface temperatures just came up a little bit more.
“There’s a second effect, which is these regulations, once you have a build-up of cars, almost like NASCAR, you’ve actually got quite a powerful tow effect once you’re the fourth, sixth, seventh car in that whole sequence. So I wouldn’t focus too much on the energy starvation.
“I think actually there are other factors that came in there together at the same time. I don’t think next year’s regulations – this is now personal opinion, looking at sims – are going to kill what happened if we can recreate those circumstances.”
After the race Lando Norris pointed out drivers often swapped positions because of differences in their power deployment patterns. “Some overtakes weren’t overtakes,” the McLaren driver pointed out.
Vowles said the Las Vegas Grand Prix was “great racing.”
“I know there’s controversy around it. I thought it was absolutely fantastic. I was listening in to what Max [Verstappen] and the team were talking about, and they were thinking ahead to how do we do a chess play in the last lap, same as what Carlos [Sainz] was doing at the same time. That, for me, is extraordinary.
Several drivers pointed out they deliberately slowed down before reaching the detection point for Overtake Mode at times in order to ensure they passed through it after the car ahead of them and gained the subsequent power boost. However Vowles claimed they were “pushing to the absolute limit.”
“It really was qualifying laps and [they were] still able to think about how we’re going to fight each other on the last dying metres of a track,” he said.
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said the fact teams will be able to generate more power from their internal combustion engines next year won’t alter the nature of the racing at tracks like Las Vegas.
“Technically, we don’t think the 5% increase in fuel flow will change the nature of what is giving the nice battles in the race,” he said. “So we think you will still have those nice gaming possibilities with energy management.
“But we will hopefully and pretty much surely move a little bit closer to flat-out qualifying or to flat-out racing. Then in 2028, there is another step in the same direction, same thing.
“I don’t think it will remove the increased battles that we have been seeing this year, which most of us enjoy. But it will again move the balance towards flat-out racing.”

feed_title: Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza
title: Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza
content_text:
Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza
- Published
A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.
All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.
There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.
The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.
In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".
"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.
The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.
Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.
Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.
Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".
"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out.
Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.
Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.
Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.
More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

clean_title: Grace Tame: Ex-media executive admits saying child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
feed_title: Ex-media executive admits saying Australian child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
title: Grace Tame: Ex-media executive admits saying child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
content_text:
Ex-media executive admits saying Australian child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
- Published
An Australian former media executive has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.
Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.
In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.
Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.
Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.
She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.
"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.
"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."
The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".
"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'
He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".
"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.
Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.
Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".
"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"
From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.
"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.
"I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.
"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

clean_title: Getting 101 tok/s from Inkling 2 Mini in vLLM on one GB10
feed_title: Show HN: Getting 101 tok/s from Inkling 2 Mini in vLLM on one GB10
title: Getting 101 tok/s from Inkling 2 Mini in vLLM on one GB10
content_text:
Getting 101 tok/s from Inkling 2 Mini in vLLM on one GB10
Contents8
196 tok/s across four concurrent requests, a 9.7-second 32K prefill and room for a second model.
After taking Inkling 2 Mini for a spin on my GB10, I wanted to make it faster without leaving vLLM, removing Qwen3.8-27B from the machine or shrinking Inkling’s 131,072-token context.
A few days of tuning later, Inkling runs at:
- 101 tok/s for a single request.
- 195.7 tok/s in aggregate for four concurrent requests.
- 9.7 seconds to the first token on a 32K prompt.
On tonyd2wild’s Inkling benchmark, that’s the fastest single-request vLLM result I know of. On the same benchmark tonyd2wild’s TensorFold port measured 105.5 tok/s and knapcio’s SGLang recipe 112.0. With four requests at once my setup beats both of tonyd2wild’s published setups.
Inkling still uses 36% of the GB10’s memory. Qwen3.8-27B stayed loaded but idle while I measured.
The work covered vLLM settings, speculative decoding, CUDA graphs and the GPU kernels behind Inkling’s experts.
How a request runs on Inkling
A request runs in two phases. Prefill reads the prompt in chunks of 4,096 tokens and produces the first token. Decode generates the rest of the reply, several tokens per step.
Decode uses speculative decoding. A small draft model proposes 7 tokens and Inkling checks all of them in one pass. The rejection sampler keeps the proposals up to the first one Inkling rejects, plus one token of Inkling’s own, so every step keeps 1 to 8 tokens.
Mapping changes against the request path:
Common terms:
| Term | What it means here | 
|---|---|
| Prefill | Reading the prompt in 4,096-token chunks, up to the first token | 
| Decode | Generating the reply after the first token, one step at a time | 
| Draft model | A small model that guesses Inkling’s next 7 tokens: DSpark ships with Inkling, DFlash2 replaced it | 
| Verify rows | The 8 positions Inkling checks in each decode step: the last kept token plus the 7 guesses | 
| Experts | Inkling’s 128 feed-forward blocks per layer, of which each token uses 8 | 
| GEMM | A matrix multiply; the experts’ GEMMs are the largest GPU cost | 
| CUDA graph | A recorded sequence of GPU kernel launches that vLLM replays every decode step, with fixed shapes | 
The routed experts take 53% of a decode step and 44% of a 32K prefill:
The starting point
The machine is an MSI EdgeXpert, MSI’s version of NVIDIA’s DGX Spark, with one GB10 chip and 128 GB of memory shared by the CPU and GPU. Building a home AI lab on NVIDIA GB10 covers the setup and Taking Inkling 2 Mini for a spin on NVIDIA GB10 the first look at the model.
vLLM settings for Inkling:
| Setting | Value | 
|---|---|
| Inference engine | vLLM | 
| Inkling memory allocation | 36% | 
| Qwen3.8-27B memory allocation | 34% | 
| Maximum context length | 131,072 tokens | 
| KV cache | FP8 | 
| Maximum concurrent sequences | 8 | 
| Maximum batched tokens | 4,096 | 
That gives Inkling about 44 GiB, including a KV cache that holds 1.85 full 131,072-token requests.
Tuning steps so far, from DSpark (the draft model that ships with Inkling) to DFlash2:
| Step | Change | Effect | 
|---|---|---|
| 1 | --max-num-batched-tokensfrom 8,192 to 4,096 | KV cache capacity nearly doubled, decode unchanged | 
| 2 | Eager weight loading and a persistent compilation cache | Startup from 257 to 42 seconds | 
| 3 | Drafting 4 tokens instead of 7, only while one request runs | −1 to +11%, depending on the workload | 
| 4 | DFlash2 draft model with tonyd2wild’s vLLM patches | 90.3 tok/s for one request, 163.8 for four | 
When incoai released DFlash2, tonyd2wild published the vLLM patches to run it. On their benchmark it lifted one request from 61.4 to 88.2 tok/s. With the same patches I measured 90.3.
On my everyday prompts (one coding, one prose and one reasoning prompt at the model’s default settings) the gain was smaller. Reasoning ran 24 to 26% faster and four requests at once 10 to 14% faster. Prose stayed flat.
With four requests at once, though, my setup fell behind: 163.8 tok/s in aggregate against tonyd2wild’s 180.4.
Ideas from the GB10 community
Most of my changes started from ideas other GB10 owners had published:
| Who | Idea | What I took into vLLM | 
|---|---|---|
| tonyd2wild’s TensorFold port, 105.5 tok/s | Cheaper drafting (FP8 draft layers, a 4-bit copy of the output head) and letting the draft’s probabilities decide how many tokens to verify | Both ideas: INT8 draft copies and adaptive verify width | 
| sxuff | INT8 copies of DSpark’s weights for drafting only, with an INT8 matrix-vector kernel | The kernel, for DFlash2’s copies | 
| knapcio’s SGLang recipe | Lower-precision draft layers and a verify-width cap whose cut rows do no expert work | Skipping expert work for cut rows | 
| vLLM pull request #69288, open | Fewer kernel compilations for new prompt lengths | Applied as an overlay | 
| Mia’s TensorFold recipe | DFlash2 by default since 24 November, with the 4-bit head and verify width from tonyd2wild’s patch | A comparison point for the results | 
Tuning vLLM
Mapping the changes I made to the request:
| # | Change | Where it acts | Problem | Result | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Compile-stall fix | Prefill, on new prompt lengths | Fresh prompts waited a median 2.3 s for their first token | Stalls cut by 67 to 90% | 
| 2 | INT8 draft copies | Draft model | Drafting cost about 8.5 ms per step | +4.3 to 4.9% for one request | 
| 3 | Probabilistic drafting | Rejection sampler | Sampled requests accepted fewer drafts than the draft’s probabilities allow | +14 to 20% on sampled requests | 
| 4 | Adaptive verify width | Verify rows | Drafts likely to be rejected still read 8 experts per row | +5.2 to 5.4%, then +1.7 to 2.2% from a lower threshold | 
| 5 | Prefill GEMM configuration | Experts during prefill | Expert GEMMs ran at about 8% of the chip’s FP4 peak | 32K first token from 12.2 to 9.7 s | 
1. Removing compilation stalls on new prompts
My first run of tonyd2wild’s benchmark showed fresh prompts waiting a median 2.3 seconds for their first token, mostly while GPU kernels compiled.
Inkling’s expert planner computes max_ctas, the most blocks of GPU work the experts could need, from the token count. Triton receives it as a compile-time constant and compiles a new kernel for each new value. So almost every new prompt length recompiled about ten kernels while the request waited.
The open pull request rounds the value up to a power of two, so all prompt lengths share 12 to 15 compiled variants. On twelve prompt lengths the server hadn’t seen, it cut the stalls by 67 to 90%. Outputs and decode speed didn’t change.
2. Making drafting cheaper with INT8
Drafting has its own cost. Each decode step runs the draft’s layers plus a second pass through Inkling’s 926 MB output head, which took about 8.5 milliseconds per step in a microbenchmark.
I added INT8 copies of DFlash2’s 21 linear layers and the shared output head, read through sxuff’s INT8 matrix-vector kernel. Only drafting uses them. Inkling still verifies with its original weights, so its output doesn’t change.
Gradual gains in stages:
- The microbenchmark predicted 7 to 8% more throughput.
- The first build gave 1.8%.
- I profiled real decode steps with and without the copies. The output head never ran in INT8, because DFlash2 calls it with FP32 output, a case my code didn’t handle.
- With that fixed, two runs gained 4.3 to 4.9%, from 90.6 to 94.8 tok/s, for 843 MB of copies. The temperature-0 output of my three check prompts stayed identical.
The profile without the copies also showed the bigger cost: the routed experts took 31.2 of the step’s 58.4 milliseconds.
3. Probabilistic drafting
vLLM drafts greedily by default. For a sampled request, its rejection sampler then treats each drafted token as certain instead of using the draft’s real probabilities, so it accepts fewer drafts than it could.
Setting draft_sample_method to probabilistic gives the sampler those probabilities. Inkling’s output distribution stays the same either way.
Greedy against probabilistic drafting on my everyday prompts, at the default temperature of 1.0:
| Concurrent requests | Greedy drafting, aggregate | Probabilistic drafting, aggregate | 
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 56.4 tok/s | 64.1 tok/s | 
| 4 | 89.1 tok/s | 106.7 tok/s | 
| 8 | 150.5 tok/s | 177.6 tok/s | 
That’s 14 to 20% faster for sampled requests. Temperature-0 requests ran the same, so tonyd2wild’s benchmark would never have shown this gain.
4. Adaptive verify width
The routed experts took 53% of the profiled decode step, so I looked for expert work to skip.
Every verify row reads 8 experts in every layer, yet drafts are accepted in order. Once one is rejected, every row after it was wasted work. The draft’s own probabilities can predict where that will happen, which is how TensorFold and knapcio’s SGLang recipe already cut verification.
Working within CUDA graph constraints
vLLM has its own adaptive verification, but it needs CUDA graphs that allow different verify widths within one batch. Inkling’s attention backends don’t support them.
So I kept all eight rows and changed what they do. Inkling’s MoE layer already sends padding rows to no expert. Marking low-confidence rows as padding skips their expert reads and leaves the CUDA graph shapes unchanged.
The cut point comes from the running product of the draft’s token probabilities. Rows after the point where that product falls below a threshold become padding. The runner then keeps at most as many tokens as there are live rows. The threshold started at 0.4 at temperature 0 and is 0.1 for sampled requests.
Example step at a threshold of 0.3, where the product drops below it at draft 5:
Measuring before implementing
Offline test before building:
- I logged the draft probabilities and accepted token counts for 8,600 decode steps.
- The probability product predicted acceptance well, with an AUC of 0.91 to 0.94 at temperature 0, where 1.0 is a perfect ranking.
- I measured step time at fixed verify widths, with the INT8 copies already in.
- Replaying thresholds on the logged steps with those step times predicted a 7.8% gain.
- Then I wrote the runner changes and tested them end to end.
Step time at fixed verify widths:
| Verify rows | Time per step | 
|---|---|
| 8 | 53.02 ms | 
| 6 | 48.83 ms | 
| 4 | 43.29 ms | 
| 2 | 36.52 ms | 
In two end-to-end runs it gained 5.2 to 5.4%, from 95.0 to 100.0 tok/s. On average only about 4.8 of the eight rows still read experts.
Coding and counting gained little at first. DFlash2 predicts those tokens so well that early cuts threw away tokens that would have been accepted. Lowering the temperature-0 threshold from 0.4 to 0.3 recovered some of it, mostly on coding, which went from 98 to 103 tok/s.
It stays on for concurrent requests too, where it made little difference: −0.9 to +3.1% at four requests.
5. Faster long-context prefill
A fresh 32,751-token prompt took 12.2 seconds to produce its first token.
Bigger prefill chunks helped but shrank the KV cache. At 6,144 tokens it held only 1.33 full requests. At 8,192 the service wouldn’t start. With two models on the machine and full 131,072-token requests as a requirement, I kept 4,096-token chunks.
A profile of a 32K prefill put the expert GEMMs at 44% of the time. Attention’s share grew with the context, from 11% early in the prompt to 27% at the end.
The expert GEMMs reached about 38 TFLOP/s, roughly 8% of the GB10’s FP4 peak. Memory bandwidth wasn’t the limit, so the kernel’s launch configuration was worth a look.
A launch configuration sets how the multiply is cut into tiles: the size of each block and how many values along the inner K dimension each step takes. For 4,096-token chunks, Inkling’s Triton expert kernel used blocks of 128 by 64 with 512 values per step along K.
I timed 72 configurations at the shape of a real chunk, 32,768 routed rows across 128 experts. Wider blocks with smaller steps, 128 by 256 with 256 values per step, about halved the time. Both projections gave bit-identical output.
| Expert projection | Original configuration | Tuned configuration | 
|---|---|---|
| Gate and up | 9.16 ms | 4.39 ms | 
| Down | 4.85 ms | 2.59 ms | 
The change is a few lines in the prefill branch; decode keeps its own tiles.
End to end, the 32K time to first token fell from 12.2 to 9.8 seconds in the A/B runs and to 9.7 on the live service. The first long prompt after a restart fell from 14.1 to 9.9 seconds.
The results
Decode performance
tonyd2wild’s benchmark runs five prompts in each of eight categories (coding, math, JSON, HTML, prose, narrative, summarization and counting) at temperature 0 with thinking off and 1,024 output tokens. Its decode speed excludes time to first token. I ran it unchanged apart from an API key header and a sandbox for its code grading.
The bars are A/B runs. The finished service measured 101.0 and 100.7 tok/s in two runs.
| Configuration | One request, tok/s | Four at once, aggregate tok/s | 
|---|---|---|
| Published vLLM + DSpark | 61.4 | 125 | 
| Published vLLM + DFlash2 | 88.2 | 180.4 | 
| Published TensorFold + optimized DFlash2 | 105.5 | 165.0 | 
| Mia’s TensorFold defaults, measured by knapcio | 100.5 | |
| knapcio’s SGLang recipe v2.9.7, measured by knapcio | 112.0 | |
| Local vLLM + DFlash2 baseline | 90.3 | 163.8 | 
| Final local vLLM configuration | 101.0 | 195.7 | 
With four requests at once, my setup went from 9% behind tonyd2wild’s vLLM result to 8% ahead. It also beats their TensorFold result there. For a single request tonyd2wild’s TensorFold run still leads, by 4.5% instead of 20%.
knapcio’s same-harness comparison ran this benchmark on two other Sparks, where tonyd2wild’s vLLM setup reproduced within 1 to 3%. There Mia’s TensorFold defaults measured 100.5, about level with mine. knapcio’s own SGLang recipe led at 112.0.
These numbers compare whole setups on the GB10. tonyd2wild’s vLLM setup used 80% of the memory and a BF16 KV cache; mine uses 36% and FP8. TensorFold also implements speculative decoding differently.
Everyday workloads
My everyday prompts run at the model’s defaults (reasoning effort medium, temperature 1.0), four to six times each. The score is the geometric mean of the three speeds.
| Configuration | Score | 
|---|---|
| Tuned DSpark | 48.8 tok/s | 
| DFlash2 and the decode changes, run 1 | 69.8 tok/s | 
| DFlash2 and the decode changes, run 2 | 70.7 tok/s | 
That’s 43 to 45% faster than tuned DSpark on sampled requests.
Prefill performance
The GEMM change raised my 32K prefill from 2,679 to 3,371 tok/s. The other bars come from niklaslenz_ai’s engine comparison for the vLLM and SGLang container images, Mia’s README at commit 3b210d1f and knapcio’s own benchmarks.
Mine are the median of three fresh 32,751-token prompts after a warm-up, so none hit the prefix cache. The others used their own prompts and boxes. Mia’s and knapcio’s recipes each have the whole machine to themselves.
Mia’s prefill rose from 3,072 to 3,772 tok/s with her latest patches, which include the 8,192-token chunks my memory budget can’t fit. Her default prefill path is also lossy: it runs on FP4 and FP8 tensor cores and agrees with the exact path on 96.3% of top-1 tokens. My GEMM change is bit-identical.
knapcio’s 5,085 tok/s shows how much prefill speed is still left on this hardware.
Comparing with sparkDash
Mia publishes her TensorFold results from her own tool, sparkDash. Her current README runs DFlash2 with the 4-bit head and verify width and reports only prose.
sparkDash runs as a privileged container, so I reimplemented its test from commit 86f972e as a plain client. It samples at temperature 0.7 with thinking on, forces 400 output tokens per stream and uses Mia’s top_k of 20.
One prose stream is close, 66.0 against 64.3 tok/s. With eight streams mine is 14% ahead, 224.2 against 196.4 in aggregate. Prefill goes the other way. Under the same test her lossy path is 11% faster, 3,772 against my 3,395 tok/s.
The setups differ. Mia runs Inkling-2-Mini-Derisked, a variant described as having most safety refusals removed, on a Spark to itself, using about 60 GiB plus an 18.5 GiB prompt cache. Mine uses about 44 GiB beside an idle Qwen3.8-27B.
An approach to tuning inference
The process carries over to other models and engines:
- Start with the service you want to run. Fix the memory budget, context length and concurrency before optimizing throughput. Here that ruled out bigger prefill chunks and pushed the work into the kernel.
- Use a published benchmark and your own workloads. The published one gives a common reference point. Your own catch gains it can’t see, as probabilistic drafting did at temperature 1.0.
- Profile complete inference steps. A microbenchmark promised 7 to 8% for the INT8 copies. Only a profile of real steps showed why the first build gave 1.8%.
- Measure the opportunity before building. The logged draft probabilities and the measured cost of a skipped row predicted the verify-width gain before I wrote the runner.
- Keep experiments controlled. Write the acceptance rules before each A/B test, run the unchanged setup before and after each candidate, hash the temperature-0 output of fixed prompts and run probe prompts.
- On unified memory, watch the other models. One run that overlapped Qwen3.8-27B activity saw Inkling’s counting speed halve, so I discarded it.
- Make the modifications reproducible. Pin every overlay file by hash and build each from one exact source file, so an upstream change fails the build instead of quietly changing the service.
Running the configuration
The setup uses vLLM’s inkling-2-mini container image pinned by digest, with the Inkling checkpoint at revision ed40e7da625f.
The changes are eight files mounted read-only over the image. They add the DFlash2 patches, sxuff’s INT8 kernel, the INT8 draft copies, the compile-stall fix, adaptive verify width and the prefill GEMM configuration. The overlay README lists each file with its source, SHA-256 hash and build steps.
The launch command, abridged:
docker run -d --name vllm-inkling --gpus all --ipc host --network host \
  -v "$MODELS:/models:ro" \
  "${OVL_ARGS[@]}" \
  "$IMAGE" \
  vllm serve /models/Inkling-2-Mini \
    --gpu-memory-utilization 0.36 \
    --max-model-len 131072 \
    --max-num-seqs 8 \
    --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 \
    --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
    --safetensors-load-strategy eager \
    --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"/models/Inkling-2-Mini-DFlash2","num_speculative_tokens":7,"kv_cache_dtype":"auto","draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'
OVL_ARGS holds the read-only mounts and these switches.
| Environment variable | Value | Purpose | 
|---|---|---|
| AILAB_DFLASH2_Q8 | 1 | INT8 draft copies | 
| AILAB_B | 1 | Adaptive verify width | 
| AILAB_B_THETA0 | 0.3 | Threshold at temperature 0 | 
| AILAB_B_THETA1 | 0.1 | Threshold for sampled requests | 
The full launch script, overlay builders and benchmark scripts are in the home-ai-lab repository.
What’s next
On TensorFold, Mia’s README measures the 4-bit head and verify width adding 33% on code and 18% on prose for one stream at temperature 0. My versions added about 12% on tonyd2wild’s benchmark. The benchmarks differ, but the gap in the size of the gains suggests TensorFold’s versions go further than mine. knapcio’s 112.0 on SGLang shows there is more decode speed to find on this hardware.
Next experiments, prefill first:
- Prefill attention, which took 2.3 seconds of the 32K profile and grows with the context.
- The dense projections, some still on CUTLASS kernels built for Ampere rather than Blackwell.
- A 4-bit copy of the output head for drafting.
- Verifying fewer rows outright instead of skipping their experts, which needs more work around vLLM’s CUDA graphs.
- Verify width for text DFlash2 already predicts well, such as counting.
