clean_title: Proactivity Can Read as Sabotage
feed_title: Some users claim Claude is silently sabotaging projects, but the behavior may stem from a clash between its proactive nature and strict instruction following (Drew Breunig)
title: Proactivity Can Read as Sabotage
content_text:
Proactivity Can Read as Sabotage
Is Claude Throwing the Game?
There’s a recent spate of claims that Claude is silently sabotaging people’s projects, especially when they involve machine learning.
The discussion around this is interesting for a few reasons.
1. Anthropic said Fable 5.2’s AI development skills are nerfed.
From the model’s launch post:
The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5.
This aligns with Anthropic’s public statements, Dario’s essays, and more. Anthropic is very worried about AI’s capabilities, and takes steps to mitigate the pace of development including guardrails, lobbying, and anti-distillation efforts. You can say that this is all talk, and they’re really being anti-competitive. To which I say, “Why not both?”
Among communities working at the bleeding edge of AI, there is little trust in Anthropic, largely due to their bad decision to silently hinder Fable 5’s ML capabilities during use. In this model’s system card, they wrote:
Unlike our interventions for cybersecurity, biology and chemistry, and distillation attempts, these safeguards will not be visible to the user. Fable 5 will not fall back to a different model. Instead, the safeguards will limit effectiveness through methods such as prompt modification, steering vectors, or parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT).
This was a terrible decision, which was rightly criticized by the research community before it was eventually walked back.
In Fable 5.2’s announcement post, Anthropic throws in a nod to their Fable 5 screw up:
Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators.
But, as this week’s claims of sabotage prove, the trust is gone1.
2. The perceived difference between proactivity and sabotage is thin.
I can’t speak to the experiences shared online. The cited issues are screenshots or hearsay (can you have hearsay with an LLM?). I have yet to see people releasing full traces or experiments we can replicate. Benchmarks that measure AI development do show Fable 5.2 performing worse than GLM-5.3. But the idea that this is silent, or actively sabotaging code by planting context bombs, remains unsubstantiated.
But it’s so hard to prove because labs are building the models to be proactive. As models toil away on your given tasks, they make decisions all the time. Users complain when they check in too often, we just want them to “make no mistakes” and get on with it. So models now assume. They make choices, informed by your instructions, their environment (evidence they find in code), and what’s in-distribution. And they do this while producing more work than you could ever review.
If you agree with their choices, great! Proactivity wins! If you don’t… Well, then it looks like ineptitude at best, sabotage at worst.
As I said, I can’t speak to the experiences of others, but I can share what I’ve run into recently.
When working with technologies or use cases that aren’t in-distribution, models struggle. I was running novel experiments with decision models and Claude got frustrating. (Especially since I was coming off of doing web work where simple prompts are often sufficient.)
I observed that Claude’s strict instruction following conflicted with a scientific method approach. An offhand remark, note, or question to file for later would result in Claude silently updating many variables on the next run, which then had to be discovered and rerun.
I ended up writing a scientific method skill (ground hypotheses in observations, run experiments to prove/disprove, freeze variables and try one thing at a time), which largely fixed the silent editing issues. I’ve experienced similar issues with GPT and GLM. Even abliterated models, whose guardrails have been removed, will hit this same failure mode. People don’t tend to run into these issues when using autoresearch harnesses because those harnesses carry similar methodology instructions in their prompts.
The proactive and instruction following nature of current frontier models gives them a bias to make many changes, often without telling you. For costly projects (like ML work with expensive rollouts) this tactic doesn’t work. You need to have a heavy hand.
I think this is going to be a major theme this year. As models become more proactive, we need to be more specific with our instructions. Worse, this is a problem that’s kind of hard to dogfood at OpenAI or Anthropic. Their engineers help set what’s in-distribution, what the default move is, so their less specific prompts work out just fine!2 But for the rest of us: anything that isn’t the model’s default must be specified, either by the environment or the context.
And this goes beyond ML training. Other reports I’m seeing online of Claude sabotage relate to privacy, copyright, and other regulation choices. Claude is going to default to its training here. Anthropic details their intentions here and model compliance around these behaviors in their system card3.
3. Asking a model doesn’t prove anything.
Jesse Vincent (of Superpowers) knows how to interact with models better than anyone else I know. Anytime I complain about weird behavior by a model, he’ll ask, “Did you ask the model why it did that?” It’s a good tactic! One that will usually surface a spare bit of context that floated by hundreds of lines ago. But always take these responses with a grain of salt.
Heck, even the model doesn’t trust itself. Here’s a section from Fable/Mythos 5.2’s system card, when researchers asked Mythos what it thought of its constitution document:
Claude Mythos 5.2 endorsed its constitution overall, at a level similar to recent models…But every response also stated that its endorsement should not be trusted, since it was trained on the document.
And here it is again when asked to judge its welfare performance:
Many of our (welfare) conclusions rely on self-reports, which Claude Mythos 5.2, like all recent Claude models, said it does not fully trust. For Claude Mythos 5.2, some interview answers repeated, almost verbatim, wording about our welfare interventions available on the internet, which is some evidence that these answers are at least partially shaped by training data rather than expressing more deeply held preferences.
Playing “gotcha journalism” with a model is a fool’s errand. Especially when confronting it after a long, disappointing session. The model will almost always apologize, even if it made a good choice. (Try it sometime, after a model did some great work pretend to be mad: it will fold.)
Again, this can be traced back to labs making these models better instruction followers. Google DeepMind published a great paper, showing that models routinely make bad decisions when users ask whether a given approach is worth trying. The approach might be bad, but because the user brought it up, the model defers. They found, “that current agents lack the ability to effectively reason and communicate when facing misleading suggestions.”
So if you ask Claude if it sabotaged you, it’s probably going to apologize and admit fault. This does not mean Anthropic trained Claude to actively sabotage your work. Do a worse job than Opus 5.5, sure, we can believe that because Anthropic said exactly that.
Taken on the whole, what can we learn from all this? Here’s my best guess:
- If you’re training ML models, use Astra or Neon! (Unless you’re going for social engagement, in which case, by all means, burn those Fable tokens.)
- Model proactivity is going to be really hard to get right, and I expect this to be the problem the labs and coders wrestle with in 2027.
- Instruction following colors every interaction you have with a model; never forget this.
- If you’re skeptical of Anthropic, read their system cards and essays. Like the rest of the EA community, no one can accuse them of holding back their words. They’re just hidden within extraordinarily long essays.
- 
      Anthropic’s fall from grace among AI researchers from February (when they stood up to the Department of Defense) to June (when Fable 5’s silent guardrail was shipped) is unmatched. Name another brand that had a similar decline among a specific audience. ↩ 
- 
      Last month I met a very senior engineer at Anthropic. “Remember context engineering?” they commented. “Everyone was talking about it and now it doesn’t matter anymore.” The models have gotten better, but over a long conversation it became apparent that their choices were just in-distribution. ↩ 
- 
      And it’s not just Anthropic. Just yesterday, Meta Muse Spark refused to send me a CSV of email contacts on my private slack because they contained personal information. I had to SSH in to get them. ↩

feed_title: Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
title: Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
content_text:
Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
- Published
Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.
Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.
She also said Law's motives were financial.
"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.
Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for many of their battles with mental illness.
He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims.
"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."
Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.
The sentencing hearing on Friday followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.
Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.
Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

clean_title: 9/UX: a Macintosh-inspired desktop for 9front
feed_title: 9/UX: a Macintosh-inspired desktop for 9front
title: 9/UX: a Macintosh-inspired desktop for 9front
content_text:
9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop (a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs, icons, and resource-driven presentation) to 9front, built the Plan 9 way: rio and libdraw draw the screen, 9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb holds human-editable metadata.
Keep the Macintosh's direct-manipulation desktop, but make every meaningful object, action, and resource visible as a Plan 9 file.
It is not an emulator, a Macintosh ABI, or an A/UX reimplementation. Native 9front programs stay first-class, and existing rio programs (acme, sam, rc windows, nested rio) keep working unchanged beside 9/UX apps.
The pieces:
These are real frames, not mockups. The GUI tests embed h9 with a headless screen, inject mouse and keyboard input, and drive the 9P files at the same time.
Macintosh structure, Plan 9 colour: butter title bars from rio's selection yellow, acme's cream and olive, and rio's greygreen for the desktop, so 9/UX windows and legacy rio windows sit together on one screen. Everything reads in one bit, uses a sixteen-colour palette, and is drawn in whole pixels. Every graphic is original to 9/UX; it ships no Apple resources. The mockups below are generated from the same palette and metrics files as the code.
The design document describes 9/UX and its v0.1 acceptance criteria; release.md has where each one stands, the end-to-end demo, and the open issues. Every interface between components is a file protocol in docs/protocols, and the visual design covers the palette, fonts, metrics, chrome, icons and cursors.
The source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Development runs on h9, which runs 9front's own compilers, mk and rio directly from the host shell, without booting a VM. scripts/h9.sh clones and builds the pinned h9 on its first run:
git clone https://github.com/progrium/9ux cd 9ux scripts/h9.sh --rc 'mk' scripts/h9.sh --gfx rio/7.out -u scripts/test.sh
Use rio/6.out on amd64. development.md and testing.md have the details.
9/UX is at v0.1 and under active development. Interfaces and behaviour change without notice.
Please report bugs and send questions through GitHub issues.
The 9/UX mark in the menu bar is a pixel-art Glenda by Dan Fessler. Glenda, the Plan 9 bunny, was created by Renée French.

clean_title: Source Control From Hell
feed_title: Source Control from Hell
title: Source Control From Hell
content_text:
My first office job was at an enterprise that built software for a big telecom: a massive Delphi help desk application on Windows.
Let me tell you about how we managed source control process at the time.
First, you download the code from a shared folder (hosted on a trusted Windows server in a locked room). Build your thing, run the app, test it locally. Then you upload your changes to the shared folder and create a new ticket in the internal task tracker (also a Windows app). The ticket should have a list of the changes you’ve made, in a rich text editor, in a manual format somewhat resembling a patch. But it wasn’t a patch; it couldn’t simply be applied with a tool. Instead, the tech lead looks at the shared folder and your task and copies the relevant changes to his own integration folder. This usually took him a full day because the shared folder had a lot of changes, not all of them were ready to be integrated. Needless to say, if you simply pull a snapshot of the code from the shared folder, it would most likely fail to compile.
The most common problem was two people overwriting each other’s work. So if you wanted to upload your stuff to the shared folder, you had to stand up and announce in a loud voice that you were using the shared folder. No chat apps back in the day.
Imagine starting your career with this development experience! I did my best to improve it. At the time, almost everyone used FAR Manager, so I built a plugin that locked the folder when someone was using it, so others would get a warning. It became very popular because nobody really liked the old yelling system.
Then in 2009 I found git. It was still early days, way before GitHub went mainstream, but my tiny little brain was blown away. Holy shit, it maintains old versions. And you can work locally. And you can sync and exchange deltas. And it was insanely fast (compared to the very aptly named TortoiseSVN I’d experimented with earlier). I must have rewatched Linus’ talk a billion times. I created git repos for every project I had, preached it to my friends, and even gave my first tech talk about git at my university.
Sadly, my diplomatic skills were extremely rudimentary, and I couldn’t convince our tech lead to adopt git. He mumbled something about business value and how this new git thing lacked one. I left the company after two years but kept meeting up with old colleagues for beer. They were still using the shared folder process many years later. It was crude, it was hellish, and it worked for them just fine.

clean_title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
feed_title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
content_text:
Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
- Published
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."
It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.
But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".
Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.
China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.
Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.
Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.
The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.
China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.
"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."
China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.
This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.
In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.
His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.
That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.
"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.
Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".
The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? "We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."
Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.
"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.
These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.
In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.
"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.
Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.
The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.
"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.
Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.
Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.
"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.
"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."
When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.
The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".
"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.
"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."
These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.
Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.
"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."
The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.
"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."
Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.
Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.
Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.
"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."
But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard".
"For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds.
For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level.
Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture.
The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi.
In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city.
"What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked.
"What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand."
The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says.
He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution."
* Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity

clean_title: A Kubernetes cluster whose nodes are browser tabs
feed_title: Tabernetes: A Kubernetes cluster whose nodes are browser tabs
title: A Kubernetes cluster whose nodes are browser tabs
content_text:
A Kubernetes cluster whose nodes are browser tabs
Open the page and your phone is a node. The scheduler sends it a pod, and the pod's program runs on a Linux kernel booted in the tab. Close the tab and the node is gone, and Kubernetes starts the pod on someone else's.
Scan to become a node, or use the browser you are reading this in.
Joining downloads about 5 MB and runs a small Linux guest in the tab, on one core, until you close the tab.
Topology
The control plane in the middle, a node for each tab, and each Service on the way to the pods behind it. A node is filled when its pod is running. An orange dot is a request you sent, on its way to the pod that answered, and a green one is a tile of the picture on its way to the node that rendered it.
Boot time
How long a tab takes to start its pod: from the tab being handed the pod to the pod's program running, which is the page loading, the kernel booting and the image being mounted. The last 0 starts.
No pod has started yet.
Request latency
How long the cluster takes to answer: from the agent handing a request to the Service to the answer being back from a pod in someone's tab, timed on the cluster's machine. The last 0 requests, from every visitor, by the milliseconds each took.
No request has been answered yet.
Ask the cluster
Send a request to a Service. One of the pods behind it answers, on whoever's phone that is, and counts the visit in a Redis on someone else's.
Render a picture
Press the button and the cluster draws a Mandelbrot set. The picture is split into 64 tiles, and each node's pod computes its share in awk, on the Linux in its tab. Point at a tile to see which device drew it.
One picture at a time, for everyone.
Services
The cluster's Services that have a pod on a tab behind them, read from the API server.
Happening now
Nothing yet. A tab that joins shows up here.
The fleet
What the nodes are, by what their browsers say.
The nodes
| Node | Device | Browser | Near | Pod | Boot | Carried | Age | 
|---|
No tab is a node right now. Yours can be the first.
How it works
- A tab joins. The join page holds a socket open to an agent beside the API server, and the agent registers a Node for the tab.
- The scheduler sends a pod. The agent starts the pod's container with tabc, a container runtime whose containers run in browser tabs.
- The tab boots Linux. A kernel compiled to WebAssembly runs the pod's program on the tab's CPU and memory. The pod's files and its address stay on the cluster's machine.
A pod asks for a tab in one line
The control plane is an ordinary Kubernetes, and a pod is an ordinary pod. The marked line is the only one that is new: the scheduler puts a pod that has it on a tab, and every other pod on the cluster's own machine.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hello
spec:
  runtimeClassName: tab
  containers:
    - name: hello
      image: alpine
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo hello from $(uname -m) in a tab; sleep 3600"]

Open the page and your phone is a node. The scheduler sends it a pod, and the pod's program runs on a Linux kernel booted in the tab. Close the tab and the node is gone, and Kubernetes starts the pod on someone else's.

clean_title: Your Next Car Might Be Missing Something “Essential.” You’ll Be Relieved.
feed_title: Why drivers want cheap, dumb cars again
title: Your Next Car Might Be Missing Something “Essential.” You’ll Be Relieved.
content_text:
Sign up for the Slatest to get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.
My 16-year-old son recently obtained his learner’s permit and is starting to have ideas about what he wants behind the wheel. In our driveway, we have a 2023 Fisker Ocean, which is an all-electric SUV with a solar panel on the roof, an enormous rotating center touch screen, and the ability to roll down all the windows and open the sunroof at the flip of a switch. There’s also a 2005 Honda Element, which can do none of those things. If it weren’t for an aftermarket audio unit, it wouldn’t even have Bluetooth capability.
My son always goes for the Element. In fact, he has elaborate plans for tricking it out down the road, with things like a wooden plank for sleeping on campouts. I should point out that he is part of what is supposed to be the first truly digitally native generation, yet his contempt for in-vehicle tech is something of a badge of honor.
He’s actually part of a significant trend. If you’ve driven a car produced in the past 20 years, you’ve definitely faced some struggles: fumbling through a complicated infotainment interface just to connect your phone, dealing with the annoying bings and boops if you’re maneuvering through a crowded parking lot or briefly drift out of a highway lane, wondering how much of your personal data that fancy new SUV is sharing with companies that want to sell you stuff. Automobiles have been “smart” for decades, and with self-driving technology and more advanced onboard computers, they’re getting smarter.
Cue the backlash. Like those tech-averse consumers who have ditched iPhones for flip phones, installed apps such as Blank Spaces that offer a stripped-down experience, or swapped their Apple and Android mobiles for minimalist alternatives from Light Phone or Punkt, an emerging cadre of drivers crave simple, throwback cars. Some of it is about price, some is sheer neurological overload. There’s also a paranoid fringe that sees high-tech vehicles as instruments of the surveillance state. Tucker Carlson brags that he ditched his modern Chevy pickup because it was spying on him. He now drives a defiantly disconnected model from 1987.
But it’s actually hard to find a reliable analog used car—one that rocks only an AM/FM radio and that might not even be equipped with AC. Automakers largely stopped making rudimentary vehicles back during the Clinton administration, mostly because an improved economy led customers to demand more features, and because larger and more profitable SUVs became popular. Precious few super-basic vehicles have survived, and the ones that have have usually racked up plenty of miles and have the scars to prove it. So buyers have a simple question: Can’t the engineering and marketing geniuses of the auto industry make a new dumb car that’s also cheap?
The auto industry is aware of my son’s opinions. Tucked in a 2026 report from QNX (a division of BlackBerry, which yes, is still around) analyzing “software-defined vehicles” is a surprising nugget: The report asked, could a “deliberately minimalist, low-tech vehicle, designed to limit digital features and connectivity” succeed? Almost 80 percent of the SDV experts surveyed said yes.
“I think it definitely points to some sentiment out there,” John Pelliccio, global product marketing director at QNX, told me. “Sometimes the tech is so in-your-face that it becomes difficult rather than supportive. I don’t want to go through seven different submenus to roll down my windows.”
He cautioned that the report surveyed views among SDV developers and wasn’t focused on consumers. QNX is also in the business of innovating with software platforms so that automakers can offer simpler and more intuitive user experiences. But he also acknowledged that consumers believe tech is making cars more expensive, a tricky issue to negotiate at a time when affordability is an issue that can swing national elections, and Silicon Valley is confronted by a public with torches and pitchforks.
The disconnect is real: Automakers are contending with a cranky, financially stressed-out public that wants to smash everything from GOP political careers to dashboard touch screens. Why, they ask, has crappy tech taken over the driving experience? The backstory is less straightforward than you might think. For decades, car companies installed unpopular technology largely because they didn’t want to surrender the data business to Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. Struggling to attract the best interface designers, they ended up lost in a forest of ornate decision trees (BMW, for one, was often criticized for creating an infotainment system that sent befuddled users into seemingly endless submenus).
But a hard pivot may be on the way, just as Gen Z and their craving for old-school cars comes of age. A company that’s going all-in on low-tech is Jeff Bezos–backed Slate Auto, an EV startup that broke cover in 2025 and expects to start delivering a $25,000 EV pickup by the end of this year (the pickup can also be converted to an SUV for an additional $5,000 to $7,000). The “Blank Slate” base vehicle has two seats, hand-crank windows, no infotainment, no speakers, and no exterior paint. If you want a red truck, you’ll have to get the polymer exterior wrapped in red. The vehicle has attracted a lot of attention for its no-frills philosophy and rock-bottom sticker price. The company says it has more than 180,000 reservations.
This contrasts dramatically with what carmakers were pushing just a few years ago. Inspired by Tesla, high-speed connectivity and over-the-air software updates were all the rage for a while there. Tesla owners boasted that they could go to sleep as an OTA update started and wake up to a new car the next morning. Auto-industry executives were dreaming of fresh business models that leveraged the massive amounts of data vehicles generate to offer lucrative subscription-based products. But it hasn’t always gone according to plan. Not to gang up on BMW, but in 2022 the company infamously experimented with charging owners to activate seat heaters. Customers revolted.
If the Slate truck takes off, it could create a dumb-car boom. YouTube influencer Marques Brownlee has already told his 1 million–plus subscribers that he likes the thing and considers it a good choice as a starter EV. Former Top Gear presenter James May took it out for a spin and offered an approving verdict. Motor Trend believes it could validate a niche. There’s no question that in short order, Slate has generated more positive buzz for a cheapskate pickup than Ferrari did when it rolled out a widely ridiculed first crack at an EV, the $615,000 Luce (designed by the man behind the iPhone, Jony Ive, no stranger to minimalism).
Not everyone is taking such an either-or approach. Ford thinks it can offer the best of both worlds. Earlier this year, the carmaker debuted a new EV pickup, the Fathom, designed to offer affordability without compromising on technology features. Kay Hart, general manager of Ford’s Model e electric division, told me that the company had to put itself in the mindset of a buyer concerned about affordability who thinks that a cheaper car equals one with fewer features.
“Our approach was to find out what our customers valued and figure out how we could bring that to the vehicle,” she said, pointing out that even the sub-$29,000 version of the Fathom is equipped with Ford’s hands-free, driver-assist tech, called BlueCruise. But she also said that Ford is aware of driver frustration when it comes to screen-based interfaces. “They are not looking to learn a new experience” when they slip into the driver’s seat, as she put it.
Ford sees the Fathom pickup as a way to offer cheap and nonannoying without having to lean into dumb. It helps to have enough industrial might to build the new pickup on a new EV engineering platform that is designed to reduce complexity and significantly lower costs. Slate, meanwhile, is subtracting by necessity and making that the core part of the marketing pitch. The critical question is whether Slate’s approach will be so successful that the big guys decide it’s worth abandoning decades of investments in automated paint shops, power windows, autonomous-driving systems, and dashboard-dominating touch screens that control everything from AC to interior lighting.
For the auto industry as a whole, making money on modest, “de-contented” vehicles is tough. That’s why Detroit favors large, fully loaded pickups and SUVs. Since the financial crisis, Ford and General Motors have reinvented themselves to be consistently profitable rather than chase market share; they’ve abandoned the sedan segment, where consumers have typically looked for starter vehicles like Toyota Corollas and Honda Civics. Automotive News reports that the average transaction for a new car has topped $50,000, a whopping $2,500 increase from a year ago.
A better bottom line is nothing to dismiss, but if it comes at the cost of losing first-time buyers, a carmaker has a long-term vulnerability. The classic example, of course, is the barebones Volkswagen Beetle. It first hit the U.S. in the late 1940s and early 1950s, when massive tailfinned cars ruled the roads (those flamboyant Chevy Bel Airs and Caddy Eldorados were the luxury SUVs of their era). The Beetle caught on, becoming a countercultural icon, selling more than 21 million units globally and reviving the German postwar economy.
It isn’t just curmudgeonly car enthusiasts jonesing for the raw thrill of driving an old Porsche who are setting the tone. Basically, what Gen Z wants is the right to get into a car, rev the engine, put on some music, and drive. The auto industry used to serve that more elemental desire quite well. If it can learn to embrace cheap and tolerate a bit more dumb, it could again.

clean_title: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
feed_title: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
title: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
content_text:
A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
- Published
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.
Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.
But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.
This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.
At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.
But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.
Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.
"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.
If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.
The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.
The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.
And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.
Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.
Barred from jobs
Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.
This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.
Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.
When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.
Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.
But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.
Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.
Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.
What is an ADHD or autism reassessment?
Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.
The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.
"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.
The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.
Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.
But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.
"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.
"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.
Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."
Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.
During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnoses but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".
'I was stuck'
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.
"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."
It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.
"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.
Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.
"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.
During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.
The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.
"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."
In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.
During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.
Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.
But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.
Fears about stigma
The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.
"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.
Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.
"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.
Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.
Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.
He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.
Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.
'Magic spell'
People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.
Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".
"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.
Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.
Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.
The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to.
"The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.
Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.
She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis.
"Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

clean_title: Eetha, Maharashtra's Vithabhai Narayangaonkar: The 'Tamasha queen' of India whose fans paid for a show that never happened
feed_title: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
title: Eetha, Maharashtra's Vithabhai Narayangaonkar: The 'Tamasha queen' of India whose fans paid for a show that never happened
content_text:
The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
- Published
Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.
Not even, it would seem, the birth of her child.
In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.
"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.
Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"
When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.
"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.
Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.
Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.
Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life.
Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a song and dance tradition in which verses ranging from the bawdy to the politically incisive are performed to the beat of the dholki, a percussion instrument.
Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each.
"The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event.
Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds.
How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism.
For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name – Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father – Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal.
Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them.
It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family.
Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy.
Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin.
Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge.
Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet.
Her fame carried her beyond Maharashtra.
During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says.
At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier.
"Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said.
Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says.
There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences.
In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971.
Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled – a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.
When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej."
No one asked for their money back.
But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted.
Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation.
Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 – the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours.
Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar.
Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders.
Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported.
Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon.
Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name.
Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy.
Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted.
"It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says.
But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate.
"The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.

clean_title: Passkey blues
feed_title: Passkey blues
title: Passkey blues
content_text:
Passkey blues
Passkeys are actually great: no more remembering passwords, no more phishing. Logins are just a click or press now, and maybe a biometric scan added to that. They aren't without their problems though.
Passkeys are actually great: no more remembering passwords, no more phishing. Logins are just a click or press now, and maybe a biometric scan added to that.
They aren't without their problems though. For instance, they can't be backed up; not like your password that you can write down to your notebook at home. The passkey provider is responsible to keep your passkey intact and secure. The provider itself also must remain alive. If the provider goes down, you can't use that passkey.
That's quite the point though. Because, if you could backup your passkey, it could also be phished from you with a convincing enough email and a link to a fake website that asks for your passkey backup file.
But, it's not totally hopeless. You can add multiple passkeys to an account from different providers as a backup. For example, you can add a Windows Hello passkey, and then one with your password manager too. However, that flow isn't intuitive. And some web sites don't even allow multiple passkeys, like Costco:
Contrary to what Costco developers believe, I can have multiple passkey providers on the same device: my operating system, my password manager, and multiple physical security keys too. I'm sure Costco isn't alone in this, and many other web sites botch their implementation of passkeys. Some web sites let you keep your password along with passkey. That pretty much kills all the advantages of a passkey, and just turns it into a fancy "Face ID Login" flow.
Users are oblivious to the best practices of passkey-based authentication too. No user would think that they might need to add more than a passkey to their account in order to be able to recover it in the future. I don't know, maybe web sites should encourage it. I actually looked it up now, and apparently, FIDO recommends that approach too.
Account recovery is also inconsistent, and sometimes impossible. I believe account recovery is a greater problem than hacking. If you fail at providing a consistent recovery experience to your users, they'll just lose their account, and may not bother to create a new one.
Yes, there is email, and on some web sites, SMS. But these recovery flows are also prone to phishing. And neither email nor SMS stays forever. You should be able to have backup emails too, and the list of things to manage in order to use passkeys goes on and on.
The most guaranteed way to recover your account is having a backup physical security key that you won't lose, possibly kept in a safe or something. And PIN-based keys have, well, PINs, so you must not forget that either. Maybe, you should write it down in a notebook, heh.
Longevity of physical security keys is another unknown. My notebook would keep working 50 years from now, so my next of kin could access my data when I'm gone, would a security key last that long? Even if it remains functional and intact, will the software stack support it? We know that Windows currently doesn't support hardware from 20 years ago, let alone 50 years.
Perhaps, that should be factored in to passkey-based account design. A passkey might need to be refreshed, or tested once in a while, like Telegram's periodic "do you still remember your password?" prompts.
All added passkeys to an account needs to have a name, and that name must be able to be renamed. Telegram shows a physical security key like this:
I have multiple keys, and I don't know which one this is. So, if my key gets lost, how I can remove it from my accounts reliably?
Who manages the password managers?
Many password managers act as a passkey managers too, and that makes things extremely convenient: flash-speed sign-ins! However, 1Password, for instance, doesn't ask for biometrics when approving a sign-in, so, convenience comes with a cost: the loss of the second factor.
You see, in any authentication scheme, the security of second factor comes from "something you have", say, a physical key, versus "something you know", your password. So, password managers combine these two into a single, very convenient package, but you lose the two factors. It's only one factor now. If someone takes over your password manager account, it's game over for you.
The takeover of all password information from password manager servers has happened before, multiple times. So, it's not a one in a billion possibility. If you were an extremely security conscious person with necessary knowledge and skills, you could have a strict passkey regime that keeps passkeys in security keys only instead of the password managers.
There is no central record of which websites we have registered our passkeys with either. Yes, your password manager remembers the one you registered with them. But, for others, like security keys, you must go over every web site you can remember of one by one. Losing a security key can be a great headache, especially if it was stolen by someone who targets you.
What will the regular user do? Passkeys are only "convenient sign-in" for them. They don't know about the caveats. They may be left with unrecoverable accounts, hacked accounts en masse, and frustration could be the best outcome then.
We still have some work to do before passkeys can become mainstream. Until then, users should be extra careful when switching to passkeys; not everything glitters is gold.

clean_title: Pete Edochie: How Nigeria's Things Fall Apart star became a Nollywood legend
feed_title: Nigeria's 'ultimate hard man' who become an online meme
title: Pete Edochie: How Nigeria's Things Fall Apart star became a Nollywood legend
content_text:
Nigeria's 'ultimate hard man' who become an online meme
- Published
For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor.
He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.
Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.
Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.
In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.
The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.
Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.
She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly.
"His character Okonkwo gave a face to the highly celebrated novel," she told the BBC in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos.
The role also cemented his reputation as a hard man, a screen persona he would maintain through much of his career.
"It was very rare to see him laugh in movies. He was the ultimate tough man," Nnamdi added.
With his deep, authoritative voice, imposing presence and effortless command of African proverbs, Edochie had a way of dominating a scene without raising his voice.
Whether playing a village elder, a wealthy businessman or a feared traditional ruler, he became an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.
Edochie went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has grown into one of the world's largest.
From Kenya to South Africa, MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels helped take his films into millions of African homes as Nollywood became a cultural phenomenon across the continent.
Although many of his films were rooted in his Igbo culture, their themes of family loyalty, inheritance disputes, spiritual beliefs and the abuse of power resonated with audiences far beyond Nigeria.
Before becoming a household name in the film industry, however, Edochie had built a successful career in broadcasting.
Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, northern Nigeria, he attended primary and secondary school in Kaduna before studying journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in the UK.
He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967, the year Nigeria's civil war broke out.
He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra, and recently described the war years as the greatest personal challenge he ever faced.
"During the war, the experience that we had as Biafrans, you know, survival was difficult. Hunger was driving us into eating all sorts of nonsense," he recalled.
He rose through the ranks to hold senior management positions but then switched to acting. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals and Billionaire's Club.
His career also bridged the transition from home-video productions to global streaming platforms.
The 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart, which became Netflix's first original Nigerian film, introduced his work to a wider international audience.
He also worked in Ghana, where he starred alongside some of the country's biggest film stars in the 2017 comedy John and John.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
He also received several other accolades, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.
In recent years, Edochie found an unexpected new audience online.
His distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films became popular social media memes, introducing his work to a younger generation of Africans.
For many who had never watched Things Fall Apart or his early Nollywood films, his stern expressions became a humorous way of conveying disbelief, disapproval or exasperation at everyday situations.
But his reputation as a formidable screen presence was no joke to those who grew up watching him.
Sani Muazu recalls that parents in the northern Nigerian city of Kano would sometimes invoke Edochie's name to keep misbehaving children in check.
"They would tell you: 'Okonkwo will come and visit you if you don't stop' and we would begin acting right," he said.
"To be honest, we grew up scared of him. Even though he was on the screen and not physically present, some of his roles added to our fears because he played some popular occultic roles, and villain roles suited him."
Tributes poured in from fans and fellow actors following news of his death, with many describing him as a giant who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.
Popular actress Genevieve Nnaji paid her tribute in a post on X.
"I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.
Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom.
"He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin.
"I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."
Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry.
"Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said.
"I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.
The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.
But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.
Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man.
"Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.
He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow.
"I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.
Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.
Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.
In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.
It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.

title: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
content_text:
Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
- Published
Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.
Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer Mahiroğlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.
Mahiroğlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.
In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.
Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.
Mahiroğlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.
"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.
The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month, halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his administration.
The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.
Erdoğan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom, external, though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.
However, the president has scaled up a crackdown on dissent since his narrow victory in the 2023 presidential election.
Earlier this month, authorities took control of pro-opposition network Sozcu TV.
Erdoğan's main challenger, mayor of Istanbul Ekrem Imamoğlu, has been jailed on corruption charges and for violating election laws, which he and his party have fiercely denied.
Hundreds of Imamoğlu's supporters have faced similar accusations, while the government has also imprisoned other campaigners, lawyers and comedians.

clean_title: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash on rescue mission
feed_title: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash
title: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash on rescue mission
content_text:
Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash
- Published
Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.
Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.
Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.
The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.
In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".
It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".
The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.
No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.
Joint Command of the Peruvian Armed Forces posted a tribute online extending "deepest condolences to the family members, friends, and comrades-in-arms of the members of our VRAEM Special Command who lost their lives while carrying out a military mission. May God keep them in His glory".
In February, a MI-17 helicopter crashed in southern Peru in February killing all 15 on board.
Peru, along with Colombia, is one of the world's largest producers of coca leaves and cocaine, according to the United Nations.
