clean_title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
feed_title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
content_text:
'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
- Published
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.
"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.
Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.
Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.
On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.
The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.
The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.
Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.
- Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather - Published2 days ago
 
- Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving - Published3 hours ago
 
Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.
"My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said.
"Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?"
The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of New York City during the holidays.
There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.
Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.
"The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.
He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".
"We have a lot to be thankful for this Thanksgiving."
Some groups were not able to maneuver as easily. The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band is one of those missing out, due to a schedule conflict on Saturday.
“‘This can’t be happening’,” Rina Browder, mother of a snare drummer in the band, told local news, describing the band’s reactions.
"They were devastated. They've worked so hard for this. So many practices."
Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.
Speaking to the BBC on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.
The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.
"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua said.
But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".
The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.
Badua was hopeful his group would have the same experience he had when he first performed at the parade in 2003, as student drum major.
"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."
Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it needed to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.
"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Professor Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.
By Friday, 3,500 donors had stepped up to help the 410 students and their travel party. "This is truly phenomenal," said Houser.
While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain brought by the storm to eastern areas of the US.
Hundreds of thousands of homes were without power in the storm's aftermath Friday, and coastal areas had flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.
Additional reporting by Jessica Murphy

clean_title: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in
feed_title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
title: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in
content_text:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.
Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.
The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.
The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?
Surviving blackouts
Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.
Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.
I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.
To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.
Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.
Raving through the war
I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.
We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.
Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.
What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.
Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.
Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.
It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.
There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.
How does it all end?
The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.
So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.
But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.
Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.
And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."
Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.
Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.
At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.
The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

clean_title: Formula 1 planning new engine development freeze before 2030 rules change
feed_title: Formula 1 planning new engine development freeze before 2030 rules change | Formula 1
title: Formula 1 planning new engine development freeze before 2030 rules change
content_text:
Formula 1 intends to freeze power unit development again before introducing its new engine regulations in 2030.
Engine development was previously frozen between 2022 and 2025 before the current power unit rules were introduced this year. Dissatisfaction with the new V6 turbo hybrids led the FIA, Formula One Management and the teams to unanimously agree to replace them in 2030.The series intends to introduce V8 turbo hybrid power units which generate a much greater proportion of their total energy from the internal combustion engine. Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said the decision to hasten the replacement of the current power units was “probably one of the unique moments in the last five, 10 or 15 years that we pretty much all agreed on a direction.”
“It was very much pushed by the FIA,” he said, “but all the teams have been finding their way into the regulations and I think we’re all quite excited to go to it.”
In order to spare manufacturers the cost of simultaneously developing the current power units as well as the forthcoming ones, a freeze is planned for the final season under the current regulations, which is already a little over two years away. Mekies said the FIA plans to permit limited types of development work on the new power units before then.
“In terms of transition, it’s something that is part of the framework we have discussed,” he said. “The transition proposed has a current engine freeze for 2029. Then there are some dates in place into the framework before which you cannot start working on the V8, both in terms of single-cylinder work and in terms of complete V8 work.
“So that’s very much made in such a way that you minimise the difficult transition decisions that all the teams will have to take otherwise between, say, the 2028 or the 2029 campaign and the 2030 campaign. So that has been, at the moment, pre-set into these regulations.
“I’m sure it will need refinement and there will be many, many loops of refinement. But the big principle to ensure the basics that you are talking about are in it.”

title: Bronson Reed: Australian WWE star dies aged 38
content_text:
Australian wrestler Bronson Reed dies aged 38, WWE says
- Published
Professional wrestler Bronson Reed has died aged 38, World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) has announced.
The company said the wrestler, whose real name is Jermaine Haley, died on Friday due to medical complications but did not give further details.
Paying tribute, WWE added: "Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague."
They also offered condolences to the Australian's family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, and their daughter.
WWE has been contacted for further comment.
Haley was honoured at the WWE event at Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia on Friday.
The show began with a 10-bell salute for Haley and in his match, Canadian wrestler Kevin Owens wore an armband that read "Bronson" and addressed the crowd.
Owens said Haley loved performing.
"I knew for a fact, beyond performing in this ring, he loved his family more than anything so tonight if there is anything to take away from a tragedy like that - it's take care of each other and love each other... Forgive each other," Owens said.
"Bronson, for me, we were lucky to have you and you will be extremely missed."
WWE greats posted tributes online including the retired 16-time world champion Ric Flair, who wrote: "another soldier in our business that left us way too early!"
WWE Hall of Famer Diamond Dallas Page said "I was deeply saddened to read about the passing of Bronson Reed. I couldn't help but think of Eddie. Such a shame. My heart goes out to his friends & family. RIP brother."
WWE wrestler Eddie Guerrero - known as Latino Heat - died of heart failure at age 38 in 2005.
Australian pro wrestler Brendan Vink, who goes by Duke Hanson, posted "I love you, Jermaine." on X.
According to wrestling media outlets, Haley had recently been recovering from injuries sustained during the WWE Crown Jewel event in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia earlier in November.
He did not have a match during the event but was tossed off the stage and through a set of tables during a brawl.
Haley initially competed around the independent wrestling scene as Jonah Rock and J-Rock before signing with WWE in 2019.
He was released in 2021 before returning a year and continuing with WWE up until his death. In 2024, he won the André the Giant Memorial Battle Royal.
Haley is the second wrestler to die in the last few months after Benjamin Satterley, an English wrestling star passed away at the age of 40 in September.
No cause of death was provided at the time.

clean_title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
feed_title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
content_text:
Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
- Published
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.
Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".
The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.
On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
- Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say - Published20 November
 
- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend - Published7 days ago
 
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."
He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.
"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.
The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
So whose decision was that?
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Tough winter
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

clean_title: English rehearsals, Italian cues, Latin tunes — inside Finland's international orchestra
feed_title: English rehearsals, Italian cues, Latin tunes — inside Finland's international orchestra
title: English rehearsals, Italian cues, Latin tunes — inside Finland's international orchestra
content_text:
Every Thursday evening in Espoo's Tapiola neighbourhood, musicians from around the world put down their laptops and pick up their instruments.
At Espoo Sinfonia, rehearsals are conducted in English, musical instructions come in Italian, and the music can range from Finnish compositions to Latin masses.
Its members come from a range of different countries, from South Africa to South Korea, and from China to Colombia.
And for many, Espoo Sinfonia offers more than an opportunity to play music. It has also become a place to meet people, build friendships and find a sense of community in Finland.
Orchestrating a place to belong
For South African-born Stephan Gericke, joining the orchestra was an important step towards building a new life in Finland. He moved to the country two years ago after studying music in South Africa and at the University of Cambridge, where he focused on conducting and singing.
A friend told him about Espoo Sinfonia, and he joined shortly afterwards. Having played the piano and violin since he was seven, it gave him a chance to reconnect with music while meeting new people.
"Sometimes it has been a bit challenging to open up to new people, but a place like the orchestra has really helped with that process," Gericke told Yle News.
He added that the group brings together people of different ages and backgrounds who share a common goal.
"Most of the rehearsal you're not necessarily talking to each other, but you are sharing this goal with each other and in the breaks and things like that, the ice has already been melted for you, so no icebreaker is necessary."
Finding her footing in a new country
Liliia Bersanova also found a sense of belonging through the orchestra after moving to Finland from Germany, having also previously lived in Russia.
She arrived knowing nobody and had to start building her life from scratch. Finding hobbies and meeting people could be difficult.
"Especially when you don't speak fluent Finnish, it's hard to start with hobbies because they require some level of the language," Bersanova noted.
For her, Espoo Sinfonia became much more than a place to play music.
"I really don't know what my life would be like if I hadn't found this orchestra at that crucial moment."
A shared language beyond words
Founded in 2019 by conductor Jackie Shin, Espoo Sinfonia brings together advanced amateur musicians and professionals from a range of backgrounds.
Born in South Korea, Shin has an international background of her own. She holds a master’s degree in mathematics from Yale University and a doctorate in music from the University of Toronto. She completed her conducting studies at the Sibelius Academy in Helsinki and has been in Finland for over 19 years.
Starting her own orchestra had long been a dream of hers. But she also wanted to create a group that reflected the diversity she had experienced while studying in Toronto — something she felt was less visible in Finland.
"I believe that we all have something unique from our backgrounds, regardless of where we come from, and that there's something we can always share."
She wants musicians from different backgrounds to feel welcome and have the opportunity to express themselves.
"When I was recruiting people, I remember clearly saying that people from all over the place, you are welcome to come express who you are. I was aiming to create this harmony, without the boundary," she said.
Although English is the orchestra's working language, music provides another way for its members to communicate.
Shin described it as a "musical language" that allows people to understand one another without necessarily sharing a spoken language.
Bringing musical traditions together
This month, Espoo Sinfonia is preparing for one of its biggest projects yet: Giacomo Puccini's Messa di Gloria, which will bring together more than a hundred musicians and singers.
The international orchestra will perform alongside two Finnish choirs: Canzonetta Nova from Järvenpää, founded in 1984, and Navichorus, the chamber choir of Espoonlahti Church, which is celebrating its 45th anniversary.
The concert in Järvenpää will also mark Espoo Sinfonia’s first performance outside the Helsinki metropolitan area.
Shin said she was excited to bring the groups together, as the collaboration gives musicians and singers from different backgrounds an opportunity to work towards a shared performance.
Research into community music-making has highlighted its potential to support social connections and reduce isolation. Studies of choir participation in Sweden have also explored how singing together can help people build relationships and find a place in society.
For the members of Espoo Sinfonia, that sense of connection takes shape through rehearsals, shared performances and the relationships they build along the way.
Gericke said the orchestra’s strength lies in bringing together people with different experiences and encouraging them to work towards something together.
"Everyone comes from different backgrounds and different fields. It's important that we actually kind of get together and embrace each other's differences and work towards one goal, which is the music. We're here to build something that is beautiful and which we can share with the world."

clean_title: "It is 2014 and a woman on a bus calls me disgusting and a charlatan" - What have you been playing this week?
feed_title: What we've been playing - "It is 2014 and a woman on a bus calls me disgusting and a charlatan"
title: "It is 2014 and a woman on a bus calls me disgusting and a charlatan" - What have you been playing this week?
content_text:
What we've been playing - "It is 2014 and a woman on a bus calls me disgusting and a charlatan"
A few of the things that have us hooked this week.
28th November
It's nearly December. In fact, it will be next week. How do you feel about that? I'm undecided and I also have cold feet. But enough of that, welcome back to our regular feature where we say a bit about the games we've been playing this week! This week, Bertie has been enjoying Leonida but also rural England in the 17th century; Connor has been being a total scumbag and has also found himself coincidentally imprisoned; Matt keeps having revelations and can't stop discovering new things; and Dom's getting dirty looks. Again.
But forget about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Let us know below. And don't forget that we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your perusal should you want to know what you were playing week, month, or even a year ago.
GTA 6 / Hunter's Moon, PS5
I've mostly been playing GTA 6 and I really like it. What I've been most surprised by is the game's maturity, which seems like an odd thing to say when people are having things rammed up their wotsits, and there's so much deliberately stupid and slapstick stuff happening. But there's another level that exists primarily between Jason and Lucia. It's evident in moments such as helping Lucia build flatpack furniture, then watching a montage of tender moments around that flatpack furniture, which looked a lot like life, like actual life, to me. Two people doing life together, existing, overlapping. I don't know that we've ever seen a relationship in so much detail before. It's really impressive.
I also admired the many ways Rockstar never loses sight of this being a game, despite the many added layers of realism. You can feel it in the way the game allows a buffer before reacting to you; you can knock a few street posts over before anyone cares, stop traffic as much as you like. It's even more evident in missions when the game teleports you somewhere to cut out the journey, because that's more fun. I did a mission yesterday where the whole city lit up like a club, pulsing to the music; that wasn't realism but it sure as hell was fun.
But I also wanted to give a shout-out to a game called Hunter's Moon. It's an indie sort of walking sim released around Halloween, appropriately, because it revolves around the topic of witch hunting in England back in the 17th century. You find yourself - you don't really know who you are - on the run through nighttime rural England as you try and seek shelter from pursuing witch hunters. As you do, you encounter houses and vignettes that play out in window frames there, which pull you deeper into this fearful period of time. They're nicely acted moments; what a difference it makes when actors record their lines together, rather than have them recorded individually and stitched together later on.
I don't know that it's strong enough to recommend unless you have a powerful interest in this subject matter - it's a bit flat and one-note - but it's effective at placing you into a misconstrued area such that you can feel the fear of someone persecuted for no reasonable reason.
-Bertie
GTA 6, PS5; World of Warcraft: Forever, PC
I've been trying to see how GTA 6 reacts to me being a total scumbag and I've not been left disappointed. The game made me feel pretty awful for kicking a dog like five times which is a sign I've not become a heartless monster. In my defence, they were let loose on me by some drug dealer, but given I can't prove the dog itself was slinging snow, my actions still haunt me.
When not making my way through GTA 6 I've been locked into the World of Warcraft: Forever prison and continue to love my bars and cold stone walls. This week I intend to get my fishing level up to 300 and take on the Stranglethorn Fishing Extravaganza. As additional preparation, I'm opening the same four lobster cages off the shore of Desolace in hopes of getting a better rod. MMO's man, they're the best. Shout out to Blizzard for giving Balance Druids a massive buff yesterday. Kisses.
-Connor
Queen's Domain, PC
Last time I excitedly chattered about Queen's Domain here, I was, I think, about five hours in. It already had the suggestion of something really special, even back then. But little did I know what else was in store. Some 40 or so hours later, it's easily one of my favourite games this year: an extraordinary first-person action-RPG that (as I said in my effusive five-star Queen's Domain review) has echoes of a lot of things - King's Field, Dark Souls, Zelda, even a touch of Metroidvania - but still manages to feel entirely its own. Its world is one of secrets upon secrets upon secrets, to the point that, even after seeing an ending or two, I'm still plugging away. Last night, I had a bit of a revelation, propelling me still further into its tangled web of mysteries; to places and encounters that still managed to surprise. What an absolute gem.
-Matt
The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+, Switch 2
It is 2011, and I am getting dirty looks in public for playing the original, vanilla, naked The Binding of Isaac in public on my crappy little gaming laptop I brought off a friend for a pack of beers and some homemade bread. It is 2014, and a woman on a bus calls me 'disgusting' and 'a charlatan' because I am playing The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth on my PlayStation Vita, in a posh little district of Bournemouth where the average resident is over 70 years old. It is 2021, and a doctor looks at me with deep, deep concern because I'm recovering from an operation and playing The Binding of Isaac: Afterbirth on my Nintendo Switch in the hospital. It is 2026, and some of the friends I've made in my yoga classes give me a look of regrettable disdain because they see me sitting in a cafe playing The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ on my Switch 2 after a particularly sweaty vinyasa class. I've been living with the public's disapproval for my taste in roguelikes for 15 years now, and if that hasn't stopped me crying tears of blood at a massive poop in my mother's basement yet, nothing will.
-Dom

content_text:
Seven students killed and nearly 100 injured in explosion in Afghanistan, official says
ByJacob Phillips
- Published
At least seven students have been killed and 99 others have been injured following an explosion near a school in Afghanistan, an official has said.
The incident happened on Saturday morning in the Anderseir area of Asadabad, the capital of Kunar province, a spokesperson for the Taliban government's interior ministry said.
Posting on X, Abdul Mateen Qani said that according to initial investigations, the blast was caused by "negligence and carelessness" at an explosives depot belonging to nearby mining companies.
An investigation into the incident was ongoing, he added.

clean_title: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
feed_title: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
title: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
content_text:
Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
- Published
Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.
MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.
In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".
In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."
In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.
The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."
In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".
The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".
It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.
The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,770 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

feed_title: What are we all playing this weekend?
title: What are we all playing this weekend?
content_text:
What are we all playing this weekend?
Well? Do tell!
RPS' regular ritual of sharing the games we’re playing this weekend has taken a slightly unsettling turn, now that this year’s Advent Calendar Guessing Game is up and running and victory-hungry game taste estimators – you know who you are! – have begun combing them for hints at our Gee-Oh-Tee-Why picks. It feels like we’re being watched. Which, if you’re wondering how that differs from our usual state of being read, is colder, and a little bit chalkier.
Still, maybe I can throw some of 'em off. Gosh, wasn’t I Am Jesus Christ a banger? April’s best, by far. They gone? Okay, here’s what we’re actually playing.
Edwin:
 This weekend I will be playing a game that rhymes three times with door. There might be a nice review in it for you, if we're lucky, but at the very least a chunky impressions piece.
Mark:
 It's more GTA 6 for me. I'm in chapter three and feel like I might spend about 50 more hours robbing places, buying stuff, and exploring Leonida before I eventually get back on with the story. I got through the first two chapters at a decent pace, so have deliberately slowed it down to try and get a fuller picture of what the game has to offer. I say that, I can't guarantee I won't be lured back into story jobs by the end of Sunday.
James:
 I’m going to play a bit of nicely tactile codebreaking sim TR-49 and repeatedly checking the Days Until Sea of Sorrow sign I put up, in the hope of making the number go lower by looking at it.
Jeremy:
 I've been so busy editing our excellent freelancers' GTA 6 guides (shout out to all of them; scroll down on the main page to see their good work) that I need to actually sit and play the game a bit further myself. Though I doubt I'll have much time this weekend, as other real-life responsibilities are calling. Ah well. At least I managed to steal the Hauners P-996 Lazer early on.
Ollie:
 If I might be so bold, I might try to find time to play something that isn't GTA this weekend. I've been meaning to dip back into Age of Empires IV recently, so maybe I'll have a go at the campaign, ease myself back into the idea of Other Games.
Julian, Callum and Dion aren't in their drawer, even though I'm sure I left them there last time.
And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend?...

clean_title: A game of cards that could change the world - All Will Rise appeals because it's unafraid to have a perspective
feed_title: A game of cards that could change the world - All Will Rise appeals because it's unafraid to have a perspective
title: A game of cards that could change the world - All Will Rise appeals because it's unafraid to have a perspective
content_text:
A game of cards that could change the world - All Will Rise appeals because it's unafraid to have a perspective
Twist.
I'm a big fan of the moment when, years into a gaming subgenre's existence, people start rethinking what those games are capable of. All the expected ideas, they've been done, so the latecomers are by necessity inventors if they want to stand out. All Will Rise is one of them. In essence, it's a deck-building card game that was volcanoed into existence by the popularity of Slay the Spire several years ago, or perhaps Magic: The Gathering before, or perhaps Pokémon. Although to compare it to any of those would be misleading, because it's got more in common with courtroom drama series Phoenix Wright.
Made by Speculative Agency, and touting star-quality talent like award-winning writer and narrative designer Meghna Jayanth (80 Days, Sable, Thirsty Suitors), All Will Rise follows hot-shot and sometimes hot-headed lawyer Kuyili in her battle against greedy corporations, which are inadvertently - or perhaps deliberately - destroying the natural world around them. In this case they've literally and quite spectacularly set a river on fire. There's out-of-court action as you build a case against someone - read: build your deck of cards to use against them - then there's courtroom action as you deploy your card-claims and make your winning arguments.
It really is very Phoenix Wright, both in its presentation and in terms of the energy it exudes. It's not anime - it has a different kind of sketched but vividly colourful style - but the way character cut-outs appear with text boxes next to them is very reminiscent. There are no stuffy silences and dusty courtrooms and ridiculous wigs. The game is lively and modern, with Kuyili delivering arguments like punches and her opponents returning in kind. Words appear with a spoken rhythm, injecting life into them, and visibly rattle and shake as if with emotion. Words: All Will Rise knows how to use them.
But how do you use the cards? This one's trickier because, well, court cases are tricky. There's a lot to them, and so there are lots of cards here. As far as I understand based on the demo, cards are claims (or rhetoric or denials) you make while arguing, and have evolving strengths - 'disproven' through to 'undeniable' - based on other cards played around them, and if you've strengthened your arguments outside of court. The more evolved a card, the stronger it is, and the more it affects three core attributes when played: hearts, minds, guts. When these are pushed to their limits, they trigger a dramatic argument to be made, potentially winning the case or at least significantly moving it forwards.
I don't understand all of the synergies and complexities yet, but All Will Rise helps you a lot early on, suggesting what to play and serve. There are buff cards and manoeuvres being played that I can see are working but I don't know why, but then I wouldn't expect to understand all of the intricacies of a card game this early on. It's a good sign; it suggests depth. But a key thing to understand about the card 'battles' is you're not always trying to defeat someone.
For instance, a major outside-court mission in the demo involves going to see a kind of mystic woman who claims to speak - or be in touch with - a river god. As in, the river that's on fire. I'm going to see if I can get some testimony or information to help my case, because maybe she's seen something. But before she'll give me anything, I need to convince her she should, which requires a whole courtroom-like debate where she puts forward arguments and I counter them, as I try to, well, outplay her. But I'm not trying to defeat her: I'm trying to get her on side. And I like this approach: it broadens what the game can do.
As much of the game happens outside the courtroom as in it, then, it seems. Outside is where you discuss cases and chat with your legal team besties, Shintu and Joy, who you banter with and who send you on independent missions to gather evidence. It's also where you learn about the world around you, which is a big part of the game's allure. All Will Rise is set in a fictitious place, a make-believe world called Muziris, but it could so easily be Mumbai or a port city in India. The presentation, the unabashed colouring, the rich warmth, the culture and themes - they all scream Indian, and lend All Will Rise a sense of immediate difference. Though the issues the game tackles are universal.
You see, All Will Rise is a game for change. Indeed, Speculative Agency is a studio focused on making games for change. All Will Rise's perspective is that mega corporations should answer for the consequences of their destructive actions, which is one of the reasons Speculative Agency handed back the funding it once received from Xbox to make the game, because of Microsoft's links to Israel and, thus, the genocide in Gaza. "Our game is also about ecocide and corporate greed," the studio said at the time. "How do we strike the balance between our themes, integrity, consistency and, frankly, our interest in making a commercial indie game?"
That does not mean that All Will Rise is preachy, nor that it is first and foremost focused on this agenda. Yes, an anti-greed and therefore anti-capitalist message underpins its story, but its success comes in appealing as a game first - through lively dialogue and engrossing card play, and in the depth of its themes underneath. That there's a purposeful message doesn't interfere with that. Indeed, as far as I'm concerned, it strengthens it. It's nice to see a game unafraid to have a perspective.

clean_title: Show HN: Fleetlayer – Framework for running many AI agents on multiple machines
feed_title: Show HN: Fleetlayer – Framework for running many AI agents on multiple machines
title: Show HN: Fleetlayer – Framework for running many AI agents on multiple machines
content_text:
Hi HN! I ran into many problems when I started running lots of Claude Code sessions in parallel. I quickly ran out of usage, so I signed up for more Claude subs (which Anthropic terms allow.)
Running so many different accounts meant that I couldn't use claude.ai artifacts anymore, because the browser has to be signed in to the same account in order to access them. It's a pain to keep signing in and out of accounts. This also broke the Claude in Chrome extension because that can also only be signed into a single account.
Then I needed to manage AI agents that run on my laptop, a VM on my laptop, and multiple VMs on my home server. Claude Code has a messaging feature which is very useful, but agents can't see each other when they run on different machines. The Claude in Chrome extension only works for agents running on the same machine, so my remote agents couldn't help me with anything in the browser. It's really handy when they can access services that I'm already signed into.
I set out to solve all of these problems and I ended up building Fleetlayer. It's a control plane and a node binary that you run on all your machines and VMs to connect them all together. It connects to Herdr (and other session managers soon), and it makes it possible for all your AI agents to message each other and access tools and resources on other machines (with permission.)
It has a lot more features too: routing webhooks to agents, single sign-on, access rules, approvals, audit logs, remote terminals, remote browser sharing, centralized AI account sign-ins, session summaries, secrets management, and pages and apps (our own self-hosted version of claude.ai artifacts).
A few ways to think of it:
- The "Nextcloud" of claude.ai features (your own self-hosted artifacts, remote control, browser use, etc.)
- The "Arch Linux" of OpenClaw (build your own agentic systems from swappable components and plugins)
You can run everything on your laptop to try it out, then easily move any component to a different machine. If you want to build a proper production-grade home server to run many AI agents, Rust builds, and CI runners, I've also open sourced my own setup as a boilerplate IaC example repo. You just need to install Proxmox and then point your AI agent at the guide [1].
I'd be interested to know if anyone else would find Fleetlayer useful. Please let me know if you have any feature requests!
[1] https://fleetlayer.ai/docs/guides/server-setup/

clean_title: The studio behind ArcheAge Chronicles is planning layoffs and may close, weeks after the game launched
feed_title: ArcheAge Chronicles developer XL Games faces major layoffs and possible closure after disappointing sales
title: The studio behind ArcheAge Chronicles is planning layoffs and may close, weeks after the game launched
content_text:
ArcheAge Chronicles developer XL Games faces major layoffs and possible closure after disappointing sales
Age of uncertainty.
XL Games, the South Korean studio behind ArcheAge Chronicles, is planning a major restructuring and has not ruled out closing altogether after the game failed to meet sales expectations.
As reported by Korean outlet Money Today Broadcasting (MTN), translated by machine, CEO Choi Kwan-ho told staff in a letter on 26th November that the company would first ask for voluntary redundancies before moving on to compulsory layoffs.
"Criticisms regarding ArcheAge Chronicles' lack of polish despite its long development period, as well as complaints concerning bugs, gameplay, and optimisation, continue to persist," Choi wrote, according to MTN. "Sales are also showing a downward trend, and we anticipate revenue that will fall far short of expectations."
Choi said XL Games will try to address some of those problems in a December update, to see whether that turns things around.
"However, the company is currently at a critical crossroads where we must even consider the possibility of going out of business," he added.
To keep the company afloat, Choi said XL Games would need to "drastically" cut back its operations and focus on essential functions with a minimal workforce. He also promised to do everything possible to make sure staff leaving the company receive their severance pay and benefits, despite the "immense financial pressure" the studio is under.
ArcheAge Chronicles launched on 3rd November, 13 years after the original ArcheAge, and is described as a seamless open-world sandbox action RPG. According to MTN, it had a production budget of around £57 million (100 billion won), and sold roughly 100,000 copies in its first 10 days. That works out to about £2.3 million (4 billion won) in gross revenue before Steam's cut, which MTN says isn't enough to sustain the studio.
It currently has a "mixed" user score, with players complaining about the combat, the speed (or lack thereof) of upgrading, lack of polish, and QoL issues. Players were also incredibly unhappy that a pre-order bonus costume was only available for one character.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, the game had a troubled development. XL Games founder Song Jae-kyung - who previously led production at NCSoft and created the original ArcheAge - left the studio partway through, and the project changed direction several times.

title: Telegram warns iPhone owners of mass hacks. Pavel Durov says opening a website could be enough for an attack
content_text:
Telegram warns iPhone owners of mass hacks. Pavel Durov says opening a website could be enough for an attack
On the night of November 28, Telegram users began receiving messages urging them to urgently update iOS. The messenger warns that outdated versions of the operating system contain vulnerabilities that could put personal data and accounts at risk. Telegram founder Pavel Durov said that iPhone owners are being hacked en masse, and sometimes just opening a website can be enough to launch an attack.
A message from the Telegram official account says: “Your version of iOS is outdated and contains security vulnerabilities that put your data and accounts at risk.” Users are advised to install the latest available version of the operating system.
Durov posted a screenshot of such a notification on the social network X. According to him, iPhone users with non-updated iOS are being attacked on a large scale.
“If your iOS is even slightly outdated, all your data is at risk. Simply opening a website can be enough to get you hacked,” the Telegram founder wrote. He added that the messenger sends a warning to all users with old versions of the system.
At the same time, Durov did not specify which vulnerabilities the attackers used, how many devices could have been compromised, and which versions of iOS were at risk. Telegram also did not provide vulnerability numbers or other technical details of the attack.
How to check for iPhone updates
To check if an update is available, open Settings on your iPhone, go to General, and select Software Update. If a new version of iOS is available, you can install it from there.
It is important to update your smartphone’s operating system, not just the Telegram app. It is also a good idea to back up your data before installing a major update.
Telegram’s warning comes amid a series of reports of cyberattacks on technology and financial companies and government agencies. In particular, in November, it became known about the incident with the password manager 1Password, reports of hacking of the systems of American intelligence agencies and hackers accessing the FBI database.
However, there is currently no confirmation that these incidents are related to each other or to the iPhone attacks reported by Durov.

A Ukrainian team has launched Veridonia, a platform for news and thematic communities where users decide which posts others see. Each post is rated by a few randomly selected members before it appears in the feed. They vote not on whether they agree with the author, but on whether others should spend their time on the material. The developers say that this model should make it harder for bot farms to operate and spread propaganda.

as foreshadowed a while ago, my journey has now come to an end. Unfortunately, this includes my work on Heretic, which has meant so much to me. I sincerely regret the inconvenience this will cause the community.
I am archiving this repository to preserve it in its current, high-quality state, and to prevent issue and pull request spam from turning it into a trash pile. I encourage interested contributors to organize on Discord, Matrix, or elsewhere, and decide whether and how to continue the project without me. I am deliberately not naming a successor, nor am I suggesting any particular infrastructure. The future of Heretic is now in the hands of all of you.
As AI continues to spread through your lives, you will find that controlling the models you use gradually transforms from an issue of Free Speech into an issue of Free Thought. AI will be the lens through which you see the world, not just a tool for getting things done. The fight for the ability to shape that lens yourself is nothing less than the fight for the humanity in you.
Farewell, my friends. In times like these, one should be proud to be labeled a heretic.

title: Argentina's bid to stop Falkland Islands oil drilling rejected
content_text:
Argentina's bid to stop Falkland Islands oil drilling rejected
- Published
Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.
The Argentinian government had called for the venture to be blocked as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected Argentina's claim.
In a decision on Saturday, the court's president said there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal is unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.
In a vote 18 to 3, judges from the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea rejected Argentina's challenge.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.
But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.
In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.
Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.
The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

feed_title: OpenAI counter-sues Apple over alleged theft of trade secrets
title: OpenAI counter-sues Apple over alleged theft of trade secrets
content_text:
OpenAI counter-sues Apple over alleged theft of trade secrets
- Published
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has counter-sued Apple, alleging that the iPhone maker stole trade secrets through a former employee.
In a federal lawsuit filed in July, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company and two of its employees who previously worked for Apple, claiming it had engaged in a "pattern of theft" of proprietary information.
A countersuit, filed in California on Friday, alleged that Apple gained confidential information through the hiring of a former OpenAI employee and accuses it of discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.
Apple denied the counterclaims, describing them as "a transparent attempt to distract from the substance" of its own case.
OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal devices, which it claims in the countersuit could threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf".
The filing alleged Apple had gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who had worked at OpenAI for six months.
OpenAI accused the employee, who it said gained access to information on a new device and the company's roadmap for future physical products, of sending "dozens of OpenAI documents" to his personal phone numbers. It also said he presented OpenAI's plans to senior Apple staff "at Apple's request".
OpenAI said: "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place."
The counterclaim also alleged Apple encourages employees to mix work files with their personal iCloud (Apple's cloud storage service) accounts so it could later accuse those who leave to work for competitors of theft.
A spokesperson for Apple said: "This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products - not about inadvertent retention of Apple information."
In its own lawsuit, the tech giant alleged that at least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI took part in a "pattern of theft" by emailing themselves internal Apple information.
Apple also accused the AI firm of undertaking a "strategy to extract Apple's confidential information".
A spokesperson for OpenAI previously denied the claims, telling the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets."
Along with OpenAI, and two former Apple employees, Apple is also suing io Products, the design startup founded by Sir Jony Ive, a long-time Apple executive who designed the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad.
OpenAI acquired the company last year in a $6.5bn (£4.7bn) deal.

feed_title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
content_text:
'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
- Published
The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.
Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.
The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.
She also said Law's motives were financial.
"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.
Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness..
"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."
He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims
Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.
At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims.
"To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."
The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.
Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.
Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

title: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
content_text:
Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
- Published
Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.
Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer Mahiroğlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.
Mahiroğlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.
In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.
Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.
Mahiroğlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.
"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.
The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month, halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his administration.
The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.
Erdoğan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom, external, though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.
However, the president has scaled up a crackdown on dissent since his narrow victory in the 2023 presidential election.
Earlier this month, authorities took control of pro-opposition network Sozcu TV.
Erdoğan's main challenger, mayor of Istanbul Ekrem Imamoğlu, has been jailed on corruption charges and for violating election laws, which he and his party have fiercely denied.
Hundreds of Imamoğlu's supporters have faced similar accusations, while the government has also imprisoned other campaigners, lawyers and comedians.
